C1.justification: V1 emphasizes normal-only few-shot detection with performance close to existing state of the art. V2 makes scalable few-shot multi-class detection central and adds broad claims about unseen-category/anomaly robustness and medical applicability. These materially expand the claimed contribution, although multi-class operation and the principal method components already existed.

C2.justification: V2 develops explanations linking class semantics to reduced inter-class confusion and attributes INP-Former's generalization weaknesses to absent textual grounding. It also interprets medical results as evidence of transferable normality cues. These extend v1's mechanism discussion substantially. V1's explicit logical-anomaly, multiple-object and shape limitations have no accessible counterpart in v2; their status in the missing supplement is unknown.

D1.justification: V1 specifies epochs, learning rates, prompt settings, SGD parameters, memory layers, hardware and code access. V2 retains backbone and crop-size information but directs additional settings to an unavailable supplement; its readable text also lacks v1's code-access statement. The full extent of revised, removed or relocated reproducibility information cannot be determined.

E1.justification: V2 adds Real-IAD and medical anomaly detection on BMAD's Brain MRI, Liver CT and Retinal OCT datasets to the retained MVTec-AD and VisA coverage. These additions substantially broaden the represented domains and imaging modalities. Multi-class anomaly detection itself was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: The main Table 1 comparison removes PaDiM, RegAD, FastRecon, AnomalyGPT and InCTRL and adds IIPAD and INP-Former, retaining SPADE, PatchCore, WinCLIP and PromptAD. V2's medical comparison also evaluates MedCLIP and UniVAD. These are substantial changes in evaluated comparator membership, independently of changed scores.

E3.justification: V2 Table 1 reports reproduced MVTec-AD/VisA baselines under a unified multi-class training configuration, replacing v1's comparison mixing single-class, multi-class and transfer settings. V2 adds image AUPR and pixel PRO, plus leave-one-class-out and targeted anomaly-description-withholding protocols. The retained backbone and image/crop resolutions do not establish changed AnoPLe training settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds held-out-category generalization tests, targeted defect-description withholding tests and analysis of PromptAD's multi-class embedding confusion. The class-name-versus-object ablation and prefix-attention analysis already existed in v1's supplement and are not new analyses. Whether v1's additional sensitivity, pseudo-anomaly and failure studies persist cannot be checked without v2's referenced supplement.

E5.justification: V1 Table 1 and supplementary Tables 6–9 report ± uncertainty terms, whereas v2 Table 1 contains point estimates only. The unavailable v2 supplement prevents determining whether uncertainty reporting was removed overall or relocated. Neither supplied text establishes a change in repeated-run counts or seeds.

E6.justification: Reported one-shot AnoPLe image/pixel AUROC changes from 94.1/95.3 to 94.5/96.0 on MVTec-AD and from 86.2/95.8 to 86.0/97.0 on VisA. V2 also adds Real-IAD, medical, held-out-category and FPS results and revises ablation scores. These are substantial result changes; revised comparison protocols and incomplete training details preclude interpreting all differences as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The documented algorithm retains bidirectional textual–visual prompt coupling, pixel- and latent-space pseudo anomalies, the lightweight decoder, three loss terms and memory-assisted scoring. V2's scale-aware prefix corresponds to v1's multi-view signal, including the same training crops and global-only inference. Renaming and rewritten explanations do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten around multi-class scalability. Method subsections are reorganized, textual and visual prompting receive separate treatments, and multi-view signal becomes scale-aware prefix. New generalization and medical sections materially restructure the narrative.

P2.justification: V2 replaces Figure 1 with semantic, speed and embedding panels, redraws the architecture figure, and restructures Table 1 around shot settings and additional metrics. Qualitative figures and ablation tables are redesigned. V2 Figure 5 redisplays the MVTec portion of v1 supplementary Figure 12, rather than introducing a new attention visualization.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work around multi-class anomaly detection, discussing CCL, IIPAD, INP-Former and UniVAD and adding medical-domain references. V1's emphasis on the prompt-learning lineage through MaPLe, VPT, CoOp and CoCoOp is reduced, with those references absent from v2's bibliography. This changes the research context beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The prompt projections, prefix definition, losses, local–global alignment and anomaly-score equations retain their mathematical substance. V2 reorganizes and renotates these expressions but introduces no new theorem, proof, formal assumption or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 adds valuable unified comparisons, generalization tests and medical evaluations, but uncertainty and reproducibility information are less accessible. Its stronger interpretation also exceeds some reported evidence: Section 4.2 describes INP-Former advantages as 0.1–1.0 points, while Table 1 gives 88.3 versus 83.2 image AUROC on 4-shot Real-IAD. These reliability concerns and the unavailable supplement prevent a confident net quality judgment despite the broader empirical coverage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AnoPLe despite the changed title, and their main text, equations, figures and tables are readable. V1 includes supplementary Sections 6–10. V2 ends with references while referring to supplementary implementation details, visual comparisons and discussion that are not supplied, limiting comparison of those materials.

after.justification: V2 reports original AnoPLe benchmark results, ablations, held-out-category evaluations, medical-domain experiments and inference-speed measurements. Its use of previously reported results for some baselines does not negate these original outcomes.

before.justification: V1 reports original AnoPLe experiments on MVTec-AD and VisA, including benchmark results, component ablations, sensitivity studies and qualitative failure analysis in the supplement.

C1.justification: V1 presents Fixed and Balanced coreset construction and claims state-of-the-art compression with approximately preserved performance. V2 redefines the contribution around gradient-based SSTP, explicitly claims one-time selection with substantial training-time savings, and emphasizes improvements over full-data training in dense scenes. The central half-data and scenario-balancing goals remain, but the proposed contribution and claimed benefits expand materially.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of why balancing and informativeness must work jointly, why moderate pretraining can outperform a converged selector, and how partition intervals should adapt to dataset characteristics. It also explicitly identifies selection overhead and performance at very low retention as limitations. These extend v1's predominantly distribution-imbalance and coreset-transfer interpretation.

D1.justification: V1 provides a detailed training recipe, including AdamW, 64 epochs, batch size 32, learning rate, weight decay, dropout and scheduling. V2 largely replaces this with references to official protocols, reducing self-contained reproducibility information. It adds a code-availability statement and repository pointer, baseline-selection descriptions, and RTX 4090 selection/training timings. The repository's availability was not externally verified.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only Argoverse 1. V2 adds actual Argoverse 2 evaluations, extending coverage to different driving scenarios and a five-second observation window with six-second forecasting, versus Argoverse 1's two-second observation and three-second forecast. Other datasets mentioned in background discussions do not establish additional SSTP evaluations.

E2.justification: V1's external selection comparator is random sampling. V2 Table 2 adds K-means Clustering and Herding against SSTP on Argoverse 1 across all three retained prediction models. Table 3 evaluates Random and Clustering on Argoverse 2. The nonrandom comparators substantially strengthen the competitive comparison.

E3.justification: V2 substantially expands the evaluation design: QCNet/DeMo configurations for Argoverse 2, alternative selection backbones, pretraining budgets of 0/5/8/10/15/64 epochs and partition intervals of 5/10/20 agents. It adds 60% retention and no longer displays v1's 1%, 2% and 5% tests. The six prediction modes and minADE/minFDE/MR metrics remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's retention, density and transfer analyses, v2 adds explicit partition-only and submodular-only controls (Table 5), pretraining sensitivity (Table 6), selection-backbone comparisons (Table 7), partition sensitivity (Table 8) and measured efficiency analysis. V1's detailed low-retention dense-scene curves and distribution-variance analysis are replaced by more limited density summaries.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, performance error bars or significance tests. V1's variance across scenario-category proportions describes dataset balance; it is not an estimate of uncertainty in model performance.

E6.justification: Numerous results are revised or newly reported. Full-data HiVT-64 changes from 0.692/1.047/0.104 for minADE/minFDE/MR in v1 Figure 2 to 0.695/1.037/0.109 in v2 Table 2, although v2 Table 5 retains the earlier values. V2 adds Argoverse 2, comparator, ablation and timing results. Changed methods and incompletely specified settings prevent interpreting cross-version score differences as controlled performance gains.

M1.justification: V1 scores squared differences between HiVT objective values and selects by maximizing gain. V2 instead constructs output-gradient/decoder-embedding features, scores their cosine similarities and minimizes the selection score (Equations 2–6). Algorithm 1 also revises dynamic budget allocation and replaces the separate Fixed/Balanced formulations with a balanced SSTP pipeline. These change the selection procedure substantially.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial portions of the remaining prose are rewritten around SSTP. Problem formulation moves inside Method; the experimental narrative is reorganized into main results, ablations, efficiency and generalizability, with explicit limitations. Terminology, contribution organization and author information also change.

P2.justification: V1's opening scene examples reappear in v2 Figure 2 with revised distribution plots, rather than being wholly new illustrations. V2 adds an opening performance/timing graphic and substantially restructures result displays: v1's twelve-panel density/retention figure and embedded tables give way to larger comparison tables, four retention plots and separate ablation tables. Typography and page layout also change extensively.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated long-tail trajectory-prediction discussion, positioning scenario-level selection against feature-learning approaches including FEND, Hi-SCL and TRACT. It also expands coverage of recent forecasting and condensation methods while removing earlier references such as Dataset Quantization and the federated submodular-selection work. This materially revises research positioning, beyond reference renumbering.

T1.justification: The central mathematical formulation changes substantially: v1 Equation 1's squared objective-value differences become explicitly defined gradient features and a cosine-kernel criterion in v2 Equations 2–6, with a different optimization direction. The budget-allocation rule is also mathematically revised. Neither version provides a theorem or proof establishing the claimed submodular properties.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's weak comparative and diagnostic evidence: nonrandom selection baselines, a second benchmark and component controls test whether the method offers benefits beyond random sampling and density balancing alone. Sensitivity studies and measured selection costs further strengthen its practical assessment. These gains outweigh reduced implementation detail and reporting inconsistencies, including differing full-data HiVT values and HPNet training times of 268.8 hours in Figure 1 versus 307.2 hours in Section 4.4. Those issues still limit reproducibility and confidence in precise efficiency claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work despite the SSTP retitling, and their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. Neither contains an appendix. However, v2 Section 4.5 references additional backbone results in Supplementary Material that is absent from the supplied PDFs. The main papers support reliable comparison; those supplementary results cannot be assessed.

after.justification: V2 reports original Argoverse 1 and Argoverse 2 experiments, component ablations, sensitivity studies and timing measurements. These are distinct from the prior-work training times compiled in Table 1.

before.justification: V1 reports original Argoverse 1 experiments with HiVT-64, HiVT-128 and HPNet, including retention-rate comparisons, dense-scene evaluations and dataset-distribution analysis.

C1.justification: Both versions claim that SSTP constructs compact, balanced trajectory datasets, preserves accuracy using roughly half the data, improves high-density prediction, reduces training cost and transfers across architectures. v3 foregrounds density imbalance and reorganizes the contribution bullets without materially changing these central claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving gradient domination and under-training of shared attention parameters, asserts asymmetric transfer from complex to simpler scenes, and interprets why naive balancing alternatives fail. It also explicitly limits demonstrated applicability to Argoverse trajectory prediction and discusses the observed degradation at extremely low retention.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 substantially expands reproducibility details through selection batch sizes, optimizers, learning rates, schedules, architecture settings and augmentations for the existing predictors. Conversely, v3 removes the RTX 4090 disclosure and explicit repository URL; its reproducibility statement mentions code and checkpoints through an unspecified anonymous link.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate trajectory forecasting on Argoverse 1 and Argoverse 2 with the same observation and prediction horizons. Additional density illustrations, model evaluations and retention budgets remain within this existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds augmentation, reweighting, epoch-wise reselection and High-density+Random comparisons. It also adds Herding to the Argoverse 2 comparison and Cluster/Herding to the existing density-stratified comparison. These substantially expand the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: The core metrics, six predicted modes and benchmark protocols are retained. v3 adds 5%, 2% and 1% retention settings, differently sized controls in Table 1, and changes the efficiency example from 50% to 60% retention. Appendix A.1 mainly discloses existing training settings rather than establishing that they changed.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of alternative balancing strategies, extreme data-budget degradation and detailed HPNet performance across density strata, while extending backbone sensitivity results across retention ratios. The existing component, pretraining-epoch and partition-interval ablations are retained, with the latter two moved to Appendix A.3.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for the experiments. Both present point estimates; varying pretraining epochs is a sensitivity experiment rather than repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial result entries for new comparators, HPNet density evaluations, smaller subsets and backbone transfers. Existing values also change: Table 2's HiVT-64 SSTP result at 50% retention changes from 0.704/1.073/0.111 to 0.706/1.074/0.110 for minADE/minFDE/MR. Revised timing results use a different retention setting and therefore do not establish a same-setting efficiency change.

M1.justification: Density partitioning, gradient extraction, cosine-based selection scores and descending-density budget allocation remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 renames DynamicBudget to DynamicSelect without changing its steps; the new biased-sampling terminology describes the existing allocation procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method narrative are substantially rewritten. Related work moves after experiments, the experimental narrative is reorganized, and several analyses move into a structured appendix. Ethics, reproducibility and LLM-usage statements are also added.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to predominantly single-column layout. Figure 1 is redesigned, timing becomes a separate figure, scene examples and density histograms are separated, and the retention plot drops its minFDE panels. v3 also adds comparison tables and appendix scene grids while relocating existing ablation tables.

R1.justification: The literature coverage and positioning against trajectory prediction, long-tail learning and sample-selection work remain largely unchanged. v3 removes Chen et al.'s Super-samples from kernel herding reference, previously cited in v2 Table 2; the citation-style conversion and related-work relocation are presentation changes.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens empirical scrutiny through alternative-strategy comparisons and extreme-budget tests, and Appendix A.1 improves implementation disclosure. However, it introduces an unsupported approximation guarantee, removes the explicit code URL, and claims over 50% time reduction in Figure 5 despite reporting 7.25 versus 7.78 hours for HiVT and about 45% reduction for HPNet. These gains in evidence and documentation coexist with material losses in rigor and access information, leaving the net quality direction unclear.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SSTP work, with readable text, equations, figures and tables that can be matched reliably. The supplied v2 ends with references; v3 includes Appendix A, which was also inspected.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and reports additional comparisons, density-stratified evaluations and low-retention experiments in its main text and appendix.

before.justification: v2 reports original subset-training experiments on Argoverse 1 and 2, including prediction accuracy, component ablations, sensitivity studies and training times.

The new safety comparison does not specify its dataset, backbone, retention ratio, or density cutoff.

E4.justification: V3's extremely low-budget, selection-backbone, pretraining-epoch, and partition-interval analyses disappear with Appendix A, including Tables 9–12. The component ablation remains as v4 Table 4. V4 adds the density/error diagnostic in Figure 1 and the full-versus-high-density safety analysis in Table 5, substantially changing the supplementary evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests for its experiments. V4's added NLL metric measures predictive quality and does not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The main benchmark scores are identical in v3 Tables 2/4 and v4 Tables 2/3. However, v4 adds safety results, omits numerous appendix and density-table results, and revises retained ablation values. For example, v3 Table 5 to v4 Table 4 changes the full-data high-density share from 6.12% to 14.83% and the proposed method's minADE from 0.704 to 0.706. These changes do not establish a same-setting performance improvement between versions.

M1.justification: The density partitioning and gradient-based greedy selection framework remains. V4 changes the stated regression loss from L2 to best-mode negative log-likelihood and corrects Algorithm 1 to assign fully retained partitions to Ck before decrementing the remaining budget. These are localized revisions; the newly documented tensor alignment does not establish a new architecture.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial method explanations are rewritten around Den-TP's curation-and-evaluation framing. Related work moves before the method, the appendix and disclosure statements disappear, and acknowledgements are added. This is extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: V4 adopts a two-column layout and substantially reorganizes the displays. It adds a density/error figure and safety table, redraws the density comparison, consolidates scenario illustrations with frequency strips, and removes detailed density and appendix tables. Other benchmark tables and plots are retained but relocated or reformatted.

R1.justification: V4 adds explicit submodular-selection precedents, including Wei, Malioutov, and Qian, and cites Weng for joint metrics. It drops much of the broad trajectory-model survey and focuses related work on scenario imbalance and sample selection. The central distinction from feature-level long-tail methods and generic subset selection remains.

T1.justification: V4 removes v3 Equation 7's claimed 1−1/e greedy approximation guarantee. It also replaces the linear O(|D|d + Bd) selection-cost estimate with partition-specific terms including O(nk|Dk|d). These materially revise the formal guarantee and computational scaling claims, beyond notation or explanation.

improvement.justification: V4 improves the algorithm description, revises mathematical claims, and adds useful safety results. However, removing implementation settings and sensitivity/backbone evidence weakens reproducibility and support for retained robustness claims; the new safety table also lacks a clearly specified experimental setup. The unchanged main benchmark evidence preserves the core empirical case, limiting the overall decline.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same density-aware trajectory-data selection work, renamed from SSTP to Den-TP. Text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. V3's Appendix A has no counterpart in the complete v4 PDF; this is a content omission, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: V4 retains original Argoverse experiments and reports additional joint prediction, likelihood, and collision results in Table 5.

before.justification: V3 reports original Argoverse 1 and 2 experiments, including selection comparisons, timing measurements, density analyses, and appendix ablations.

C1.justification: v2 presents the headline contribution as pre-training a unified, factorizable model, replacing v1's emphasis on the first joint size- and task-adaptive initializer. It drops the first-multitasking and 5x storage-saving claims and explicitly extends its claimed generality to classification and alternative architectures. The central factorization and initialization-performance claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations: pruning/distillation failures are attributed to disrupted denoising hierarchy and temporal coherence; long-horizon curves are used to argue that initialization affects the entire training trajectory; and PCA alignment is interpreted as cross-scale structural coherence. It also qualifies domain independence as holding 'to a certain extent.' These explanations extend v1's discussion of adaptive transfer.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds factorization pseudocode, dataset counts, a VAE identifier and detailed optimizer, dropout and dataset-specific training settings; the main text identifies RTX 4090 hardware. However, v1's explicit EMA decay of 0.9999, guidance scale of 1.0 and 50K-image evaluation sample count are no longer disclosed. Their omission does not establish that those settings changed.

E1.justification: v2 retains ImageNet-1K, CelebA-HQ and LSUN generation experiments, adds Hubble, MRI and Pokemon generation domains, and introduces ImageNet-1K classification with DeiT (Table 3). These substantially extend the represented domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: BK-SDM and Laptop-diff are added to both corresponding diffusion comparisons in Tables 1–2, introducing pruning/distillation comparators. GHN-3, previously only discussed, is evaluated in the new classification comparison. Direct pre-training remains a comparator, presented in Figure 3 rather than v1 Table 1.

E3.justification: Reported factorization training changes from 30K steps with batch size 256 to 300K with batch size 64; ImageNet downstream training changes from 10K to 100K steps. v2 adds DiT-L and DeiT configurations, 800K-step trajectories and controlled ablation protocols. Sigma-sharing settings also change. Table 2 replaces downstream FID/sFID reporting with FID for natural-image datasets and FDD for the new domains.

E4.justification: v1 has no component ablations. v2 tests shared factorization against independent layer-wise SVD with matched transferred components (Table 4), and trainable Sigma against random, identical and linear initialization (Table 5). Figures 3–5 add long-horizon convergence, qualitative training trajectories and PCA analysis of Sigma across depths.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent repeated-run counts, seeds, uncertainty intervals, error bars or significance tests. The n=5 in v1 Table 1 describes the five model configurations, not documented independent repetitions.

E6.justification: Main-table results are extensively replaced under revised conditions: FINE's DiT-B L6 FID is 83.79 after 10K steps in v1 Table 1 and 51.58 after 100K in v2, not a same-setting gain. v2 adds DiT-L, new-domain, classification and ablation results, convergence curves and Appendix B samples. Earlier downstream sFID entries are no longer reported.

M1.justification: v2 Section 3.2 expands the stated factorized weight types from qkv, o, in and out to include adaLN. The central procedure remains joint training of shared U/V and layer-specific Sigma, followed by Sigma-only initialization and ordinary downstream training. v1 already trained a factorized auxiliary model, so the new pre-training framing does not establish an entirely new algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanation and results discussion are extensively rewritten around factorizable pre-training and adaptive initialization. Method preliminaries are reorganized, the results section expands from two principal subsections to six, and detailed settings and baseline descriptions are organized in Appendix A.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws Figures 1–2, substantially restructures Tables 1–2, and adds classification, ablation and implementation tables. New Figures 3–5 display comparisons, convergence and PCA; Appendix B adds eight generated-image figures. Direct-pretraining results are presented graphically rather than as v1's table row.

R1.justification: The main PEFT, initialization and Learngene context, including the KIND/SVDiff contrast, remains. v2 updates its relationship to WAVE toward constrained pre-training, adds pruning/distillation and newer learngene references, and removes the Weight Selection discussion. Publication updates to retained WAVE and KIND references are not new works.

T1.justification: v2 corrects v1's malformed attention-normalization expression and restores the omitted GELU in the feedforward equation (Section 3.1). Section 5.2 adds explicit amortized training-cost expressions. The central factorization and denoising objectives remain substantively equivalent, and neither version provides theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps in v1: Tables 4–5 directly test the two central design choices, and Figure 3 examines sustained convergence beyond short-budget results. Appendix A substantially improves implementation transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of some evaluation details. The retained 3n speedup claim remains problematic: v2's stated costs imply 3n/(n+3), not 3n. Overall, the paper provides substantially stronger evidence for its central method.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FINE, and their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and contains no appendix; v2 includes readable Appendices A–B. Revised experimental settings limit direct score comparisons but do not prevent comparison of the work.

after.justification: v2 reports original generation and classification experiments, component ablations, convergence analyses and generated samples in the main text and Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 Tables 1–2 report original diffusion-model initialization experiments on ImageNet-1K and three downstream datasets.

C1.justification: Beyond retained gradient-separability and time/memory-efficiency claims, v2 adds a central claim of strong online-learning performance without increased power consumption. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion also recast the contribution around hybrid firing/reset and explicitly foreground surrogate-gradient alignment.

C2.justification: V2 introduces a substantive energy tradeoff: binary weights incur more SOPs at matched time steps, ternary sparsity reduces this cost, and fewer time steps can provide comparable accuracy at lower cost. V1's discussion of SECA inference slowdown and its mitigation through parallel computation disappears. The interpretation of deployment efficiency consequently shifts substantially.

D1.justification: V2 adds per-experiment weight-precision assignments in Table S1, specifies convolution-only SOP accounting, and clarifies Table 2's parameter-memory scope. Conversely, v1's explicit binary quantizer, straight-through derivative, membrane-parameter gradient formulas, and deployment-binarization instruction are omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate classification on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-200, ImageNet-1k, and DVS-CIFAR10. Replacing the ImageNet-200 SECA ablation with DVS-CIFAR10 and adding SOP measurements do not introduce new datasets, tasks, or input environments.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains the same comparator membership within every dataset, including the corresponding GLIF, SLTT, OTTT, and NDOT comparisons. Vanilla online learning remains the efficiency reference; the new weight-precision cases are variants of the proposed model.

E3.justification: The appendix changes the reported ImageNet-1k configuration from 120 to 300 epochs, learning rate 0.01 to 0.025, weight decay 0.0005 to zero, and binary to ternary weights. V2 also introduces accuracy-versus-convolutional-SOP evaluation across time-step settings, replacing the earlier CIFAR-10 speed-ratio experiments.

E4.justification: Section 5.2 replaces random-backpropagation and parallel-computation timing ablations with binary/ternary accuracy–SOP analyses on CIFAR-100 and DVS-CIFAR10. Table 3 retains the CIFAR-10/100 SECA ablations but removes the ImageNet-200 ablation and adds DVS-CIFAR10, substantially changing the supporting analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. Both present point estimates; batch-normalization statistics are not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2 changes reported CIFAR-10 accuracy from 95.51% to 95.59%, CIFAR-100 from 79.91% to 78.45%, and DVS-CIFAR10/ResNet-18 from 78.10% to 81.70%. ImageNet-1k changes from 68.07% to 69.77% under revised training and precision settings, so this is not a same-setting gain. SECA outcomes are revised, including a new 83.50% DVS-CIFAR10 result, and accuracy/SOP results replace the previous speedup results.

M1.justification: The neuron firing/reset equations and main online-learning procedures survive the renaming. V2 adds a 1.5-bit ternary-weight option alongside binary weights and removes Sign binarization between GAP and Conv1d in SECA (v1 Eq. 9; v2 Eq. 8). These are limited but actual procedural changes.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, changes the author list, systematically renames EM-PF to HM-DF, revises selected explanations, and switches to numbered citations. Experimental configuration and proof subsections exchange appendix positions. Most section organization and substantial portions of the prose remain matched.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn with reset and gradient-alignment illustrations. V1 Figures 2–3 are redrawn and merged into v2 Figure 2; the speed plot is removed and an accuracy/SOP plot added. Tables gain revised styling, explanatory captions, and a weight-precision column, while appendix and algorithm layouts are reorganized.

R1.justification: V2 adds literature on ternary weights, neuron models, normalization, and spiking transformers. A new passage acknowledges LIAF-Net's similar model structure and distinguishes its lightweight-processing objective from online training and deployment. The overall related-work organization and principal positioning remain intact.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.2 and its proof are retained; the additional silent-neuron equation merely expands the existing argument. Substantive localized corrections occur in Corollary 4.3 and the reparameterization equations: normalization thresholds change, leakage terms move outside the normalization fraction, and batch-normalization bias signs are corrected.

improvement.justification: V2 corrects normalization algebra and adds useful accuracy–SOP evidence, precision settings, and positioning against LIAF-Net. However, it removes the empirical training/inference-speed validation while retaining speed claims, and its new power-consumption claims rest on convolutional SOP counts rather than measured energy. These gains and losses affect central efficiency arguments, leaving no reliably assessable net direction in overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same online SNN framework, renamed from EM-PF to HM-DF. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original classification and SECA results in Tables 2–3, plus accuracy and synaptic-operation experiments in Figure 3.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification results in Table 2, SECA ablations in Table 3, and training/inference-speed experiments in Figure 4.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly acknowledges additional training costs from learnable parameters and explains that vanilla HD-LIF offers no neuron-operation advantage without parallelization. Section 5.4 interprets static-image and event-data temporal behavior as ANN/SNN duality. V2 discusses related temporal observations but lacks these explicit qualifications and interpretation.

D1.justification: V3 adds a code-access link and clarifies some model/block selections. However, the supplied PDF omits v2 Appendix A.1 and Table S1, losing the documented optimizer, scheduler, learning rates, weight decay, augmentation, batch sizes, epochs and configuration mapping. Algorithm 1 is retained in the main text rather than removed. The linked code was not accessed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same classification coverage: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-200, ImageNet-1k and DVS-CIFAR10. Spike precision and parallel-neuron configurations change within these retained tasks.

E2.justification: V2 Table 2 and v3 Table 1 retain the same dataset-specific comparison methods. The efficiency analyses continue using vanilla LIF/online training as the baseline. Newly cited Relaxation LIF and FPTT are discussed but not evaluated as additional comparators.

E3.justification: V3 Table 2 introduces controlled configurations with 4-bit emitted spikes and 50% parallel-neuron substitution. Evaluation expands from accuracy, parameter memory and SOP-based power proxies to reported training seconds per epoch, GPU memory, neuron operations and an mJ energy metric. These are new evaluation configurations; the PDFs do not establish reruns of the retained benchmark experiments.

E4.justification: The new Table 2 isolates spike-compression and parallelization effects on accuracy and training/inference costs, substantially strengthening component analysis. V3 Figure 4 adds temporal comparisons with SECA, while v2 Figure 3's weight-precision-specific SOP sweep is absent. The existing three-dataset SECA ablation remains.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Random time-step selection is part of the training algorithm, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The benchmark values in v2 Table 2/v3 Table 1 and the SECA results in Table 3 are unchanged. V3 adds substantial efficiency results: its compressed, partially parallel configuration reports 78.61% accuracy, 4.40 MB parameters, 4.62 million NOPs and 0.02 mJ in Table 2. This differs from the retained 78.45% benchmark configuration. Temporal result curves also change, and the earlier weight-specific SOP curves disappear.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming HM-DF to HD-LIF, v3 introduces an explicit spike-output quantizer Q with bit-width, scaling and rounding controls, separates transmitted spikes from the unquantized reset signal, and incorporates quantization into the backward chain (Equations 4–5). This substantially extends the method; P2-Reset, Mem-BN, SECA, parallel neurons and random backpropagation already existed in v2.

P1.justification: V3 retitles the paper, renames the model throughout, rewrites the abstract and contribution summary, reorganizes four method subsections into three, and redistributes the efficiency discussion. It also restructures the experimental analysis, introduces a temporal-processing subsection and moves the pseudocode into the main text.

P2.justification: V3 switches to a two-column layout, adds a radar overview, substantially redraws the model overview, revises block diagrams and introduces a numerical efficiency table. The earlier dual-axis accuracy/SOP figure is replaced by accuracy-only temporal plots. Tables are reformatted, Algorithm 1 is relocated, and the appendix configuration table is absent.

R1.justification: V3 adds discussions or citations concerning Relaxation LIF, FPTT with liquid time-constant neurons, and neuromorphic robustness. Five optimizer, scheduler and augmentation references associated with v2's appendix disappear. The broader positioning relative to existing SNN and online-learning approaches remains similar.

T1.justification: Definition 4.1 is reformulated, and Theorem 4.2 changes from sufficient conditions for uniformly firing or silent neurons to gradient-product formulas covering more general firing sequences and an explicit online/STBP gradient relationship. V2's Mem-BN Corollary 4.3 and Appendix A.2 proof are absent from the supplied v3, which provides no corresponding theorem proof.

improvement.justification: V3's efficiency ablation and explicit training-cost tradeoffs strengthen evidence for its deployment claims. However, the supplied version loses v2's detailed training recipe and theorem proof while broadening the theorem; the gradient treatment of the new rounded spike outputs also remains unclear. These substantive gains and losses prevent a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, model lineage, datasets and retained benchmark results. Text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. V2 includes Appendix A; the supplied v3 ends after the references despite referring to an appendix. This is an observable omission, not an extraction failure.

after.justification: V3 retains original benchmark and SECA results and reports additional efficiency ablations and temporal accuracy results in Table 2 and Figure 4.

Table 3 supplies rare/common/frequent thresholds of below 2%, 2–20%, and above 20%. Existing training details are retained; the V100 timing disclosure moves from the Table 2 caption into the complexity discussion.

E2.justification: The comparator methods remain Scan2Cap, X-Trans2Cap, Vote2Cap-DETR, TOD3Cap, and BEVFormer in their respective comparisons. InternLM2 adds another configuration for TOD3Cap and MTA, rather than a new comparison method.

E3.justification: v2 adds an InternLM2 experimental configuration and evaluates mAP separately across frequency, weather, and time-of-day groups. The original Llama-3.2-1B setting, dataset splits, metrics, IoU thresholds, ten-epoch training budget, and learning rate remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Table 3 examines whether detection improvements persist for rare objects and different weather and lighting conditions. The existing component, attachment-layer, and alignment-loss ablations are unchanged, moving from Tables 3–6 to Tables 4–7; the qualitative example is also retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. v2 continues the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 substantially extends the reported evidence with another language model and condition-specific detection results. The new InternLM2 comparison reports TOD3Cap/MTA CIDEr@0.5 of 105.1/113.0 and mAP of 26.8/27.6; Table 3 adds rare-object mAP of 17.1/18.9 and nighttime mAP of 12.4/13.1. Original Llama results and ablation values are unchanged.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.4 retain the same BLA and DCA components, alignment losses, prompt pooling, training objective, and inference procedure. Testing InternLM2 does not introduce a documented change to the MTA algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammar and wording corrections, revises experimental discussion, and introduces a labeled Computational Complexity paragraph. Jingru Luo is added to the author list. The section sequence and most explanatory prose are retained.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain language-model columns, additional rows, and grouped headers; a new Table 3 is inserted. Existing ablation tables gain Captioning/Perception group headings and are repositioned. Figure 2 is reduced in size, but its content and the framework diagram remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to the InternLM2 Technical Report, BEVDiffuser, and Position: Prospective of Autonomous Driving, while removing Driving with LLMs. The related-work organization and positioning around joint perception-captioning alignment remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and objectives are equivalent. Changes to transpose notation, definition symbols, and caption-metric notation do not alter the mathematics; no new assumptions, derivations, or proofs appear.

improvement.justification: The additional language-model comparisons and condition-specific analysis provide useful support for portability and robustness beyond v1's single-model, aggregate evaluation. These are limited extensions of otherwise unchanged evidence. A small reporting inconsistency remains: the text gives rare/nighttime gains of 10.7%/5.7%, whereas Table 3's caption gives 10.5%/5.6%. Overall, the added evidence modestly improves the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MTA work, and all ten pages, including equations, figures, tables, and references, are readable. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix; both mention separate supplementary materials that are unavailable for this comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and additionally reports InternLM2 comparisons and detection results stratified by object frequency, weather, and time of day.

before.justification: v1 reports original MTA detection and captioning experiments, qualitative examples, and component, layer, and loss ablations in Section 4.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims: unified detection across three OOD settings, virtual outlier synthesis from ID data, standardized-feature training, and effectiveness across six datasets without external OOD data for ASCOOD.

C2.justification: The synthesis rationale changes substantially: v1 describes gradient addition as reducing the true-class logit, whereas v2 explains that it raises that logit while disrupting invariant features, producing challenging outliers. Appendix B.8 develops the corresponding addition-versus-subtraction interpretation. v2 also qualifies decreasing-alpha benefits as specific to spurious detection and removes v1's recommendation that masking is unnecessary in fine-grained settings.

D1.justification: v2 adds a consolidated per-dataset configuration table, Table 8, and documents exposure datasets and CIFAR training initialization for OE/MixOE. Existing software, preprocessing, validation procedures, and code-access information are retained. The additions improve documentation, although alpha descriptions in Table 8 and Appendix B.5 are not clearly reconciled.

E1.justification: The six ID datasets, spurious and fine-grained tasks, conventional OOD datasets, and CIFAR-10 near-OOD coverage are retained. The added OE/MixOE experiments reuse already represented datasets as exposure data; they introduce comparison protocols rather than new domains or test scenarios.

E2.justification: v1 discusses external-outlier methods without evaluating OE or MixOE. v2 adds both across the six benchmarks through Table 3, Appendix B.9, and conventional-OOD tables in Appendix F. This substantially broadens comparisons beyond methods operating without external OOD training data.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: Waterbirds uses lambda=0.1 instead of 1 and an alpha schedule of 300 to 30 instead of 2 to 0.1; fine-grained defaults change from full gradients to 10% masked gradients. Sensitivity grids are revised. New OE/MixOE protocols specify external exposure datasets and training from scratch on CIFAR. These are reported setting changes, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds logit-gradient versus probability-gradient comparisons and gradient-addition versus subtraction controls, including Tables 13 and 18. It also adds CelebA sparsity analysis and extends lambda sensitivity to Car. Existing Aircraft/Car synthesis and sparsity studies are merged and revised, while several alpha and sigma studies are updated.

E5.justification: Both versions use the existing plus/minus uncertainty notation without documenting run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures. Additional rows and changed uncertainty values do not introduce a new reporting practice.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced or added. Table 1 changes Waterbirds spurious FPR@95 from 12.97 to 11.37, and Table 2 changes Car fine-grained FPR@95 from 45.37 to 40.76. Waterbirds MSP FPR@95 instead changes from 20.11 to 24.11 in the appendix. Revised settings prevent interpreting these as uniform same-setting gains. New comparator and ablation results substantially expand the evidence; existing CIFAR headline and near-OOD scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed framework retains gradient-based perturbation or pixel shuffling, standardized features, and cross-entropy plus weighted KL training. Both full and masked gradients already appear in v1. Revised hyperparameters and newly tested gradient alternatives do not establish a new proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the synthesis explanation and results discussion, introduces Sections 5.1 and 5.2, reorganizes Appendix B, and separates complete results into Appendix F. It also renames p_i to p_inv. The introduction, related work, conclusion, and much of the remaining prose are retained.

P2.justification: The empirical displays are substantially revised through new comparator, configuration, and gradient-control tables, merged Aircraft/Car ablation tables, and an expanded Waterbirds sparsity table. It interprets caption-count saturation as redundancy in geometric information. C1.justification: The central claim that collective contributions improve detector explanations is retained. However, v2 adds the π*-index and its asserted axiomatic properties as a principal contribution, and reframes efficient computation of Shapley quantities as their incorporation through a heuristic. It also claims novelty in analyzing greedy patch selection through game-theoretic indices, substantially changing the stated theoretical contribution.

C2.justification: New Appendix A explicitly distinguishes the method's goal from accurate Shapley approximation, leaves approximation analysis and reward design unresolved, and discusses evaluation validity. Section 4.3 acknowledges that greedy ordering need not recover the optimal ordering. v2 also adds redundancy-based interaction explanations and interpretations of detector failures through background correlations. Existing pointing-game limitations and insertion-versus-deletion interpretations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix C.6 newly explains how patches selected together for r >= 2 receive individual reward values: their ordering is chosen by examining r! permutations. Appendix C.7 revises the documented search-window parameters. These improve or change implementation documentation without establishing that the newly explained ordering procedure was introduced in v2. Both versions still promise future code release.

E1.justification: MS-COCO, PASCAL VOC, and the seven-class synthetic marker dataset are retained. v2 adds dedicated misclassification and mislocalization test scenarios, extending coverage to explaining naturally occurring detector failures. Grounding DINO is evaluated on MS-COCO; its addition alone does not establish a new dataset or open-vocabulary task.

E2.justification: v2 adds two directly relevant comparator families: Monte Carlo estimated Shapley values in Appendix D.2 and the greedy-search method VPS in Section 5.5 and Appendix D.13. VPS is evaluated with Grounding DINO, DETR, and Faster R-CNN. The original six baselines remain in Table 1; BSED and FSOD remain citations rather than reported evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New protocols include 200 detections per failure type, Grounding DINO evaluation on 100 instances above confidence 0.6, and VPS comparisons on 500 instances above 0.7. v2 also adds a 200-sample Monte Carlo baseline evaluated on 100 detections, weight-randomization checks using SSIM and rank correlation, and blur-versus-zero masking. The search-window settings are explicitly revised, but the PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds masking-sensitivity tests, model-weight randomization sanity checks, and quantitative and qualitative analyses of misclassification and mislocalization. It also expands the existing weighted-reward analysis to additional examples and patch deletion. The original patch-combination, computational ablation, biased-model, and detector-comparison analyses are largely retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for experimental results. The new Monte Carlo sampling budget describes how a comparator estimates feature contributions, rather than uncertainty reporting or repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 is unchanged, but v2 adds substantial failure-case, VPS, Monte Carlo, masking, and randomization results. For example, its Grounding DINO comparison reports overall AUC 0.751 for VX-CODE versus 0.646 for VPS. Retained pointing-game results are also revised: insertion PG(M) changes from 0.953 to 0.905, EPG(B) from 0.644 to 0.520, and EPG(M) from 0.443 to 0.351 (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 6). These revisions do not establish a same-setting performance change.

M1.justification: The core reward, greedy insertion/deletion, patch selection, and step restriction remain. However, the documented rule restricting eligible patches changes: v1 Appendix B.8 applies it when Rbox <= 0.1 with margins w/5 and h/5; v2 Appendix C.7 uses Rbox <= 0.2 and margins w/7 and h/7. This changes the explanation search region. The new π*-index provides theoretical interpretation rather than a new selection algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Preliminaries become a separate section, biased-model examples move into the motivation, detailed bounding-box evaluation moves to the appendix, and the supplementary material is reorganized around limitations, related work, method details, and experiments. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond renumbering or adding scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the method overview, compacts and relocates the opening illustration, and adds performance curves, failure-case panels, and new comparison tables. It merges the former aeroplane bias table into a broader appendix table and expands the weighted-reward figure. Several existing visualization grids are preserved and relocated, rather than constituting new results.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against SAG, REX, VPS, and logic-based explanation approaches, alongside new references supporting masking, error diagnosis, and sanity checks. Section 2 and Appendix B distinguish the contribution through game-theoretic analysis of patch search and sequential coalitional games. This goes beyond v1's positioning primarily as an extension of MoXI to object detection.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the π*-index, an optimal ordering objective, and a sequential coalitional-game interpretation in Section 4.3. Appendix C.8 adds the elimination variant and arguments concerning null-player, linearity, and efficiency properties, while excluding symmetry. It also revises the accelerated complexity expression to include the early-step factor γn/r. These additions substantially extend v1's self-context and full-context derivations.

improvement.justification: The added masking and weight-randomization checks, direct VPS and Monte Carlo comparisons, and clearer limitations strengthen empirical credibility beyond v1. However, the new linearity argument in Appendix C.8 holds π* fixed across reward functions although Definition 5 makes its optimum reward-dependent, leaving a prominent theoretical claim unsupported. The empirical and documentation gains support a limited net improvement despite this theoretical gap.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds failure-case evaluations, comparisons with VPS and Monte Carlo Shapley estimates, and masking and weight-randomization tests.

C2.justification: v2 substantially revises interpretations of open-source versus proprietary performance and adds explanations involving partial lip-reading ability, ineffective use of audio, and explicit timestamp cues. It removes the class-wise emotion-bias discussion and the suggestion that audio mitigates speaker-emotion degradation. The appendix also newly states the benchmark's applicability to videos lasting at most 10 seconds.

D1.justification: v2 adds model sizes, decoding settings, memory usage, and runtimes for the new models, and revises existing runtime reports in Table 6. It newly discloses approximately three minutes of annotation per question, ten workdays in total, and 4.7 hours of video. Most operator settings, construction prompts, evaluation hardware, and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: v2 removes the MELD-derived, seven-class Emotion Recognition in Conversation task, including its dialogue-history inputs and 210-question evaluation. This eliminates a distinct dataset and contextual emotion-understanding scenario, reducing coverage from 17 to 16 tasks. These extend represented domains, although the non-human coverage consists of qualitative demonstrations.

P2.justification: Table 1 moves from page 6 to page 7, Figures 1–2 receive caption edits, and Equation (2) is reformatted. The four figures and three tables retain their underlying visual content and structure.

R1.justification: New Section 2.3 discusses motion generation through MDM, MAS, and Motion-2-to-3, all already cited in v1. Section 2.2 compresses the MVLift comparison and removes the explicit architectural-similarity statement. This modestly revises positioning while retaining the same 39 referenced works.

T1.justification: The ground-plane equation and local-to-global transformation retain their mathematical content. v3 changes coordinate symbols, relocates tensor dimensions, and explicitly writes the concatenation already described in v1 Section 3.1. These are notation and exposition changes, without new derivations, assumptions, or proofs.

improvement.justification: The dedicated motion-generation discussion, clearer method overview with section pointers, and cleaner presentation of Equation (2) modestly improve readability and context. The polish is uneven: v3 drops the explicit MVLift architectural-similarity statement and introduces a coordinate-subscript typo in Section 3.3.1. With experiments, conclusions, and reproducibility information unchanged, the overall benefit is limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Mocap-2-to-3, and all ten pages of each are readable, including equations, figures, tables, and references. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains the original quantitative evaluations, ablations, and qualitative reconstructions reported in Tables 1–3 and Figure 4.

before.justification: v1 reports original RICH and AIST++ evaluations in Tables 1–2, ablation results in Table 3, and qualitative reconstructions in Figure 4.

C1.justification: The central claims about 2D pretraining, multi-view lifting, generalization and absolute positioning persist. v4 newly characterizes absolute-depth recovery as a novel task and foregrounds accelerated trajectory convergence as a contribution of ground-plane conditioning. These refine the claimed novelty and component roles without replacing the paper's central contribution.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly interprets pointmaps as accelerating convergence rather than being essential for eventual learning, based on the longer-training control. It attributes worse foot sliding than GVHMR to omitted post-processing and adds detection-confidence, foot-sliding and SLAM-based future directions. Detector-quality and calibrated-camera applicability constraints remain, although their presentation changes.

D1.justification: The supplied v4 omits v3 Section 4.1's architecture dimensions, Adam optimizer, learning rates, batch sizes, two-stage epoch schedule and maximum sequence length. It newly identifies a ResNet-18 pointmap encoder and lists camera augmentation parameters, but camera and pointmap details also point to missing appendices. This substantially changes the available reproducibility information without proving that the omitted settings changed. Both versions still promise a future code release.

E1.justification: The evaluation datasets and SMPL/COCO lifting tasks remain RICH and AIST++. Training coverage expands modestly: v3 explicitly excludes AIST++ training data, whereas v4 Table 2 adds an AIST++ 2D-pretraining variant while retaining a variant without that data. The other named training datasets remain unchanged.

E2.justification: v4 adds WHAM+SMPLify to the RICH comparison and extends qualitative comparisons to optimized baselines. GVHMR+SMPLify was already evaluated in v3 and is not a new comparator. The AIST++ baseline set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v4 substantially broadens evaluation with Accel, Jitter and foot-sliding metrics on RICH, a 3500-versus-8000-epoch pointmap convergence comparison, and additional decoupling and AIST++ pretraining controls. Existing pose and trajectory metrics remain. The complete training schedule is no longer supplied, so changed benchmark scores cannot be assumed to come from otherwise identical settings.

E4.justification: Table 3 adds a control without pose/global-motion decoupling and an extended-training control without pointmaps, directly testing representation necessity and convergence speed. Table 2 adds the effect of AIST++ 2D pretraining. New failure illustrations and AIST++ qualitative cases supplement the retained RICH analyses, substantially strengthening investigation of the method's components and behavior.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added epoch counts describe training duration, not statistical replication or uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: RICH Table 1 changes Ours PA-MPJPE/MPJPE/Abs-MPJPE from 25.8/38.7/152.5 to 26.2/39.6/156.8, and W-MPJPE/WA-MPJPE from 85.3/56.1 to 82.6/50.1. Several baseline scores also change. New motion-quality results show foot sliding of 3.5 for Ours versus 2.5 for GVHMR. AIST++ and ablation results are expanded and revised, including a new pretraining variant. These are revised or added results, not established same-setting gains. v4's prose gives Abs-MPJPE as 111.5 mm, conflicting with Table 1's 156.8 mm.

M1.justification: The two-stage diffusion, view attention, pointmaps, triangulation and SMPLify pipeline persists. However, v4 specifies J−1 non-root local joints and J+1 total output slots, versus J local joints and J+2 slots in v3, and replaces the reconstruction factor (scale+1)/2 with s. The PDFs do not establish whether these differences reflect an implemented parameterization change or clarified bookkeeping and normalization.

P1.justification: v4 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, method explanation and experimental discussion. Motion representation moves after pretraining and fine-tuning, pointmap conditioning becomes a separate convergence section, and limitations merge into the conclusion. The title, author list, affiliations and citation style also change. This is substantial narrative and structural revision.

P2.justification: The overview and pipeline figures are redrawn, the pointmap illustration is redesigned, and a new representation/failure diagram appears. The former combined RICH qualitative figure becomes expanded separate comparisons, and AIST++ gains a qualitative figure. Table 1 becomes a grouped full-width display with motion-quality columns and camera-input markers; the tables also gain result highlighting and revised structures.

R1.justification: Related work expands to discuss HMMR, DSD, SLAHMR, PACE, PromptHMR, HumanMM and TRAM/ZoeDepth, adding distinctions concerning drift, computation and input requirements. The basic positioning relative to Motion-2-to-3, MAS and MVLift remains. Hartley–Sturm and MonoUni citations disappear, while triangulation now cites Wikipedia. MVLift remains the same cited work despite changed bibliographic attribution.

T1.justification: Neither readable main text introduces a theorem or proof. v3 explicitly presents the ground-plane equation and coordinate-construction reasoning; v4 summarizes the geometry and defers its computation to unavailable Appendix B.3. It is therefore unclear whether that derivation was moved unchanged or revised. The changed root and scale notation alone does not establish a substantive mathematical change.

improvement.justification: v4 improves empirical scrutiny through direct decoupling and convergence controls, motion-quality measurements and an additional optimized baseline. However, the supplied revision loses much of v3's reproducibility information, refers to unavailable appendices, and contains an Abs-MPJPE discrepancy between prose and Table 1. These evidential gains and documentation/reporting losses, together with unclear settings behind revised scores, prevent a reliable judgment of net overall quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs clearly describe Mocap-2-to-3, and their main text, equations, figures and tables are readable. All 10 pages of v3 and 9 pages of v4 were inspected. Neither contains appendices or embedded supplements, although v4 references Appendices B.2 and B.3, limiting comparison of camera configuration and geometric derivation details.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark results, motion-quality measurements, qualitative reconstructions, and expanded component and convergence ablations in Section 4 and Tables 1–3.

before.justification: v3 reports original RICH and AIST++ evaluations, qualitative reconstructions, and pointmap and 2D-pretraining ablations in Section 4 and Tables 1–3.

C1.justification: v6 drops v4's explicit characterization of absolute monocular pose recovery as a novel task. The principal claims about 2D pretraining, absolute positioning, generalization, and comparative performance remain. Listing ground encoding as a separate contribution restates an existing component.

C2.justification: v6 adds rationale for diffusion over deterministic regression and calibrated cameras over potentially drifting SLAM estimates. It reframes inaccurate detector inputs as an upstream issue rather than an intrinsic framework limitation, and replaces planned SLAM-based camera estimation with future interaction applications. The ground-plane coordinate requirement is also more explicit.

D1.justification: v6 newly specifies 175 in-domain RICH sequences, identifies the RICH training set as a pretraining source, and clarifies baseline input requirements. These disclosures do not establish changed sample counts or inputs. A project-page link replaces v4's future-code promise, but the PDFs do not establish whether code is available.

E1.justification: Both use HumanML3D, BEDLAM, and Human3.6M for training and evaluate ground-truth SMPL keypoint lifting on RICH and ViTPose-derived COCO keypoint lifting on AIST++. The added COCO teaser panel does not introduce a new task or dataset.

E2.justification: v6 adds TRAM to the RICH comparison and GVHMR+SMPLify to the AIST++ comparison, while retaining the other evaluated comparators. MetricHMR appears in the new related-method feature table, without reported benchmark evaluation.

E3.justification: Metrics, detector inputs, and reported ablation budgets remain unchanged. However, v4 Section 3.2 specifies test-set camera perspectives during testing, whereas v6 specifies random sampling of pretraining camera poses during fine-tuning and omits the testing rule. These concern different stages; the missing camera-configuration supplements prevent establishing whether the test-time protocol changed.

E4.justification: v6 removes the AIST++ control without AIST++ 2D pretraining and its associated robustness argument from v4 Table 2 and Section 4.3. The RICH ablations testing motion decomposition, pointmaps, convergence, and in-domain pretraining remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Added result rows retain the same single-value reporting practice.

E6.justification: Retained numerical results are identical. v6 adds TRAM's RICH results, including 36.3 PA-MPJPE and 533.8 Abs-MPJPE, and AIST++ GVHMR+SMPLify results of 62.2/102.8/112.3 for PA-MPJPE/MPJPE/Troot. It removes the no-AIST++-pretraining results of 61.2/92.4/64.7. It also removes v4's inconsistent 111.5-mm Abs-MPJPE statement; both RICH tables report 156.8 mm.

M1.justification: The documented pipeline retains single-view diffusion pretraining, four-view fine-tuning, view attention, local/global decomposition, pointmap conditioning, and triangulation. Section 3.5 clarifies that existing SMPLify fitting is optional when mesh parameters are required; it does not establish a different lifting algorithm.

P1.justification: v6 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, and method explanations. It creates numbered related-work subsections, renames method subsections, separates limitations from the conclusion, and changes author, affiliation, acknowledgment, and citation formatting.

P2.justification: Figure 1 becomes a redesigned full-width teaser preceding the abstract, with an added COCO-results panel. v6 adds the method-feature comparison table, revises diagram labels and quantitative-table legends, and substantially changes the opening layout and document formatting. Figures 5–7 retain their underlying qualitative comparisons.

R1.justification: v6 adds MetricHMR, removes the ZoeDepth citation, introduces a related-method feature comparison, and sharpens the distinction between calibrated-camera and SLAM-based absolute recovery. The central positioning around 2D pretraining and absolute localization remains. Updated MVLift and SLAHMR bibliographic entries represent retained methods.

T1.justification: The coordinate decomposition, global-recovery Equation (1), and pointmap geometry remain mathematically equivalent. Notation changes and expanded explanations do not introduce a new derivation, theorem, or proof in the supplied material.

improvement.justification: The added baseline comparisons and clearer input/data disclosures improve transparency, while removing the 111.5-mm prose error resolves a contradiction with the RICH table. Deleting the AIST++ pretraining control weakens one generalization argument, but the retained RICH ablations preserve relevant evidence. The net improvement is limited; core results are unchanged and referenced supplementary details remain unavailable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Mocap-2-to-3, and all supplied text, figures, tables, and equations are readable. However, both end with references: v4's cited Appendices B.2/B.3 and v6's referenced supplementary material are absent. This limits comparison of detailed camera configurations and implementation procedures.

after.justification: v6 retains these original evaluations and ablations in Tables 2–4 and Figures 5–7, with additional baseline results.

before.justification: v4 reports original RICH and AIST++ evaluations, qualitative reconstructions, and component ablations in Tables 1–3 and Figures 5–7.

C1.justification: v1 explicitly claims new metrics, particularly pAPE, as a distinct contribution. v2 instead presents the metrics as adaptations of existing subject-consistency and pose-AP measures, materially narrowing the methodological novelty claim. The central claims about WYD's diversity, difficulty, and diagnostic value remain.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new controls as evidence that generation, rather than reconstruction capacity or pose-detector choice, drives the observed difficulties. It adds a size-dependent tradeoff between pose adherence and visual detail. Existing distribution-shift and disappearing-object limitations remain, while the explicit limitation concerning face and emotion assessment is omitted.

D1.justification: v2 documents the manual pose-annotation workflow and interface, expands model training-data disclosures, and revises reported annotation effort and computation from over 5,000 to over 6,000 A100 GPU hours. It omits v1's explicit description of autoregressive extension for short-video models. These documentation changes do not establish changes to retained experimental settings.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluations on HumanVid's 71 videos and VACE scenarios using text-only or image-only inputs without pose guidance (Figs. 5–6). These extend evaluation coverage while retaining WYD's videos, source datasets, and categories.

E2.justification: VACE-Wan2.1 joins the pose comparisons and replaces TF-T2V in category-level comparisons. MagicAnimate and depth/edge models remain evaluated elsewhere. Metric validation adds an explicit pICD-versus-ICD comparison and drops PSNR; most existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4 narrows the recommended six-metric suite to FVD, OFE, pICD, and pAPE, dropping standalone ICD and pFVD. New evaluation designs compare generation with autoencoder reconstruction, substitute pose detectors, and use manually annotated poses on 100 videos. The existing 16-fps setting and Appendix D human-study design remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial controls testing reconstruction capacity, OpenPose versus DWPose, and sensitivity to pose errors using manual annotations (Figs. 44–46), plus VACE modality ablations (Fig. 6). Earlier category analyses remain with revised model membership. The separate pFVD/pJEDi and frame-similarity metric comparisons are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated generation runs, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or experimental error bars. Human validation retains the same sampling and reporting practices, including rank correlation and pairwise accuracy.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial numerical and qualitative results for VACE, HumanVid, and the new controls. For example, text-conditioned VACE reports FVD 276, pICD 19, and pAPE 47 in Fig. 4. Table 2 changes the attribution of 72.67% agreement from ICD to pICD, reports ICD at 67.33%, and removes the PSNR and VMAF agreement entries.

M1.justification: The seven-step dataset curation procedure and mask-based pICD/pAPE approach are retained. Revised explanations, attribution to existing metrics, and experiments with additional models do not establish a change to the underlying proposed procedures.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, evaluation discussion, and diagnostic narrative are extensively rewritten. Detailed filtering and categorization descriptions move into Appendix B, the main method description is condensed, and limitations are incorporated into the conclusion. These are substantial structural changes beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, adds a metric schematic and several experimental plots, separates pose results from appendix depth/edge results, and adds VACE rows to existing qualitative grids. Category plots are redrawn, tables are restructured, and the pose-annotation interface is added; several older metric plots disappear.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises metric positioning by acknowledging prior pose-AP use and crediting ConsistI2V for the consistency-metric inspiration. Related work expands discussion of HumanVid and reference-video requirements, and introduces works including AIGCBench, T2V-CompBench, and VACE while removing numerous earlier background citations.

T1.justification: Neither version contains theoretical propositions or proofs. The retained metric definitions, including pAPE as the complement of mean pose AP, are explained and attributed differently without an established substantive mathematical revision.

improvement.justification: The reconstruction and pose controls address important alternative explanations absent from v1, while the revised novelty attribution improves scientific positioning. However, reporting inconsistencies temper these gains: Table 2 reassigns 72.67% from ICD to pICD without explanation, and Fig. 47's FVD-labeled actor-count trend conflicts with Fig. 7 and the accompanying interpretation. The added validation supports a positive but limited net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WYD benchmark, retaining 1,544 videos and nine annotation categories. Their main text, figures, tables, and appendices A–E are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original evaluations and adds VACE results, HumanVid comparisons, and experiments involving reconstruction and manually annotated poses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, category-level analyses, and human preference studies validating automatic metrics.
