C1.justification: The central depth-prior, fine-patch, and competitive-accuracy contributions remain. v4 emphasizes resolving the accuracy–efficiency trade-off and broadens one introductory contribution from using less than 11% of diffusion models' parameters to less than 11% of their computational cost. That is a stronger resource claim, although the abstract retains the parameter-based wording.

C2.justification: v4 introduces binarization as a possible explanation for metric differences with DiffDIS, interprets the loss-transfer experiments, and discusses foundation models' boundary weaknesses. It also explicitly identifies failures involving ultra-fine detail and erroneous monocular depth, suggesting higher resolution or better depth generators (Supplement (9), Figure 12). These add substantive explanations and applicability boundaries absent from v1.

D1.justification: v4 adds baseline backbone specifications and identifies ImageNet-21K pretraining more precisely than v1's generic ImageNet description. It documents new gating thresholds and ablation controls. Conversely, v1's explicit statement that training uses randomly selected depth qualities is omitted. Hardware, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, training duration, and depth-generation pipelines remain documented, and both versions identify the same code repository.

E1.justification: Both versions use DIS-5K and the HRSOD/UHRSD training and test sets. The latter experiments already appear in v1 Appendix F and move to v4 Supplement (5). Added comparisons and analyses use existing coverage; ground-truth box prompts are an added comparator protocol, not a new dataset or target task.

E2.justification: v4 retains the original benchmark comparators but adds RGB-depth-concatenated MVANet* to Table 1 and SAM, HQ-SAM, and Pi-SAM to supplementary Table 10. Its patch-count comparison also adds MVANet configurations with 2×2, 3×3, and 4×4 patches (Table 4), whereas v1 Table 5 evaluates only PDFNet configurations.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include ground-truth-derived box prompts for foundation models, with/without pre-metric binarization, and separate all-ones replacements for the S and Bd controls. v1 exempts FP-DIS and DiffDIS from its standardized 1024×1024 evaluation by using published scores; v4 states that all models are tested at that resolution. This is a reported protocol revision, not proof that every experiment was rerun. The principal dataset splits and 100-epoch training budget remain.

E4.justification: Beyond retained depth-quality, loss, and patch-count ablations, v4 adds dataset-level foreground/background depth-variance analysis (Figure 1), separate integrity and boundary controls (Table 2), direct MVANet patch-density tests (Table 4), loss-transfer tests on MAGNet and DACOD (Table 6), a binarization study (Table 8), and concrete failure cases (Figure 12). These substantially expand tests of the method's motivation, components, and limitations.

E5.justification: v4 Figure 1 adds descriptive statistical reporting through density curves and box plots of depth variance across DIS-TR foreground, background, and full-image regions; v1's corresponding motivation figure contains qualitative examples only. These summarize data distributions and dispersion, not experimental uncertainty. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests.

E6.justification: Many existing scores change alongside substantial new results. In Table 1, PDFNet's DIS-TE (ALL) values change from 0.925/0.874/0.943/0.915/0.031 to 0.915/0.876/0.944/0.916/0.030 for maximum F-measure, weighted F-measure, E-measure, structural measure, and MAE. Its HRSOD/UHRSD maximum F-measures change from 0.971/0.970 to 0.965/0.963 (v1 Table A2; v4 Table 9). Comparator scores, ablations, and efficiency results also change. These are reported revisions, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The overall architecture and 8×8 patch strategy remain, but FSE changes from continuous amplified boundary responses and averaged patch scores to thresholded binary boundaries and any-boundary patch selection, with revised feature gating (v1 Equations 2–5; v4 Equations 2–7). The reported auxiliary depth-supervision sum expands from four to five stages. Averaging the integrity loss is offset by removing its outer half-weight, preserving that contribution's effective weight.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and much of the method and experimental prose are extensively rewritten around an accuracy–efficiency narrative. The title changes, and PDFNet expands to Prior of Depth Fusion Network instead of Patch-Depth Fusion Network. Main headings lose numbering, ablation subsections are reordered, and lettered appendices become reorganized numbered supplementary sections.

P2.justification: v4 adds statistical plots to the motivation figure, redraws the conceptual comparison and pipeline diagrams, revises the FSE diagram, and introduces a failure-case figure. Tables gain backbone, control, metric, and efficiency information, with new loss-transfer, binarization, and foundation-model tables. Existing qualitative panels are retained but relocated and resized within a substantially revised layout.

R1.justification: v4 adds references and discussion for SAM, HQ-SAM, Pi-SAM, and several backbone architectures, while removing the JL-DCF reference. It credits diffusion methods' strong generative priors and emphasizes their computational expense, refining v1's broader criticism of previous methods' dependence on local features. The three principal related-work areas remain DIS, monocular depth, and depth-aware dense prediction.

T1.justification: FSE's mathematical definitions change substantively: v4 introduces binary threshold and existential patch-selection predicates in place of continuous responses and averaged scores. The depth-supervision summation also changes its stage count. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs, and the compensating integrity-loss rescaling does not constitute a new mathematical objective.

improvement.justification: v4 better substantiates the depth prior and component contributions through dataset-level variance evidence, stronger controls, and loss-transfer tests, while making failure conditions explicit. These improve the paper's explanatory value. The gains are tempered by unexplained score revisions, apparently duplicated RISNet entries across different subsets in Table 1, and a broader computational-cost claim that the parameter ratio does not establish. The net improvement is useful but limited.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable 16-page PDFs describe the same PDFNet research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and supplements support comparison despite substantial rewriting, renaming, and reorganization.

after.justification: v4 retains and revises these empirical results and adds depth-variance analysis, additional controls, foundation-model comparisons, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original DIS-5K comparisons and ablations in Tables 1–5, plus HRSOD/UHRSD experiments in supplementary Table A2.

C1.justification: The central efficiency claim is substantially narrowed: v4 emphasizes 94M parameters and less than 11% of diffusion-model parameters or computational cost; v5 includes DAM-v2 and claims less than 50% of parameters. V5 also explicitly claims the first incorporation of depth as a DIS modality and elevates DIS/HRSOD generalization into the conclusion.

C2.justification: Core depth-loss and patch-density interpretations remain. V5 adds an explanation connecting background depth variance to disconnected surfaces and extends the robustness interpretation to other generators. It removes the explicit limitations concerning ultra-fine details and monocular-depth errors, together with suggested remedies. The binarization qualification survives in Table 1's caption.

D1.justification: V5 newly states that comparator evaluations use official model parameters and were rerun on an RTX 4090, and explains inference-time auxiliary parameter accounting. The code-access pointer changes from a direct repository link to a project website. V4's explicit PyTorch declaration and default-Large reporting convention are omitted; most implementation details remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use DIS-5K, HRSOD and UHRSD. The HRSOD experiments move from v4's supplementary material to v5 Section 4.5 and Table 6. Additional depth generators are model configurations within retained data and tasks, rather than new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V5 removes RISNet, DACOD and FP-DIS rows from Table 1, although FP-DIS remains named in its caption. The SAM, HQ-SAM and Pi-SAM comparison in v4 Table 10 disappears. The loss-transfer comparison replaces DACOD with CPNet, while the HRSOD comparator set remains unchanged.

E3.justification: V5 expands generator-substitution testing and changes parameter accounting to include external depth estimators and diffusion VAEs. Its stated augmentation list omits random cropping, without establishing that cropping was removed from implementation. Data splits, input resolution, optimizer, batch size and DIS/HRSOD training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V5 retains component, loss and patch-count ablations and expands depth-generator robustness testing beyond DAM-v2 to DAM-Small and DepthPro. However, it removes the loss-weight case study, the quantitative pre-metric binarization experiment in v4 Table 8, and the failure-case analysis in supplementary Section 9 and Figure 12.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests for the performance comparisons. Figure 1 retains the depth-variance distribution analysis. The added results introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Reported evidence changes substantially through removal of foundation-model, binarization and baseline result sets. New DIS-VD results include Fmax-beta 0.904 with DAM-Small and 0.917 with DepthPro; CPNet's loss-transfer comparison reports 0.892 without versus 0.895 with the loss. Retained Table 1 scores, all PDFNet-S/B/L scores and HRSOD scores are unchanged after matching relocated tables.

M1.justification: The shared encoder, 64-patch branch, FSE/CoA modules, depth-refinement decoder and training losses remain unchanged in Figures 3–4 and Equations 1–22. The expanded PDFNet name and additional depth-generator tests do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: V5 substantially reorganizes the narrative, rewrites the abstract and introduction, expands the conclusion, and introduces numbered section hierarchies. Selected supplementary content becomes main-text material under ablation and generalizability sections, while the separate supplement disappears. Author-date citations become numerical, and PDFNet's expanded name changes.

P2.justification: Table 1 replaces the backbone column with modality, reorganizes comparison groups and incorporates previously supplementary PDFNet variants. Other retained tables move into compact main-text layouts. Qualitative panels are reduced and rearranged, including Figures 1, 5 and the loss comparison; several supplementary figures, including the CoA schematic and failure panels, are removed.

R1.justification: V5 distinguishes DIS from saliency-focused HRSOD and explicitly positions depth incorporation as a first for DIS. It adds references including Segment Any Motion in Videos and Source-free Depth for Object Pop-out, while removing SAM-family and RGB-D COD references. The central positioning against non-diffusion and diffusion approaches remains.

T1.justification: V5 Section 3.3 adds the explicit boundedness-based justification that diff lies in [0,1], making the depth-stability loss nonnegative. This is a limited mathematical qualification; the loss definitions and Equations 1–22 otherwise remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V5 improves transparency by correcting the headline parameter accounting and placing the existing binarization caveat beside Table 1; additional depth-generator tests also strengthen robustness evidence. However, it removes the supporting binarization experiment, explicit failure conditions and substantial comparison evidence. With the core method and principal scores unchanged, these gains compete with losses in auditability and limitations disclosure, leaving the net quality direction uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PDFNet research. Their text, equations, tables and figures are readable, including v4's supplementary material. V5 has no separate appendix, but retained content can be reliably matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V5 retains original DIS-5K and HRSOD/UHRSD results and ablations, and reports additional depth-generator evaluations in Table 7.

before.justification: V4 reports original PDFNet experiments on DIS-5K, component and loss ablations, and HRSOD/UHRSD results in supplementary Table 9.

Totals cover reported usage only; unknown or launched attempts without usage may still have consumed tokens. Finalized known pre-launch failures are counted as not launched.

C1.justification: The central claims of efficient, zero-shot semantic reconstruction without scene-specific training remain. The abstract changes the quantitative speed claim from a minimum nine-fold speedup to up to nine-fold faster inference, narrowing its stated scope despite unchanged runtime results.

C2.justification: v2 newly discusses scene-dependent benefits, attributing weaker ScanNet/DTU performance to repetitive textures, limited viewpoints, and semantic ambiguity. It also interprets the added sensitivity studies through noise suppression, detail preservation, and diminishing refinement returns. These provide specific qualifications absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information: SAM/SAM2 initialization and re-detection rules, overlap thresholds, four-frame ScanNet++ processing, shared geometry for embedding comparisons, projection-based evaluation, quasi-optimal source-view selection, A100/i7 hardware, and refinement defaults. Much of this is newly disclosed information rather than demonstrated changes to existing experiments. The code link is retained.

E1.justification: The same eight datasets, open-vocabulary segmentation and depth-estimation tasks, and indoor/outdoor coverage remain. RobustMVD explicitly names the existing five-dataset depth benchmark. Additional backbones and parameter studies do not establish new data or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds OpenNeRF and LSM, and Table 3 adds LSM embeddings. Table 4 adds Fast3R and VGGT while removing MVSNet variants, Vis-MVSNet, MVS2D, DeMoN, DeepV2D, and Robust MVD comparison rows. This substantially revises the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 adds a VGGT-backbone configuration and controlled sweeps over anomaly thresholds, window sizes, smoothing strengths, and refinement iterations. Table 4 removes the legacy pose/depth-range/alignment-specific comparison groups. Core metrics remain unchanged; newly documented four-frame processing and projection procedures do not establish that existing experiments changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component-removal studies, v2 Table 6 compares uniform, area-weighted, and confidence-weighted aggregation strategies. Supplement Tables 8–11 test anomaly thresholds, neighborhood size, smoothing strength, and repeated refinement, substantially expanding evidence about design choices and sensitivity.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new confidence-weighted aggregation methods and refinement iterations concern algorithm settings, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Most retained benchmark scores are identical, but v2 adds substantial baseline and ablation results and removes legacy depth rows. New VGGT-backed PE3R reports average rel/tau of 3.7/75.2, while the retained DUSt3R-backed result remains 4.5/68.0; these are different configurations. The no-semantic-reconstruction ablation changes from 5.3/60.2 in v1 Table 6 to 4.9/64.4 in v2 Table 7.

M1.justification: The three-stage pipeline remains. However, v1 replaces anomalous pixels' RGB values with their semantic-region mean, whereas v2 specifies blending that mean with the original value and selects alpha=0.1 (Section 3.4 and Supplement Section 7.3). This changes the reported refinement procedure; expanded tracking details alone do not establish another algorithm change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, experimental discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v2 creates a dedicated framework subsection, changes component terminology, moves proofs into supplementary material, removes the Impact Statement, and adds acknowledgements.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and caption formatting, relocates Figure 1, substantially restructures Table 4, and adds aggregation and supplementary sensitivity tables. The reconstruction ablation gains a runtime-difference column. The six existing figures retain their visual evidence, with resizing and revised captions.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion or citations for MASt3R-SfM, Spann3R, VGGSfM, Fast3R, VGGT, OpenNeRF, and WildSeg3D, while removing references associated with several discarded depth baselines. The central positioning around semantic guidance and efficient reconstruction remains.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 5 introduces a parameterized mathematical definition of RGB refinement, replacing v1's full mean replacement. The two interpolation propositions and their proofs are otherwise retained and moved to Supplement Section 6; renaming Semantic Vectorization to Semantic Guidance does not change the proposition or reasoning.

improvement.justification: The added aggregation controls, sensitivity studies, and explicit evaluation details strengthen design justification and reproducibility relative to v1. These gains outweigh the loss of older depth comparisons, but the improvement is limited: core results largely remain unchanged, and the interpolation proof still incorrectly assumes a+b=1 (v1 Equation 11; v2 Equation 16).

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PE3R, with matching authors, core pipeline, benchmarks, and figures. All pages are readable, including v2's supplement; relocated proofs and renamed components can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, a VGGT-backed evaluation, aggregation experiments, and supplementary sensitivity studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation, depth-estimation, runtime, and component-ablation results in Tables 1–6 and qualitative experiments in Figures 1–6.

C2.justification: v2 substantially revises the mechanism explanations, attributing advantages to preserving pretrained features and describing cosine matching as prone to collapse outside CLIP's aligned space. Appendix E.2 replaces the earlier freezing explanation with one based on RMOT-specific textual discrimination. New Appendix B discusses data quantity/diversity requirements and claims a tracking-based performance ceiling; v1 has no corresponding limitations discussion.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the detector's approximately 10-epoch training budget, car/pedestrian setup and runtime, and identifies the supplied detection/tracking outputs used for Refer-Dance. Conversely, bounding-box query construction, FPN connections and iKUN's inference stride are no longer explicitly documented. These disclosure changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun. Both versions still promise future code release.

E1.justification: v1's evaluations use KITTI-derived tracking and referring data. v2 adds a separate Refer-Dance evaluation in Appendix E.1 and Table 9, extending evaluated data coverage beyond the retained Refer-KITTI and Refer-KITTI-V2 benchmarks. The task remains referring multi-object tracking.

E2.justification: The principal benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged. Within the decoder comparison, v2 adds cosine similarity and removes two sequential-decoding variants. Its encoder-adaptability comparison also drops the iKUN variant with a trainable RoBERTa encoder reported in v1 Table VII.

E3.justification: v2 removes DeiT configurations from the reported experiments and narrows metric reporting by dropping detection/association recall and precision columns. The added Refer-Dance evaluation uses iKUN's supplied detector and tracker outputs. The retained KITTI input resolution, frame sampling, expression sampling, optimizer and 20-epoch training schedule are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a direct test of replacing PCD with cosine similarity, reduces the sequential-decoder ablation from four variants to two, and removes iKUN's text-unfreezing control. The proposed model's freezing, backbone-scaling, annotation-correction and tracker analyses are retained, as are the qualitative case studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Both present point estimates; references to significant improvements do not introduce statistical testing.

E6.justification: The reported evidence changes substantially through additions and removals, although retained main benchmark scores match exactly. New results include Refer-Dance HOTA of 31.83 for JustHook, 29.06 for iKUN and 9.58 for TransRMOT; cosine-ablation HOTA of 28.29; and detector costs of 12.4 training hours and 2.99 inference minutes. DeiT results, recall/precision entries and several controls disappear. The MLP and parallel-decoder ablation HOTA entries change from 42.82 to 42.81.

M1.justification: Grid sampling, motion-feature concatenation, masked parallel decoding and the weighted loss substantially match after renaming CVSA/PSS to VFH/PCD. However, v1 explicitly constructs queries from bounding-box sequences and specifies convolutional FPN connections; v2 describes learnable queries and omits those connections. The PDFs do not establish whether these reflect procedural changes or reduced documentation.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming the paper and components, v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, framework explanation and experimental interpretations, while shortening the loss discussion. It reorganizes the supplementary material into Appendices A-F, moves references before the appendices and relocates the main qualitative-results discussion.

P2.justification: v2 switches from two-column to single-column presentation, redraws the framework diagrams, adds bilinear-sampling and motion-aggregation illustrations, and combines decoder illustrations. It removes v1's MOT-versus-RMOT illustration, restructures tables with fewer columns and configurations, and relocates/reformats retained qualitative examples in the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds SCLIP and ClearCLIP to support its discussion of CLIP's fine-grained capabilities, plus references on hooking and attention. It removes several references, including DeiT, ViT, LLaMA and PyTorch. The main RMOT literature remains, but the critique of iKUN now stresses disruption of pretrained representations alongside restricted encoder compatibility.

T1.justification: The coordinate-grid and entropy-weighted loss mathematics are retained, and neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs. v2 adds the standard bilinear-interpolation formula for an operation already specified in v1 and omits the explicit standard cross-entropy formula; these are explanatory changes rather than new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: Refer-Dance results, the cosine-similarity control and explicit detector overhead strengthen validation and make the efficiency claim more assessable. However, v2 removes the stronger trainable-text iKUN control that achieved 46.23 HOTA in v1 Table VII, reduces reported configurations and metrics, and leaves query/FPN construction less explicit. These gains in coverage and cost transparency coexist with losses in comparative completeness and reproducibility, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: The authors, research task, corresponding components and extensive matching results identify the same work despite its renaming from CPAny to JustHook. Both PDFs are readable, including their complete appendices, equations, tables and figures.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark and ablation results and additionally reports Refer-Dance evaluation, a cosine-similarity ablation and detector timing.

before.justification: v1 reports original Refer-KITTI and Refer-KITTI-V2 experiments, component ablations, runtime measurements and appendix analyses of encoder freezing, scaling and tracker combinations.

C1.justification: v3 elevates systematic analysis of tracking/referring interactions to a principal contribution and claims first identification of grid sampling's suitability for RMOT. v2 primarily claims efficient feature extraction and combined-space decoding. Flexible-encoder, accuracy, and efficiency claims remain, while the headline Refer-KITTI-V2 HOTA advantage changes from 7.77 to 6.9 percentage points.

C2.justification: v3 adds information-sufficiency and redundancy arguments, a ground-truth-versus-predicted-trajectory explanation for augmentation, and a distance-based rationale for long-range sampling. It qualifies long-range benefits by backbone and revises the freezing interpretation to distinguish CLIP alignment disruption from RoBERTa domain shift. The earlier limitations concerning dataset complexity, diversity, and scaling are retained.

D1.justification: v3 specifies new implementation parameters, including four-of-eight frame sampling, 0.02% localization-noise standard deviation, 1% recombination, and ten reference points. It omits v2's explicit positive/negative sampling balance, custom-loss parameter choices, and Refer-Dance statement identifying official iKUN detector/tracker outputs. Both PDFs still promise future code availability.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Refer-KITTI, Refer-KITTI-V2, Refer-Dance, and pure tracking on KITTI. Refer-Dance moves from v2 Appendix E.1 to v3's main experiments; it is not new coverage. The added training perturbations do not introduce a separate evaluated domain or test scenario.

E2.justification: Table 1 drops EchoTrack, DeepSORT, and FairMOT from the Refer-KITTI comparison; FairMOT remains on Refer-KITTI-V2. The principal TransRMOT, TempRMOT, and iKUN comparisons remain. Sequential-decoder alternatives disappear, while an Avg-Pool comparator is added to the OME ablation. Newly discussed LaMOTer is not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: The reported expression sample count changes from 8 per target to 36, and training introduces four-of-eight frame sampling and tracking-error perturbations. The encoder configurations are substantially revised: BERT and ordinary Swin combinations disappear, while CLIP is added across the supplementary tracker combinations. New Hook/PCD controls disable OME and long-range enhancement. FPS is additionally reported; the principal accuracy metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 Tables 4–6 add a temporal-pooling control, isolate Hook and PCD under a CLIP configuration, and test neighboring-grid augmentation and long-range reference-point counts across backbones. v2's sequential-decoder comparison and loss-parameter sensitivity study are removed. Freezing, backbone-size, tracker, dataset-correction, and qualitative analyses are retained, although several quantitative results change.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The Gaussian standard deviation introduced in v3 specifies training perturbations, not uncertainty in experimental results.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes best-model HOTA from 53.83 to 53.91 on Refer-KITTI and from 42.81 to 41.94 on Refer-KITTI-V2. Reported JustHook inference time changes from 27 minutes to 69 minutes. Freezing, scaling, and tracker-combination scores are extensively revised, and new ablation results replace removed entries. These accompany method and setting changes, so they are not controlled version-to-version performance comparisons. Refer-Dance results, including 31.83 HOTA, remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming VFH to Hook, v3 introduces trajectory fragmentation, localization noise, and grid recombination to simulate tracking errors. It adds optional text-conditioned long-range reference-point sampling and incorporates the resulting features into PCD. The loss is now described as Focal Loss rather than v2's explicitly entropy-weighted objective, although no replacement formula is provided.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem formulation, and method narrative are substantially rewritten around subtask interactions. VFH becomes Hook, OME receives a separate subsection, and RBT/TBR terminology is introduced. Supplementary sections are reordered, Refer-Dance moves into the main experiments, and references move after the supplementary discussion.

P2.justification: The document changes from one-column to two-column layout, with extensively redrawn framework and decoder diagrams. v3 adds paradigm and long-range-enhancement figures and removes the dedicated bilinear-sampling illustration. Benchmark tables are condensed, and the timing table adds detection-time and FPS columns. The retained qualitative panels are enlarged and relocated.

R1.justification: The positioning expands from one-stage versus two-stage RMOT to one-stage RBT, two-stage RBT, and Tracking-by-Referring, incorporating LaMOTer and GroundingDINO. v3 relates grid sampling to ROI pooling and Deformable Attention and frames novelty around subtask information transfer. References also add recent vision-language tracking work and remove several earlier citations.

T1.justification: v2's explicit entropy-weighted loss definition and detached hard-sample weighting in Equations 3–4 are removed, leaving a brief Focal Loss statement. The bilinear interpolation remains mathematically equivalent. v3's task-relation notation largely reformulates the existing task; its new information-flow discussion introduces no theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 Tables 4–6 better support component claims through a pooling control, controlled Hook/PCD comparisons, and evidence that long-range enhancement can hurt Transformer backbones. These provide a limited improvement in experimental support and applicability guidance. The gain is tempered by narrower encoder/decoder comparisons and omitted sampling-balance and Refer-Dance proposal details; the revised headline scores alone do not establish improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JustHook for referring multi-object tracking. Their complete main texts, supplementary sections, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results and analyses, including new neighboring-grid, long-range enhancement, and controlled Hook/PCD ablations, alongside retained supplementary results.

before.justification: v2 reports original JustHook benchmark results, component ablations, timing measurements, encoder and tracker analyses, and qualitative examples, including Refer-Dance results in Appendix E.1.

C1.justification: v3 foregrounds a systematic analysis of subtask interdependence and information sufficiency/necessity. v4 redefines the principal contributions around sampling-based feature construction, language-conditioned cues and learned pairwise correspondence, and expands its headline performance claim to LaMOT. This materially changes the claimed contribution structure and empirical scope.

C2.justification: v3 interprets auxiliary sampling as long-range enhancement that benefits CNNs but not Transformers; v4 interprets it as language conditioning that benefits all tested backbones. v4 also introduces reference-point boundary collapse as a failure condition and replaces v3's CLIP alignment-disruption explanation for partial freezing with a broader performance–efficiency interpretation.

D1.justification: v4 documents dataset-specific detector/tracker choices, four sampled-feature resolutions, expression length and regularizer hyperparameters. Conversely, v3's explicit sampling strides, augmentation probabilities and annotation-correction recipe are absent from the supplied v4. Code wording changes from future availability to availability in supplementary materials, but neither that code nor the promised pseudocode is supplied locally.

E1.justification: v4 adds LaMOT evaluation covering its TAO, SportsMOT, VisDrone and MOT17 subsets. This substantially broadens the driving and dance coverage of v3 to sports, aerial imagery and more diverse object-tracking environments.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds CGATracker, SKTracker, HFF-Tracker and DKGTracker on both KITTI benchmarks while dropping older comparators such as DeepRMOT, CStrack, TrackFormer and FairMOT from their corresponding comparisons. ByteTrack disappears from the KITTI comparisons but participates in the new LaMOT comparison alongside MOTRv2 and LaMOTer.

E3.justification: v4 introduces subset-specific LaMOT detector/tracker protocols, specifies D-DETR for Refer-Dance instead of v3's stated TempRMOT detector setup, and uses ten reference points in the best Swin configuration instead of disabling enhancement. The reported TempRMOT timing budget also changes from 50 to 60 epochs. Whether v3's Refer-KITTI annotation correction remains in use is unspecified.

E4.justification: v4 recasts the component ablation around a tracker-matched FlexHook-iKUN variant, includes temporal integration in that comparison, and adds frozen-encoder timing. Reference-point, noise and encoder-freezing analyses already existed in v3. However, the unavailable v4 supplement prevents determining whether v3's aggregation-strategy, annotation-correction, tracker, backbone-scaling and qualitative analyses were retained, revised or removed, leaving the overall extent uncertain.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its results. The Gaussian noise described in v3 is training augmentation, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Reported best-model HOTA changes from 53.91 to 53.83 on Refer-KITTI, 41.94 to 42.53 on Refer-KITTI-V2, and 31.83 to 32.17 on Refer-Dance. v4 newly reports 56.77 HOTA on LaMOT and revises numerous ablation and timing values. These are revised or newly reported results; changed objectives and settings prevent interpreting them as controlled same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The sampling, language-conditioned reference points, optical-flow fusion and masked decoder largely carry over under new names. A substantive but localized change appears in v4 Section 3.6: boundary-collapse regularization is added, and focal supervision changes from all intermediate/final outputs to averaged multi-scale outputs.

P1.justification: The title, framework and component terminology change, and the introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. Methods and experiments gain a numbered subsection hierarchy and reorganized explanations. Encoder-freezing analysis moves from v3's supplementary material into the main experimental narrative.

P2.justification: Figures 1–3 are substantially redrawn or reorganized, including an explicit multi-scale decoding diagram, while Figure 5 reduces three aggregation illustrations to the MLP pipeline. Tables gain new structures for detector/tracker configurations, LaMOT comparisons and separated timing costs. The freezing table moves into the main text; v3's qualitative figures are absent from the supplied v4.

R1.justification: v4 substantially updates the RMOT comparison landscape with recent methods and adds literature supporting LaMOT's datasets and tracking pipelines. Positioning shifts from subtask-correlation analysis and the suitability of grid sampling toward language-conditioned correspondence and incremental deployment. This exceeds a limited citation or bibliographic update.

T1.justification: v4 Equations 3–4 introduce a boundary-distance definition, softplus regularizer and combined training objective. The existing many-to-many RMOT formulation remains unchanged, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 strengthens empirical breadth through LaMOT and newer baselines, clarifies implementation details, and explicitly accounts for detector training costs. However, v3 supplies annotation-correction procedures, extensive supplementary analyses and limitations whose v4 counterparts are unavailable. The continuing use of corrected Refer-KITTI annotations is also unclear. These gains and material uncertainties about evaluation continuity and retained supporting evidence prevent a reliable judgment of net overall quality.

improvement.justification: v5 provides a specific code repository link where v4 only points to Supplementary Materials, modestly improving code discoverability. C1.justification: v2 makes HAVS and theoretical consistency central contributions and asserts that Hier-COS is the first unified hierarchy-aware/multilevel framework with adaptive capacity absent from existing methods. v1 already discussed multilevel prediction and adaptive dimensionality, but did not make these broad exclusivity claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds a numerical-stability explanation for the weight function and interprets the new ablation as evidence supporting leaf-emphasized weights. M1.justification: The orthogonal-subspace construction, transformation module, weighted KL loss, sparsity regularizer, and projection-based inference remain unchanged. The new HAVS definition and proofs formalize the existing method without changing its procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, related-work discussion, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The method narrative is reorganized around HAVS, detailed HOPS construction moves to the appendix, and the supplement is restructured around proofs and geometric properties.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 6 gain rows, and a weight-ablation table is added. v1's conceptual Figure 8 and notation table are removed; Figure 6 is compressed from a full-width display to one column. Most existing graphics and table structures are retained, with revised placement and captions.

Formal definitions and conditional proofs also clarify the construction. These gains are limited by consistency claims broader than the proof's ideal-feature setting and by removal of explanatory displays and specific notebook access guidance.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds tieredImageNet-H ViT results and a level-weight distribution ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on four datasets, including backbone comparisons, hierarchical-consistency measurements, ablations, and qualitative analyses.

C1.justification: v2 broadens the central contribution to separately evaluated LiDAR and vision-only variants and claims state-of-the-art vision-only performance. TRBF shifts from a central component to optional smoothing. The headline 46% improvement, 2.6 FPS and 56% memory-reduction claims disappear, while the core claims of occupancy prediction without dedicated network training, flexible resolution and open-vocabulary support remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of depth-scale ambiguity, optical-flow error amplification and the decision not to accumulate camera-derived dynamic objects. It contrasts LiDAR sparsity with camera density and depth errors, identifies runtime bottlenecks, and interprets TRBF mainly as visual denoising with negligible aggregate accuracy effects. These considerably revise v1's emphasis on consistent component gains and general temporal coherence.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 supplies previously undocumented details, including 294 × 518 VGGT inputs, triangulation using calibrated cameras, full-resolution OpenSeeD inputs, the segmentation prompt list, mask refinement and instance matching/discard rules. v2 also specifies the 10% ablation subset and runtime accounting. The abstract adds a planned code-release URL, without establishing availability. v1's explicit K=10 recommendation is removed.

E1.justification: Occ3D-nuScenes and nuCraft remain the benchmarks, with the same driving domain and resolutions. However, v2 evaluates camera-only occupancy on both alongside LiDAR-assisted occupancy, substantially extending the evaluated sensor conditions beyond v1's reported pipeline.

E2.justification: The external comparator sets in Tables 1–2 are retained. VEON is relabeled VEON-LiDAR with unchanged accuracy entries; SelfOcc and C-CONet remain the nuCraft comparators. VGGT and RAFT are pipeline components, not newly evaluated competing occupancy methods.

E3.justification: v2 redesigns ablation controls around single-frame prediction, temporal accumulation and dynamic tracking for both modalities, adding bus, pedestrian and manmade IoUs. It adds per-stage timing measurements and removes the nuCraft IoU and VRAM metrics. improvement.justification: V2 makes the efficiency evaluation easier to assess through per-stage timings, explicit sampling details, and more legible tables and plots. Its prompt-diversity rationale is better supported by the retained analyses than v1's leakage and overfitting assertions. These gains are limited by removal of one DPG comparator and the 2048/4096 timings, and by the absence of an isolated BridgeFlow ablation. The larger reported speedup alone does not establish a major quality improvement.

before.justification: V1 reports original NAMI benchmark scores, human evaluation on NAMI-1K, training ablations, inference measurements, and generated images.

The inference-component timing analysis is retained from v2's Appendix C, not newly added.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 revises the specified training interpolation to use normalized within-window time and global-time conditioning. Appendix D adds an editing procedure that shares first-stage outputs and switches subsequent prompts. The architecture and linear BridgeFlow remain unchanged; these revisions do not establish that existing models were retrained.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 6–7 and the editing Figure 27, relocates v2's timing Figure 26 to main-text Figure 9, and moves table captions above their tables. Existing figure imagery is retained, with limited reflow and a new supplementary-material heading.

It does not provide a formal proof of the asserted velocity consistency.

improvement.justification: Compared with v2, the new training-resource measurements and bridge alternatives directly strengthen empirical support for the efficiency claims, while Appendix E improves data transparency. The gain is limited: main benchmark results remain unchanged, and the revised interpolation still conflicts with the unchanged velocity-target signs in Equations 2 and 4. The new Gaussian discussion also does not prove its stronger stability assertions.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds training-resource measurements, bridge-strategy comparisons, and image-editing examples.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark scores, human evaluations, inference timings, ablations, and generated-image examples.

Existing image-setting equivalence cannot be established from v2's abbreviated documentation.

These investigate substantive questions beyond v1's image analyses. The component-ablation results themselves are retained unchanged from v1 Table 2 in v2 Table 4.

E5.justification: The matched DIV2K table changes noisiness reporting from mean plus standard deviation in v1 to a single value in v2. This reduces reported dispersion information; the earlier deviations describe the noisiness distribution, not documented variability across training runs.

E6.justification: DIV2K Table 1 changes extensively: SASNet PSNR changes from 35.52 to 39.82 and SIREN from 32.16 to 34.64, without enough setting information to establish comparable performance gains. It explicitly credits the frequency embedding to prior work and removes the main-text BACON/MFN discussion. These changes extend beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The central Bessel-expansion theorem is retained, and v2's explicit masked expansion restates v1's spatially dependent amplitude argument. However, v1 supplies an inductive proof and supplementary formal details; v2's unavailable supplement prevents determining whether those were retained, revised, or omitted.

improvement.justification: The new 3D evaluations and scalability study strengthen evidence for generality and parameter efficiency, while clearer attribution improves positioning. However, revised image scores cannot be reconciled with the available settings, substantial supporting material is unavailable, and the all-shapes SDF claim contradicts Table 3's Armadillo results. These benefits, reporting problems, and evidence gaps prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

Merging the limitations into the conclusion does not materially change their meaning.

D1.justification: v2 removes Appendix B and Table 8 without an equivalent replacement, eliminating per-model learning rates, batch sizes, optimizers, and training-step counts for all six models. This substantially reduces reproducibility information. User-study details and augmentation strengths remain available through relocation.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain the same diffusion models, directly tuned AR baselines, diffusion-student controls, and data-augmentation comparator. The four approaches compared in the user study also remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The stated evaluation sampling, CLIP-I/CLIP-T/DINO metrics, model variants, and augmentation settings remain unchanged. The nine-participant, three-case user-study protocol moves from Appendix A into Section 5.5. Removing the training table establishes lost documentation, not a revised experimental protocol.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed variability, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. The user-study participant count is retained through relocation from Appendix A.

E6.justification: Tables 1–6 retain their numerical results. For example, SDXL-supervised Lumina-mGPT remains at 0.8074 CLIP-I, 0.3118 CLIP-T, and 0.7834 DINO in Table 2. The qualitative images and ablation curves also match across versions.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same three-stage procedure: fine-tune a diffusion supervisor with LoRA, generate subject-conditioned proxy images, and fine-tune the AR student with LoRA. No algorithmic component or objective changes.

P1.justification: v2 makes limited wording and paragraph edits, adds Shengju Qian and a corresponding affiliation, incorporates Appendix A into Section 5.5, and merges Conclusion and Limitation into one section. Most prose and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 and Table 1 move within page 2, Table 6 moves to page 7, and v1 Figures 5 and 6 become v2 Figures 6 and 5. Some image grids are resized; Table 7 becomes prose and Table 8 disappears. The retained displays preserve their underlying content.

R1.justification: v2 removes two cited works: A Systematic Survey of Regularization and Normalization in GANs and Domain Re-modulation for Few-Shot Generative Domain Adaptation. The remaining related-work discussion and central research positioning are substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The metric descriptions and informal token-distribution reasoning are unchanged. Neither version contains formal theorems, proofs, or derivations that are added or revised.

improvement.justification: The method, results, ablations, and user-study protocol remain intact, but removing Appendix B's complete training table makes the experiments less reproducible. The limited editorial reorganization does not compensate for losing these practical details, yielding a modest overall quality decline.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Proxy-Tuning study and are readable throughout. Text, tables, figures, and v1's appendices can be reliably matched, including material relocated into v2's main text.

after.justification: v2 retains the original quantitative experiments, qualitative results, ablations, and human-study outcomes.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-generation experiments, quantitative comparisons, ablations, multi-subject evaluations, and a human study in Sections 3–5 and Tables 1–6.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on systematically demonstrating GT-quality bias and correcting it with RQI. v3 reframes the contributions around broader FR/NR evaluation challenges, emphasizes fine-grained discrimination and fidelity, and adds the substantive claim that RQI improves SR models when used for optimization.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations connecting dense pairings and regression to fine-grained discrimination, and weaker SwinIR training gains to limited generative capacity. Appendix F newly restricts meaningful score comparisons to a shared reference and distinguishes perceptual texture quality from pixel-accurate fidelity. The cross-content restriction remains in tension with the retained across-content generalization discussion.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies Huber regression, exact test downsampling factors, SR-loss weighting, staged training budgets and model-specific integration details. It also adds a project website link, without establishing its contents in the PDFs. Existing IQA learning rates, batch sizes, crop sizes and validation splits are retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds SRIQA-Bench evaluation and LSDIR training/validation for the new SR-optimization task. The original five SR benchmarks, three IQA training datasets and BSD-SR/QADS/Kadid-10K evaluations remain. Set5 and Set14 were already evaluated in v1, so their prominence in v3 is not new coverage.

E2.justification: AFINE and DeQA-Score are added to the existing user-study and public-benchmark metric comparisons. The new SR-training experiment compares original-loss, AFINE-assisted and RQI-assisted versions of SwinIR, SeeSR and PiSA-SR. The seven SR methods in the original user study remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 introduces controlled SR retraining on LSDIR, with original-loss and AFINE-loss comparison arms, and testing on LSDIR/DIV2K using five quality metrics. Appendix E specifies staged training schedules. The original 2AFC study, scene-separated 80/20 IQA split and multiscale patch evaluation are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds L1/L2/Huber loss ablations and an AFINE failure case involving subtle quality differences. It removes v1's systematic GT-quality filtering analysis, including MANIQA-based filtering and random-discard controls, rather than relocating them. The same-distortion and single-scale ablations are retained as Table 5; StableSR/PASD behavior case studies are removed.

E5.justification: v3 supplementary Figure 5 identifies the retained user-score error bars as 95% confidence intervals. v1 Figure 7 already displays those bars but does not define them. Neither version supplies repeated-training-run counts, seeds or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 adds benchmark, comparator, SR-training and loss-ablation results while retaining the original user-study scores. DeQA-Score's added Set5/Set14 SRCC of 0.699 exceeds RQI's unchanged 0.664. Table 3 appears to interchange the earlier BSD-SR/QADS PLCC-mean and SRCC-all values, and changes QADS RQI PLCC-all from 0.822 to 0.832; these do not establish performance gains.

M1.justification: v3 adds an SR-training procedure using the original objective plus an RQI term weighted by -0.1 (Section 5.4). Appendix E explains its integration into SwinIR, SeeSR and PiSA-SR, including image-space feedback through SeeSR's frozen decoder. The core asymmetric MOS-difference metric and IQA backbones remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. User-study and metric analysis now precede and motivate RQI; the method receives separate training, evaluation and implementation subsections. Supplementary material is reorganized and consolidated after the references, with several earlier figure-reference errors resolved.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the RQI diagram, replaces the opening visual presentation, expands comparison tables, moves user-preference plots into the supplement and removes GT-quality distributions/filtering plots. It adds SR-training comparison figures and new experimental tables. Several qualitative panels are retained or recomposed rather than newly generated evidence.

R1.justification: v3 substantially revises positioning around AFINE, distinguishing RQI's general training framework and use of existing IQA datasets from AFINE's SR-specific approach. It adds discussion of DeQA-Score, NeuralSBS, probability-based formulations and recent diffusion SR methods. The KonIQ++ citation and associated GT-analysis context disappear.

T1.justification: The stated training-pair domain changes from indices 0 through n in v1 Section 4 to 1 through n in v3 Section 4.1, excluding the pristine reference as written. v3 also formally defines the new SR-optimization objective in Equation 3. No theorems or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: Comparisons with AFINE and DeQA-Score, SRIQA-Bench testing, loss ablations and controlled SR-training experiments strengthen evidence for RQI's relevance and practical utility. Clearer implementation and limitations also help. These gains are qualified by the apparent Table 3 row transpositions, removal of direct GT-quality controls and unresolved cross-content interpretation, supporting a limited overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RQI research, despite the changed title and substantial revision. The complete main texts, tables, equations, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original user-study and benchmark results and adds comparator evaluations, loss ablations and experiments training SR models with RQI.

before.justification: v1 reports original GT-quality analyses, a user study covering 2,496 images, IQA benchmark evaluations and RQI ablations.

C2.justification: v2 newly identifies server access to class names as a confidentiality limitation. It also interprets robustness across LLMs through overlapping world knowledge and multiple descriptions per class, and interprets the privacy results as preserving utility. Most existing explanations of generalization and convergence remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, identifies GPT-4o as the main prompt-generation model, and documents privacy parameters. However, v1's pseudocode, resource analysis, 75/25 data split, architecture lists, and detailed hyperparameters cannot be matched against the unavailable v2 appendices. The full change in reproducibility information is therefore unresolved.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate image classification on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet. v2 additionally uses WordNet-derived semantic rankings for evaluation. However, whether v1's cross-device scenario remains covered cannot be established because it is absent from the available v2 body and the referenced appendices are unavailable.

However, v1's separate model-heterogeneity and cross-device comparisons cannot be fully matched against v2's unavailable supplementary material, preventing a complete comparator-membership judgment.

It also introduces four-LLM comparisons and a privacy evaluation with clipping radius 2.5, delta = 10^-5, and epsilon values 1, 2, 4, and 8. The shared main cross-silo protocol remains 20 clients and 300 communication rounds.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative tests of semantic preservation in Figure 1, sensitivity to GPT-4o, Claude-4-sonnet, Gemini-2.5-pro, and LLaMA3-8B-Instruct in Figure 5, and privacy–utility analysis in Table 4. Existing component and prompt-richness ablations remain. Retention of v1's other hyperparameter analyses cannot be verified without v2's appendices.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix C.4 explicitly reports three repetitions and mean plus standard deviation. v2 reproduces the retained tables' uncertainty values and uses similar notation for privacy results, but its available text does not explain repetition counts or uncertainty estimation. The missing experimental appendix prevents determining whether those reporting practices changed.

E6.justification: All 160 mean-and-uncertainty entries in v1 Tables 1, 4, and 5 match v2 Tables 1, 2, and 3. Substantial new results appear in the semantic, LLM-choice, and privacy analyses: for example, Figure 1 reports FedTSP Spearman correlations of 0.684 and 0.291 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and Table 4 reports 45.28±0.29% under epsilon = 1 and Dir(0.1). These are additional evaluations rather than revisions to retained benchmark scores.

M1.justification: The original prototype construction and training objectives remain, but v2 Section 3.5 adds a privacy-preserving variant. One selected client generates and embeds class descriptions, then clips and perturbs the embeddings with Gaussian noise before uploading them. This introduces a substantive alternative procedure for withholding class identities from the server.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much technical prose remain intact. Changes include targeted introduction and conclusion rewrites, renamed method subsections, a condensed homogeneous-setting explanation, and reorganized experimental subsections. Author and affiliation information is updated, and acknowledgments are added.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands from four heatmaps to six panels with quantitative charts; Figure 2 is redrawn; Figure 5 replaces its local-epoch panel with an LLM-comparison table; and a new privacy table appears. Retained tables and figures are repositioned, table captions move above tables, and several captions omit previously stated experimental conditions.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantive positioning against CLIP-based federated learning, including pFedPrompt, PromptFL, and other prompt or alignment approaches. It distinguishes transferring semantics into client image models from adapting CLIP itself. WordNet, differential privacy, and additional recent federated-learning references further expand the research context beyond v1's FedPL and HtFL discussion.

The original optimization equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens support for the semantic mechanism, tests dependence on the chosen LLM, and addresses class-name confidentiality. However, its referenced appendices are absent, leaving important experimental coverage, uncertainty reporting, and reproducibility details unavailable for comparison. These benefits cannot be weighed reliably against the unresolved preservation of v1's supporting material, so an overall quality improvement is uncertain.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reproducibility through detailed calibration procedures and pseudocode, adds denoising evidence, and clarifies much of the presentation. However, conflicting main-text/supplement optimization and NMSE definitions, a changed tracking norm paired with identical scores, and the missing density factor in Equation 4 introduce reliability concerns. The TinyViT coordinate-classification architecture and original projection method remain.

(2025) as foundations for the new approach. T1.justification: v3 introduces a formal f-FDP definition and its (ε,δ) specialization, restricting neighboring records to those with identical public representations ψ(x) (Equation 6). improvement.justification: Relative to v1's MPII-focused projection study, v3 improves experimental breadth and inspectability through component controls, Human-Art evaluation, and explicit hybrid pseudocode. However, Equation 6 restricts privacy to records sharing public features, while the text claims identical privacy constraints and complete raw-image protection. Public-feature-only finetuning also scores 83.61% (Table 1), above the hybrid's 82.62% (Table 5). These unresolved issues affect the central privacy-utility claim, preventing a reliable net quality judgment despite the substantial additions.

It also compares dimensionality and sensitivity dependence across the component methods. The bound is stated as a corollary rather than fully derived.

The broad concern about unfaithful explanations remains.

It adds interpretations of concept-count plateaus and differing logit/probability responses to attacks. v1's interpretations concerning learned spatial information, OF generalization and OF's unresolved interpretability tradeoff disappear; the final-layer restriction remains explicit.

It removes OF optimization instructions and v1's explicit logit-shift correction documentation; omission does not establish whether that correction was discontinued. The abstract adds a future code-release statement, without establishing an actual release.

It removes the Fashion-MNIST, DTD and Omniglot OOD evaluations reported in v1 Section 6.3.1 and Appendix H.1. These changes substantially alter the evaluated tasks and represented data.

CDISCO, ICE, CRAFT and ConceptSHAP remain, with ConceptSHAP renamed C-SHAP. The surrogate comparison removes the PACE-derived logistic regressor, adds ICE-Eval, and evaluates both cross-entropy and L1-trained C-SHAP-Eval variants.

E3.justification: v1's main classification experiment uses ResNet-50 without global pooling and 49 concepts; its appendix also evaluates pooled ResNet-50 with one concept. v2 uses pooled ResNet-50 with five concepts for benchmarking. It adds randomized controls, rank correlation and normalized-L1 measurements. PGD now maximizes changes in the model's predictions instead of disagreement between surrogate and model, materially changing the attack protocol.

E4.justification: v2 expands the perfect-explanation check with randomized-importance and fully random controls, adds concept-count sensitivity curves, and redesigns adversarial robustness analysis. It removes v1's importance/spatial-learning ablations, weight-alignment analysis, deletion-strategy and off-manifold diagnostics, OOD robustness tests and qualitative failure cases from Appendices B, C, H and I.

It also newly reports averaging the metric-comparison results over ten seeds, without seed variability. This establishes new replication reporting, not an explicit increase over a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: v1's OF results, including 0.269 MAE and 0.023 EMD in Table 2, and its OOD result tables disappear. v2 reports new results including MCD's 1.42 MAE/0.079 EMD on classification and CDISCO's 32.6-year regression MAE, alongside new randomization, concept-count and adversarial findings. Its SURF surrogate instead uses each U-CBEM's projection operation P and concept importances, including nonlinear projections, rather than v1's prescribed inner products. The method is explicitly restricted to the final linear layer; MAE and EMD remain.

A new preliminaries section precedes related work, while metric discussion is reorganized around a taxonomy and desiderata. The experimental narrative and appendices are substantially rebuilt, beyond changes attributable solely to added results.

P2.justification: v2 adds metric-taxonomy tables, a grouped three-setting comparison, a three-task benchmark table and concept-count plots. This substantially changes the mathematical scope.

improvement.justification: v2's clearer evaluation focus, randomized controls, MCD comparison and new prediction tasks strengthen its validation. Its new statistical reporting is also unclear: Table 5 retains negative differences despite describing one-sided tests for increases and suppression of nonsignificant entries. These benefits and losses leave the net quality direction uncertain.

However, v1 Algorithms 1-2 explicitly define adaptive covariance as Sigma_i = sigma(1 + alpha times average entropy_i)I; v3 leaves covariance adaptation verbal and does not supply its referenced algorithm appendix. These change input conditions and generalization requirements without introducing a new named dataset.

Figure 2's caption also changes validation from clean to corrupted images, although its diagram still labels validation as clean; the actual validation procedure is therefore uncertain.

It also adds failure interpretation and per-corruption/error analyses. The original severity and denoising comparisons remain, but the Gaussian-noise desk example and three feature-map corruption examples are removed.

Table 1 changes DPL+Ours corrupted SGDet mR@100 from 6.4 to 5.7 and VCTree+Ours clean SGDet mR@50 from 7.2 to 7.3, while most existing scores remain. This changes normalization and aggregation, while IN, gated fusion, and the training loss remain.

This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

Positioning against key predecessors also changes: coordinate embeddings are explicitly credited to prior work, SHA is contrasted through fusion under unreliable detections, and HiKER is criticized for dependence on external knowledge graphs.

C2.justification: v1 attributes weaker PSNR improvements to difficulty with reflective surfaces; v2 replaces that discussion with an explanation of how SH initialization improves view-dependent appearance, especially indoors. It also adds substantive interpretations separating geometric consistency, spatial coverage, and raw point count, plus arguments about initialization sufficiency under sparse supervision.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands the implementation recipe: confidence and reprojection thresholds, NDC units, handling of underdetermined SH estimation, coefficient-unfreezing instructions, and ADC settings. These materially extend v1's reproducibility information.

A5–A6) are removed. Motion, noise robustness, and extreme-viewpoint analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

Neither PDF defines what those bands represent, so their status as statistical uncertainty reporting is unclear. Neither version otherwise specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: For 30K EDGS+3DGS, Mip-NeRF360 PSNR/LPIPS change from 27.80/0.175 to 28.02/0.141, while LPIPS changes from 0.124 to 0.132 on Tanks&Temples and 0.219 to 0.223 on Deep Blending. C1.justification: The abstract and three principal contributions remain intact. The introduction adds the qualified claim that architecture/data co-design may be necessary for robust non-Lambertian stereo, extending the earlier statement about current networks' difficulties. Its additional camera-baseline and rendering-cost takeaways summarize existing findings.

C2.justification: The introduction attributes fully realistic scenes' data inefficiency to insufficient geometry diversity rather than insufficient dense geometry, and adds the possible need for architecture/data co-design. Section 4.3 interprets the new mixture results as evidence that WMGStereo can complement existing datasets.

D1.justification: Sections 3.2 and 4 newly specify training from random initialization. Appendix 8.5 distinguishes basic clipping prevention from optional 5 m nature filtering and states that both filtered and unfiltered nature splits are released. Dataset counts are revised; the code link is unchanged.

E1.justification: The same indoor, dense-floating-object, and nature coverage and evaluation benchmarks remain. FSD and WMGStereo were already evaluated individually; combining them adds a training condition, not new dataset or task coverage. Newly cited datasets are not evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 5 adds DLNR trained on FSD+WMGStereo-150k as a comparison against the individual training datasets. The existing comparators remain; FoundationStereo is renamed FSD in this table, not replaced.

E3.justification: The reported dataset size changes from 163,666 to 163,396 pairs. Appendix B.5 becomes Section 8.5 and describes the 5 m nature filter as optional rather than mandatory. Table 5 adds combined-source training, and Figure 5 changes the terminal CREStereo sample count from 100k to approximately 200k. These reported revisions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The added combined-versus-individual dataset comparison tests whether WMGStereo complements FSD. Figure 5 also revises the high-sample end of the sample-efficiency analysis. Existing generation-parameter, cost, object/material-error, and appendix analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed values, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Newly specifying random initialization does not add uncertainty estimation or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: Table 5 adds FSD+WMGStereo results, including 3.24 on Middlebury 2014 (H), 2.08 on ETH3D, and 7.42 on Booster. Figure 5 replaces CREStereo's approximately 100k/1.6-EPE endpoint with approximately 200k/1.8-EPE, so this is not a fixed-setting performance decline. Existing table scores remain unchanged. The unquantified claim that sky/exterior masking provides a small performance boost is removed.

M1.justification: The procedural generator, object placement, material handling, solver and rendering optimizations, and stereo architectures are retained. Newly stated random initialization and revised dataset post-processing documentation do not establish a new model or generation algorithm.

P1.justification: Localized rewriting expands the introduction, related work, and dataset-comparison discussion and shortens several passages. Appendix sections A/B become 7/8. The overall narrative and main section sequence remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Tables 2, 5, and 6 gain row highlighting; Table 5 adds and reorders rows and changes its caption. Tables 2 and 4 relocate, and Figure 5's curve changes. Appendix Figures 6–9 retain their content but use substantially lower-resolution images.

R1.justification: v3 adds references to XR-Stereo, DISC, TartanGround, and StereoCarla. It expands the FoundationStereo discussion to emphasize disentangling dataset design choices and customizing generated data for particular tasks, while retaining the existing research positioning.

T1.justification: No formal assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations are added or revised. The evaluation-metric definitions remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: The combined-dataset comparison adds useful evidence about complementarity, while explicit initialization and filtering/release details modestly improve reproducibility. These gains are limited by unspecified mixture sampling and Figure 5 no longer explicitly plotting the 100k CREStereo comparison retained in the prose. Downsampled appendix figures retain the substantive evidence, and the main method and most results remain stable.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WMGStereo study and contain readable main text, references, and complete appendices. All tables and figures can be matched, including appendix Table 7 and Figures 6–9.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and additionally reports DLNR results using combined FSD and WMGStereo training data.

before.justification: v2 reports original generation-parameter experiments, stereo-network training and evaluation, cost analyses, and qualitative results, including additional appendix metrics.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion replace perturbation co-adaptation as the central diagnosis with over-reliance on a small parameter subset. V2 introduces the stronger claim that random pruning is equivalent to an importance-equalization regularizer and emphasizes training-free positioning. The broad transferability and compute-scaling claims remain.

C2.justification: The mechanism explanation shifts from dependent perturbation pixels/features to shortcut parameters and balanced parameter importance. V2 explains importance-pruning failure through degraded surrogate capacity and interprets trained-surrogate results as compatibility evidence. The diversity/utility tradeoff and limitation of weak CLIP-to-CNN transfer are retained.

D1.justification: New Appendix B documents the importance approximation, DepGraph parameter grouping, exponential transformation and Gini aggregation. Table 7 specifies omission of Weight Scaling in SASD-RaPA. V1's direct dataset-location link is replaced by a citation, while the core attack hyperparameters remain documented and unchanged.

E1.justification: The ImageNet-compatible dataset, targeted classification task and CNN/Transformer/CLIP coverage remain. V2 adds evaluation under diffusion-based input purification through DiffPure in Section 4.4; no additional dataset or application domain is evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 adds SIA throughout the main and appendix transfer comparisons, FTM to the RN50/DN121-to-Transformer comparison, and DSM and SASD-WS with their RaPA combinations in Table 7. These substantially expand evaluated comparators. DWP is discussed but has no reported comparison row.

E3.justification: The diagnostic design changes from perturbation masking to pruning the top/bottom 0.5% of parameters, measuring exponentially transformed importance with layerwise Gini coefficients, and sweeping importance-pruning rates. New trained-surrogate comparisons omit Weight Scaling for SASD-RaPA. The existing main attack budget, step size, batch size, iterations and inference count remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1's perturbation-masking pilot and DropP/DropF experiments are removed. V2 adds importance-ranked pruning diagnostics, Gini analysis, a most-important-parameter masking sweep and training-framework compatibility analysis. Layer-selection, pruning-probability, compute-scaling and heatmap studies remain; the diversity/utility analysis moves to Appendix D.4.

E5.justification: V2 Tables 3–4 introduce ± values for RaPA where the corresponding v1 tables contain point estimates. Their statistical meaning, run counts and seeds are unspecified, so additional repeated runs cannot be established. The standard deviation across pruning-probability settings was already reported in v1.

E6.justification: Many new result entries accompany the added comparisons and diagnostics. Under retained main settings, reported RN50/DN121-to-Transformer averages change from 45.2/40.2 to 45.0/40.3. The strongest listed comparator changes from CFM at 32.2/22.3 to FTM at 33.3/22.8. Newly reported settings include 4.0% against DiffPure and 58.3% for DSM-RaPA; these are additions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The written mask distribution changes from Bernoulli(p) in v1 Equation (3) to Bernoulli(1-p) in v2 Equation (5), correcting the retention probability for the stated pruning rates. Otherwise, Algorithm 1 retains the same selected layers, gradient averaging and projected updates. The PDFs do not establish a changed implementation beyond this specification correction.

P1.justification: The title, method terminology, abstract, motivation and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Background and related work are reorganized, detailed related work moves to Appendix A, compute scaling joins the ablation section, and diversity/utility moves to the appendix. New mathematical and ethical sections further restructure the document.

P2.justification: V2 removes v1's perturbation-masking Figures 2 and 8, adds pruning/Gini/compatibility tables, expands baseline rows and the defense table, and reformats main tables to accommodate ± values. Existing comparison tables are reordered and the diversity/utility figure moves to Appendix D with a corrected caption. Heatmaps and compute-scaling plots are retained.

R1.justification: V2 expands positioning against FTM, DSM, SASD-WS and DWP, emphasizing training-free random pruning versus feature tuning, retraining and importance-based pruning. New OBD, importance-estimation and DepGraph references support the revised foundation. The original Dropout reference and its central motivational role are removed.

T1.justification: V2 adds Hessian-based parameter importance, its squared gradient-times-parameter approximation, and a second-order expected masked-loss derivation in Equations (3), (4), (7) and (8). Appendix B also formalizes the exponentially transformed importance metric and layerwise aggregation. V1 has no corresponding theoretical treatment.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens empirical assessment through newer comparators, parameter-pruning diagnostics and trained-surrogate combinations. However, its new central regularizer-equivalence claim is undermined by Appendix B.2: the stated mask gives E[Delta_i] = -p theta_i, so dropping that first-order term while retaining other order-p terms is unjustified; the derivation also confuses the second moment with variance. The added ± values remain undefined. These empirical benefits and substantive new theoretical problems leave the net quality direction uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. Despite the title change and MCD-to-RaPA renaming, the shared algorithm and experiments clearly identify the same research work.

after.justification: V2 retains original attack experiments and adds parameter-importance diagnostics, defense results and trained-surrogate comparisons in Section 4 and the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original targeted-attack experiments, defense evaluations, ablations and visualization results in Section 5 and Appendices A–B.

E5.justification: The existing ± entries in Tables 3–4 remain unchanged, and no new run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical testing procedure are documented. The new assertion that untargeted results are statistically indistinguishable supplies no test or uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: v3 adds DWP scores, Tables 11–12, and ensemble and untargeted findings while retaining existing numerical results.
