P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 11–12, inserts DWP rows in Tables 3–4 and a DWP column in Table 8, and relocates Table 5 and Figure 7 through reflow. Existing figures retain their visual content; there is no broad redesign.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for MambaVision, DINOv2, ConvNeXt V2, and ImageNet-V2 to support the expanded evaluation. The related-work discussion and positioning against existing attack methods remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The parameter-importance definition, masked-loss approximation, Appendix B derivation, and Gini definitions are retained. Added parentheses around loss arguments in Equations (3) and (7) clarify notation without changing the mathematics.

improvement.justification: The added generalization experiments and direct DWP comparisons strengthen empirical support beyond v2, and the code pointer improves access information. E3.justification: Both retain the same models, bit widths, metrics, guidance scales, and sampling procedures: 20 steps for ImageNet and 50 for LSUN and MS-COCO, with 50k image-benchmark samples and 30k text-to-image samples. Appendix training settings also match.

E4.justification: Table 4 retains the same trajectory-alignment and cosine-loss ablations. Appendix D preserves the same multi-order trajectory visualization and qualitative comparisons; no new robustness or sensitivity analysis appears.

E5.justification: The predefined-seed description for paired trajectory sampling is unchanged. Both report point estimates without repeated-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–5 match. For example, ImageNet W4A8 SA-QLoRA retains FID 8.55 and sFID 8.51, and its MS-COCO CLIP-Score remains 0.3017. The result images and reported findings are also unchanged.

Figure 1 moves onto the first page, diagrams and appendix image grids are enlarged, and Table 5's model header moves into its caption. R1.justification: Appendix B adds dParallel and SparseD, describing parallel decoding and sparse attention as complementary efficiency approaches, with corresponding bibliography entries. The central positioning against diffusion quantization and sampling methods remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, Appendix A assumptions, Runge-Kutta derivation, and quantization-error bounds are retained. Equation reformatting and equivalent derivative notation do not change the mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 replaces the code-release promise with a concrete access link and enlarges diagrams and appendix images, modestly improving reproducibility guidance and visual inspection. Some appendix cross-references become less precise, but the net benefit is limited and positive. The methods, theory, and experimental evidence remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from a large pairwise-labeled dataset and ranking-based self-supervision to demonstrating and improving weak-to-strong generalization. v3 explicitly foregrounds learning beyond individual teachers and difficulty-guided iterative training. It drops v1's abstract-level claim of state-of-the-art performance after human-labeled fine-tuning, while retaining strong in-domain and OOD performance claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations involving larger pseudo-labeled datasets, noisy supervision, confidence reinforcement, and teacher-student disagreement, together with a VQA foundation-model outlook. It removes v1's explanation of the LIVE-VQC performance gap and its explicit limitation that comparison against five anchors substantially increases inference time, although multi-anchor inference remains.

D1.justification: Appendices A-C newly document distortion parameters and encoding settings, preprocessing resolution, model sizes, optimizer details, confidence-loss scheduling, and probability-to-score calculations. These are largely additional disclosures rather than demonstrated changes to previously unspecified settings. v3 supplies a code repository address instead of only promising release, but no longer specifies v1's minimum-variance anchor-selection rule.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same web-video sources, authentic and synthetic distortion categories, and ten evaluation splits spanning UGC, gaming, high-frame-rate, and compression scenarios. PLVD is renamed Dw2s, with the same 438k-video and 700k-pair totals. The new teacher-student experiments reuse this coverage; additional dataset descriptions do not establish new domains or benchmarks.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains MinimalisticVQA VII/IX, FAST-VQA, DOVER, and Q-Align, but adds evaluated VQA2 and VQAThinker baselines. It removes the six opinion-unaware comparators reported in v1 Table 2, including NIQE, IL-NIQE, VIIDEO, STEM, TPQI, and BUONA-VISTA. v1's separate supervised fine-tuning comparison also disappears.

E3.justification: The reported sampling target changes from aggregated distributions of four UGC datasets to LSVQ alone. For ranking training, v1 specifies learning rate 1e-5 and total batch size 4; v3 Appendix C.2.1 specifies 1e-4 and batch size 2 per device. v3 separately introduces a 200k-video single-teacher protocol with 200k iterations and a supervised-student control, while removing v1's downstream fine-tuning protocol. These documented changes do not establish that retained result rows were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds individual-teacher generalization diagnostics and an isolated confidence-loss comparison through models II and III. It retains the synthetic-distortion contribution comparison, but removes v1's hard-versus-soft ranking comparison, motion-encoder ablation, and equal-data control testing label refinement against merely adding samples. The questions isolated by the analyses therefore change substantially.

E5.justification: v1 Table 3 explicitly reports ten-fold cross-validation for KoNViD-1k, LIVE-VQC, and YouTube-UGC; that evaluation and its resampling information are absent from v3. Neither version reports seed-wise variability, confidence intervals, or performance significance tests. v3's confidence loss concerns training, not statistical uncertainty in evaluation.

E6.justification: v3 model II repeats v1's Stage 1 soft-ranking scores, but later-stage results change substantially. Reported final-model overall OOD SRCC/PLCC changes from 0.716/0.752 to 0.745/0.789; in-domain results change from 0.861/0.868 to 0.865/0.872. These involve revised models and protocols, not established same-setting gains. Table 5 adds individual-teacher student results, while the earlier fine-tuning and several ablation results disappear.

M1.justification: v3 adds difficult-sample selection through teacher-student gMAD disagreement and misclassified synthetic-distortion pairs (Section 4.2). It also adds an entropy-based confidence loss with adaptive weighting (Section 4.3, Appendix C.2.2), beyond v1's standard supervised fine-tuning objective. These substantially change training, while the core visual architecture and anchor-based scoring remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution list, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around weak-to-strong learning. The original dataset-method-experiments progression becomes an initial W2S investigation followed by an enhanced framework, with technical material moved into appendices and a new Discussion section.

P2.justification: v3 changes the two-column presentation to a single-column technical report, redistributes the original composite overview, and redraws the architecture and iterative-training diagrams. Dataset statistics and distribution plots move into the appendix; distortion illustrations, model-size and dataset-description tables, and the teacher-student results display are added. The main comparison table is substantially restructured, while the former fine-tuning and dedicated ablation tables disappear.

R1.justification: v3 replaces the dataset-centered related-work subsection with substantial weak-to-strong positioning, citing Burns, Guo, Liu and Alahi, and Sang, and adds a ranking-method discussion. It newly attributes the student architecture to LMM-VQA and discusses newer VQA competitors. This changes the paper's intellectual positioning beyond citation maintenance.

T1.justification: v3 introduces a formal constrained gMAD selection rule (Equation 1) and mathematical definitions for the entropy objective and adaptive weighting (Equations 23-26). These extend the methodological formalism without adding a theorem or proof framework. The retained feature-fusion equations and expanded description of previously used MAP inference do not establish a new theoretical foundation.

improvement.justification: v3 directly supports its revised W2S claim through individual-teacher student comparisons and a supervised-student control (Table 5), while Appendices A-C make data generation, training, and inference substantially more inspectable. These improve evidential clarity and reproducibility. The net gain is limited by removing v1's equal-data label-refinement control and explicit inference-cost limitation, leaving the iterative mechanism less cleanly isolated.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe the same research lineage despite the changed title: the backbone, video corpus, ranking framework, and several result rows match. The supplied text, figures, tables, and equations are readable, including v3's Appendices A-D. v1 references a separate supplement that is not included; judgments concern the supplied PDFs.

E2.justification: V2 Table 2 adds PixArt+MHCA to the main comparisons on both retained datasets. CoDi, Sound2Scene, the three AudioToken configurations and GlueGen remain. An MHCA alternative already appeared in v1's SoundingSVI ablation, but was not a comparator in its main results table.

E3.justification: SoundingSVI changes from 334,495 to 169,221 pairs, with newly reported temporal-gap filtering; SonicUrban changes from 250,310 to 236,674 pairs. Scene-classifier annotations are replaced by Qwen2.5-VL-7b prompts. V2 also introduces controlled two-expert component ablations and a 2/4/6/8-expert sweep. These are substantial reported setting changes; comparable reruns of the retained baselines are not documented.

E4.justification: V1's TA-PMoE-versus-MHCA and retrieval-on/off ablations are replaced by individual and joint removal of SLRCM/S-AdaLN and expert-count scaling experiments in v2 Tables 3–4. V2 Figure 4 additionally tests scene control by varying prompts for fixed bird and traffic soundscapes.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's disclosure of 17 user-study participants adds sample-size information, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: SounDiT's reported FID changes from 28.173 to 16.839 on SoundingSVI and from 33.246 to 11.553 on SonicUrban; other scores also change. These are revised-model/dataset results, not established same-setting gains. External benchmark results disappear and new component/scaling results appear. The retained original baseline scores and user-study accuracy of 86.13% remain identical.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 substantially redesigns SounDiT. Separate audio/T5 conditioning becomes shared ImageBind conditioning; scene cross-attention is replaced by SLRCM and S-AdaLN. The audio experts gain shared keys/values, low-rank queries and gated top-k aggregation. The geo-contextual retrieval and initialization pipeline described in v1 is removed.

P1.justification: The Abstract and Introduction are extensively rewritten, and the method narrative and metric explanations are substantially reworked. Terminology changes from audio2image to A2I, practical applications receive a dedicated discussion, and limitations are replaced by acknowledgements. The broad seven-section sequence remains recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 switches throughout to a two-column layout and redraws the architecture diagram. It removes the dataset-sample and PSS-framework figures, replaces the qualitative comparison grid, and adds scene-conditioned examples. The dataset table loses two descriptive columns, PSS formulas move from a table into equations, and the results/ablation displays are reorganized.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly distinguishes its contextual conditioning from earlier geographic diffusion work, including the newly cited Soundscape-to-Panorama. It adds Qwen, OmniBind and planning/noise/restoration references while dropping T5 and several navigation/ecology references. The broad positioning against generic audio-to-image synthesis remains.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.3 adds substantive mathematical definitions for scene-dependent low-rank modulation, residual strength, low-rank expert queries and gated top-k aggregation in Equations 5–11. Router prototypes are redefined from expert representations to learnable parameters. The diffusion preliminaries, task objective and PSS definitions remain equivalent; neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 improves architectural documentation and adds a closer PixArt+MHCA comparison, targeted component ablations and expert scaling. However, it removes both external benchmark evaluations and explicit limitations. All retained original baseline scores remain unchanged despite revised dataset construction, without documentation establishing comparable evaluation. The stronger architectural evidence and reduced generalization evidence create material tradeoffs whose net effect on paper quality cannot be reliably determined.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SounDiT/GeoS2L and provide readable text, equations, figures and tables supporting reliable comparison. All supplied pages were inspected. Neither PDF includes an appendix, although v1 contains unresolved 'Appendix ??' references.

after.justification: Section 6 reports original results on SoundingSVI and SonicUrban, component and expert-count ablations, scene-conditioned examples, and a matching user study.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original generation results on four dataset groups, architectural and retrieval ablations, and a matching user study.

Totals cover reported usage only; unknown or launched attempts without usage may still have consumed tokens. Finalized known pre-launch failures are counted as not launched.

C1.justification: v2's abstract newly presents the implementation and investigation of two action-routing styles as a contribution. The principal claims about adapting π0, combining vision and action MoE, handling rare behaviors, and achieving Bench2Drive state-of-the-art performance remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting additional fixed views to convergence difficulty, nuScenes results to real-world generalization, and computational cost to extra views and expert activation. Appendix 8 adds unsupervised-selection and distillation directions. Although the dedicated limitations/social-impact section disappears, the important expert-load-imbalance caveat remains in the main text.

D1.justification: v2 substantially revises the numerical training recipe, specifies the existing flow-matching objective, discloses a rear-view annotation fallback, and adds parameter counts, FLOPs, memory, latency, and GPU-hour costs. Implementation details move to Appendix 7. The explicit code/model-release promise and supplementary-movie pointer disappear, although the project-page link remains; actual resource availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix 10 adds actual open-loop planning evaluation on nuScenes, extending coverage from CARLA/Bench2Drive simulation to real-world driving data. Bench2Drive's 220 routes, 1,000-clip base dataset, and five driving-skill categories remain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds DriveMamba-L and Raw2Drive to the Bench2Drive comparison while retaining the earlier external comparators. The new nuScenes comparison uses UniAD and VAD-Base, alongside Drive-π0; these should not all be counted as entirely new baseline families.

E3.justification: The reported training recipe changes from 10+5 epochs and effective batch size 1,024 to 12+6 epochs and batch size 128. Vision/action router loss weights change from 0.05/0.03 to 10/10 in stage one and from 0.05/0.025 to 5/5 in stage two. Added experiments introduce further camera/expert configurations, resource measurements, and horizon-wise nuScenes L2/collision evaluation. These are documented setting changes, without establishing that all retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 expands the camera ablation to multiple fixed-view combinations with latency and memory measurements, adds a controlled token-versus-trajectory routing comparison, and tests action supervision and shared-expert counts. Earlier component-removal, non-shared-expert-count, and router-accuracy analyses are retained under new table numbers. The additions test substantial previously unexamined design and efficiency questions.

E5.justification: v2 newly states that results are averaged over three runs; v1 gives no corresponding repeated-run count. Neither version reports seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This establishes added reporting, not an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises Drive-π0's driving score from 60.45 to 55.85 and average L2 from 0.56 to 1.13. The main DriveMoE row retains 74.22 driving score and 48.64% success but changes L2 from 0.38 to 1.01. Baseline ability scores and fixed-camera results also change, while routing variants, expanded ablations, nuScenes outcomes, and resource results are added. Given revised training settings, these are revised reported results rather than established same-setting gains or losses.

M1.justification: v1 presents one supervised Action MoE. v2 Section 2.4 introduces separately specified and evaluated token-level and trajectory-level alternatives: independent token routing versus routing after averaging the token sequence, with trajectory routing designated as default. This substantially extends the routing design while retaining Vision MoE and the overall two-stage framework; it does not establish that every retained result used a changed implementation.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, splits Action MoE into dedicated routing subsections, moves Related Work and Implementation Details into the supplement, and reorganizes the experimental narrative. The supplement receives a new structure covering the loss, implementation, discussion, annotations, nuScenes, and efficiency. These are substantial organizational changes beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document to two columns, redraws the conceptual and architecture figures, and adds a separate trajectory-router diagram. The camera table becomes a view-selection matrix with resource columns, the expert table gains shared-expert and supervision columns, and new routing, nuScenes, and cost tables appear. Existing tables are also relocated.

R1.justification: v2 substantially refreshes the research context through newer driving/VLA citations, expanded discussion of DriveGPT-4 and DriveLM, new treatments of LeapAD and SimLingo, and connections to DySS, LightVLA, and distillation. Several earlier trajectory/perception references disappear. This broadens the substantive positioning beyond merely moving Related Work to the supplement.

T1.justification: v1 names the flow-matching loss without defining it. v2 Appendix 6 adds Equation 7 and specifies the conditional expectation, noisy-action interpolation, and target vector field. This adds mathematical specification of an existing objective, rather than a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The new routing controls, efficiency evidence, and nuScenes evaluation strengthen the paper's empirical breadth. However, v2 introduces material conflicts between tables and retained claims: Table 2 gives Raw2Drive higher success than DriveMoE (50.24% versus 48.64%), and DriveMoE's revised L2 of 1.01 is no longer lowest, although Section 3.2 still claims both distinctions. Its retained 22.8% driving-score improvement also conflicts with the revised baseline, which implies approximately 32.9%. These gains and reporting problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DriveMoE and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, references, and appendices. Their shared framework and experiments can be matched despite substantial reorganization and additional material in v2.

after.justification: v2 reports original Bench2Drive results and expanded ablations, plus nuScenes planning results and computational-cost measurements in the supplement.

before.justification: v1 reports original Bench2Drive evaluations of Drive-π0 and DriveMoE, component and expert-count ablations, camera-selection experiments, and router accuracies.

C1.justification: The central efficiency claim changes from a subquadratic-space speed/memory trade-off to linear time and space with memory comparable to on-demand sampling. Abstract maxima change from 90%/95%/50% to 92%/99%/63% for sampling runtime, memory, and end-to-end savings. V2 drops the first reference-based ultra-high-resolution evaluation claim and emphasizes the accuracy/runtime Pareto frontier.

C2.justification: V2 adds specific qualifications: only the forward pass is optimized, and the default sampler can remain faster at some small sizes on particular GPUs. Section 9.4 attributes Kubric's preference for lower-resolution inference to less-detailed objects. V1's discussion of cache overhead and future kernel fusion is replaced by interpretation of the fused implementation.

D1.justification: V2 adds actual CuTe DSL implementation listings, including GEMM helpers, sampling functions, and the fused kernel. It documents Ampere targeting, bfloat16 inputs, float32 accumulation, MMA instruction sizes, and shared-memory/register handling beyond v1's pseudocode and implementation outline. The Blender setup script is retained, but the explicit Spring subvalidation-split disclosure disappears.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluated Kubric-8K scenes with generated moving objects, including accuracy and resource measurements in Tables 6-7. V1's ultra-high-resolution evaluation used only Charge's movie scenes. This substantially broadens the central high-resolution evaluation to another scene distribution; Charge, Spring, Sintel, and KITTI remain represented.

E2.justification: The Charge comparisons add DPFlow, ReCoVEr-CX, and WAFT and remove CCMR+ (v1 Tables 2/7 versus v2 Tables 1/11). The Spring/Sintel/KITTI comparison set is narrowed to RAFT, MS-RAFT+, SEA-RAFT, and newly added DPFlow. V2 Table 9 also evaluates a mixed default/on-demand sampler against the proposed sampler.

E3.justification: The main Charge comparison selects each method's lowest-1px-error resolution instead of its highest feasible resolution. V2 also introduces alternative low/high-resolution iteration budgets and changes the iteration/channel sweeps from 256 x 112 to 512 x 224 feature maps. The latter is supported by Section 9.1 and Table 10, although Section 5.1 inconsistently retains the earlier default.

E4.justification: V2 Table 9 adds tests of whether reallocating iterations toward lower resolutions or mixing existing samplers can reproduce the proposed efficiency benefits. The original caching ablation is removed, and the component analysis is replaced by measurements of fused-kernel stages using early exits (Section 8.4, Table 4). Resolution, iteration, feature-dimension, and hardware sensitivity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions specify one run per image for isolated benchmarking and report means and standard deviations across image samples, including shaded standard deviations in plots. V2 adds no repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing procedure; changed uncertainty values retain the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Sampler timings and memory measurements are extensively replaced: at corresponding GH200 8K-input/1024-feature width, reported values change from 1004 ms and 15384 MB to 347 ms and 2829 MB. Charge results also change, including full-resolution RAFT EPE from 45.56 to 59.94 pixels, while cascaded SEA-RAFT retains 13.3% 1px error and 2.70-pixel EPE. Kubric and inference-strategy results are added; auxiliary-dataset accuracy entries are removed. Main-table changes also reflect the revised resolution-selection rule.

M1.justification: V2 Section 4.3 introduces a fused sampler using per-thread block lists, inter-thread minimum voting, and immediate computation and sampling of correlation tiles. This avoids the explicit mask, globally stored blocks, and cross-iteration cache used by v1's implementation. The mathematical sampling target and main cascaded SEA-RAFT procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction and conclusion are substantially rewritten around operator efficiency, and Section 4 is reorganized from separate mask/computation/sampling/cache subsections into high-level and fused implementations. Component analysis moves from the main evaluation to the method supplement, whose explanatory structure is expanded and reorganized. These changes exceed the title and terminology edits.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces the qualitative teaser with an accuracy/runtime comparison, and Figure 4 gains a fused-execution diagram. V2 adds a block-mask illustration and resolution-dependent comparison plots, changes plot axes and scales, and restructures several tables. The same three appendix image examples are retained with revised comparator rows, rather than constituting new case studies.

R1.justification: Related work receives a targeted update with DPFlow, ReCoVEr, and WAFT. V2 acknowledges DPFlow's concurrent synthetic 8K evaluation and discusses cost-volume-free approaches, qualifying the earlier evaluation-novelty positioning. The broader positioning as an exact, RAFT-compatible correlation operator remains.

T1.justification: V1 Section 8.3 derives O(P^1.5) memory with block size B=P^(1/8). V2 Section 8.5 replaces this with separate time and memory derivations that are linear in pixel count for fixed sampling parameters. It also revises the requested-block bound to account for the bilinear sampling footprint, obtaining at most nine blocks per pixel for r=4 and B=8.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's acknowledged mask/cache overhead bottleneck through a documented fused design and supporting measurements. A second 8K scene distribution, contemporary comparators, alternative-strategy controls, and best-resolution comparisons strengthen the empirical case, while kernel listings materially improve reproducibility. Conflicting default-size descriptions and omitted Spring split information reduce clarity, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in technical completeness and validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same correlation-sampling and cascaded optical-flow research despite the title change. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, figures, and code listings support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments with the revised sampler, Charge and Kubric-8K evaluations, and additional inference-strategy analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original sampling-pattern measurements, runtime and memory benchmarks, component ablations, and optical-flow evaluations on Charge, Spring, Sintel, and KITTI.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list shift from temporal differencing, dimensionality constraints and two new metrics toward complementary Td/Tcl mechanisms and foreground-focused continuous motion. Metrics cease to be a headline contribution, and MSE is attributed to prior evaluation protocols. The central joint-policy-learning and zero-shot-transfer claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 interprets dimensional expansion as introducing noise and motivates limiting motion size; v2 argues that Tcl structures the representation and permits scaling. S-PCFC receives a controlled, motion-centric applicability qualification. Section 6 replaces the explicit gap to fully labeled training and proposed temporal supervision with discussion of modest task-specific policy gains, fine-manipulation benchmarks, and occlusion-related multi-frame/multi-view extensions.

D1.justification: v2 adds a promised project-code address, explicit per-source video counts, the contrastive temporal-offset range, and autoregressive MSE/cross-entropy training details. Appendix A.6 specifies the new absolute-action encodings. Most existing hardware and policy hyperparameters remain documented, while v1's explicit 2,000-video metric-analysis count is omitted. The PDFs do not establish that code has been released.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained datasets, v2 evaluates RoboTwin dual-arm and EgoVLA humanoid absolute-action prediction. Real-world coverage expands from three to five tasks, adding drawer closing and pouring, replacing combined drawer-opening-and-placement with opening alone, and revising the insertion task.

E2.justification: The LIBERO comparison adds Dynamo and explicitly includes GR00T, corresponding to the retained pre-quantized baseline, while removing DP with five times the labeled data. RGB-Diff disappears from simulation ablations; Tcl-only variants and a naive continuous real-world comparator are added. O2-Fea/Future features and w/o. VQ/Con. are renamed counterparts.

E3.justification: v2 standardizes encoder training on out-of-domain Internet videos, replacing in-domain LIBERO/CALVIN training in the main ablations. The reported CALVIN encoder budget changes from 150,000 to 50,000 steps. The discrete codebook changes from 128 to 8 for LIBERO/real-world experiments, and real-world demonstrations increase from 20 robot plus 20 human trajectories to 25 plus 25 per task.

E4.justification: v2 adds separate Td/Tcl component tests, absolute-action prediction ablations, and cross-environment FDM visualizations diagnosing background leakage and foreground accuracy. Dimension scaling is reexamined through 512 dimensions. The RGB-versus-feature-difference analysis and v1's human-motion cosine-similarity case study are removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports CALVIN means and standard deviations over the last three epochs; v2 reports point estimates without that aggregation description. Deviations also disappear from the LIBERO comparison table. However, the LIBERO ablation table retains uncertainty values and the stated three-run reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced: v1 reports LIBERO averages of 80.8 in-domain and 81.8 with Internet training, versus 80.1 in v2; CALVIN changes from 2.848 to 3.070, with 3.247 at 512 dimensions. These use changed methods/settings, so they are not matched performance gains. New embodiment and real-world results are added. v2 Table 1 also contains an inconsistent discrete S-PCFC average: 0.4810 despite four negative suite values.

M1.justification: v2 adds temporal contrastive learning to the existing temporal-difference IDM/FDM. Nearby-future embeddings form positive pairs and temporally reversed embeddings form negatives; an InfoNCE objective supplements reconstruction and perceptual losses. This materially changes representation learning, while the joint diffusion/autoregressive policy framework remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, mechanism explanation, experimental questions, findings and limitations are extensively rewritten. Metrics move from Method Section 3.3 to Experiments Section 4.2.2; Internet training receives a separate subsection. Appendices move before references and gain Sections A.5–A.6. Terminology is revised throughout.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is redrawn around Td/Tcl; the metric diagram, cosine-similarity illustration and execution montage are removed. New FDM visualizations, redesigned scaling plots, expanded comparison tables, and updated task/hardware photographs substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning by distinguishing CoMo from action-supervised continuous IDMs, including CLAM, and continuous world models such as AdaWorld and DreamDojo. It adds related work including UniVLA, VILLA-X and Dynamo, while removing older discussion of 3D policy approaches. These changes go beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 introduces mathematical definitions of three pairwise similarities and their temporal contrastive objective in Equations 1–4. The S-PCFC definition remains equivalent. Neither version provides formal theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: The contrastive objective and its component/scaling tests provide stronger support for addressing v1's dimensionality limitation, while new embodiment tests strengthen applicability evidence. These gains are tempered by loss of CALVIN uncertainty reporting and the LIBERO full-data reference, together with v2 Table 1's inconsistent S-PCFC average. The added evidence supports a net improvement, but the reporting regressions limit its extent.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoMo research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original simulation experiments, five-task Franka evaluations, component ablations, and dual-arm/humanoid action-prediction results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LIBERO and CALVIN experiments, representation analyses, and three-task Franka robot evaluations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same claims about continuous latent motion, mitigating shortcut learning, zero-shot pseudo-label generation and unified policy learning.

C2.justification: The explanations of Td/Tcl synergy and the relationship between representation metrics and policy performance remain unchanged. Section 6 retains the same applicability qualifications and limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix A and Tables 6–8 retain identical hardware, data-processing, architecture and training details. Code availability and access information are unchanged.

E1.justification: Both retain SAM-V, EgoVid and Droid training data, and the same LIBERO, CALVIN, Franka, RoboTwin and EgoVLA evaluation coverage. No tasks or test scenarios are added or removed.

E2.justification: Table 3 renames GR00T to GR00T-like without changing its scores or comparator membership. Section 4.2.3 already describes incorporating comparator designs into the shared diffusion policy in both versions.

E3.justification: Evaluation settings remain identical, including 10 labeled trajectories per LIBERO task, CALVIN ABC→D evaluation, real-world demonstration budgets and rollout counts, and the appendix training configurations.

E4.justification: The same component ablations, latent-dimension scaling analysis, embodiment comparisons and FDM visualization studies are retained. The Table 1 summary-value correction does not introduce or redesign an analysis.

E5.justification: Both retain three LIBERO evaluation runs and mean/standard-deviation reporting. No run counts, uncertainty-reporting practices or statistical procedures change.

E6.justification: Table 1 changes the discrete baseline's average S-PCFC from 0.4810 to -0.0678. The four unchanged suite values (-0.0501, -0.1521, -0.0649 and -0.0040) average to -0.067775, supporting the correction. Other results and rankings remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The temporal difference mechanism, temporal contrastive loss, IDM–FDM architecture and unified diffusion/autoregressive policy procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Table 3 changes the name GR00T to GR00T-like, and the first-page arXiv version/date stamp is updated. The remaining prose, terminology and document organization are unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 3 receives a limited displayed row-label refinement from GR00T to GR00T-like. Figure designs, captions, table structures and page layout remain unchanged; the number-only correction in Table 1 is assessed under E6.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion and all 85 references are unchanged. GR00T-like clarifies a table label consistently with the adaptation already documented, without substantively revising research positioning.

T1.justification: The contrastive-loss equations and mathematical definition of S-PCFC remain identical. No formal assumptions, derivations or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: v3 fixes an internally inconsistent Table 1 average and clarifies that the Table 3 comparator is GR00T-like, matching the existing implementation description. These changes provide a limited improvement in numerical accuracy and clarity while leaving the methods, evidence coverage and conclusions unchanged.

A1.justification: Both complete 17-page PDFs describe the same CoMo work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and Appendix A.1–A.6 are readable and directly comparable.

after.justification: v3 retains these original simulation, real-world and representation-analysis results, including the appendix visualizations.

before.justification: v2 reports original LIBERO and CALVIN experiments, real-world Franka evaluations, and dual-arm/humanoid analyses in Tables 1–5, with additional qualitative results in Appendix A.5.

token_usage.accounting_note: Input totals include cached input; output totals include reasoning output. These subsets are not added again. Totals cover reported usage only; unknown or launched attempts without usage may still have consumed tokens. Finalized known pre-launch failures are counted as not launched.

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds VGBench as the first dedicated visual-geometry benchmark, the 28K SpatialScore collection and Hard subset, and SpatialAgent. V2 redefines the central contributions around a curated 30-task benchmark, the 331K SpatialCorpus training resource, and complementary fine-tuning and expanded agent approaches. VGBench and SpatialScore-Hard cease to be separately claimed contributions.

C2.justification: V2 attributes larger fine-tuning gains on Repurpose to training-distribution alignment, discusses potential forgetting and uneven task improvements, and adds limitations concerning SpatialCorpus diversity. It also interprets measured failure rates as evidence of ReAct's greater stability. The RGB-input and rudimentary-toolbox limitations already existed in v1; their relocation to Section 7 is not a new limitation.

D1.justification: V2 documents the new fine-tuning recipe: one epoch, batch size 512, learning rate 1e-5, 3% warm-up, and a frozen visual encoder. It expands construction templates, distractor rules, scoring prompts, and tool specifications, and reports eight rather than four A100 GPUs. Explicit code and dataset links are added, although the PDFs do not establish actual resource availability.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from 11 integrated datasets to 23, adding tasks such as maze navigation, paper folding, mental rotation, velocity estimation, and size compatibility. V2 also introduces real-world and simulated training coverage through SpatialCorpus. Geometry tasks persist within the repurposed data; that component adds Omni3D and PointOdyssey and stops sourcing ScanNet.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparators including Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, SpaceThinker, and SpaceR, while Cambrian-8B and SpatialBot-Phi2 disappear from the quantitative comparisons. Proprietary comparisons shift from GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Haiku, and Gemini-2.0-Flash to newer systems. Human, random, and text-only baselines are also added.

E3.justification: V1's 28,093 samples and 1,400-sample Hard subset give way to 5,025 samples selected using text-only filtering and manual verification. SpatialScore numerical scoring changes from factor-two tolerance to MRA with parser/LLM score averaging; MRA already appeared in v1's separate VSI-Bench evaluation. Video sampling changes from eight frames by default to 32 for open models and 16/8 for proprietary models. The agent token limit increases from 2,048 to 4,096.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Figure 4 cases, v2 adds annotation-error examples (Figure 5), analyses of fine-tuning versus agent generalization across OpenSource and Repurpose subsets (Appendix C.1), quantitative reasoning-failure analysis (Appendix B.3), and new qualitative cases (Figures 9–10). These provide substantial new evidence about data quality, distribution dependence, and agent reliability.

E5.justification: Both versions specify a fixed random seed and deterministic decoding. Neither reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's human-participant count and agent failure percentages do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and source-dataset result tables are replaced by results for the redesigned benchmark and new training/agent comparisons. For example, v2 Table 3 reports Qwen3-VL-8B scores of 45.48 zero-shot, 54.71 after fine-tuning, and 53.81 with ReAct; Table 2 adds human performance of 86.60. These are newly reported results under revised conditions, not direct gains over v1's scores.

M1.justification: V2 adds supervised fine-tuning on SpatialCorpus using cross-entropy, absent from v1. SpatialAgent retains Plan-Execute and ReAct but substantially changes its toolbox: Rex-Omni replaces OWLv2 localization and supports counting, while DetAny3D and MapAnything add 3D detection and metric-distance capabilities (Sections 3.2–3.4).

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution narrative, and substantial portions of the main text are rewritten. Baseline evaluation moves into the benchmark section, methodology is reorganized around two improvement approaches, limitations move into the main text, and six appendix sections are reorganized into three. This exceeds renaming or routine editing.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview, construction pipeline, toolbox diagram, and dataset-flow visualization. Result tables adopt new task columns, grouping, rankings, and highlighting; benchmark-comparison, annotation-error, and additional qualitative displays are added. Figure 4 is substantially retained and relocated, while the document typography, prompt boxes, and page layout are extensively reformatted.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands engagement with recent spatial benchmarks, training approaches, and perception tools, including SpatialEval, OmniSpatial, SPAR-Bench, MMSI-Bench, Rex-Omni, and MapAnything. The new benchmark-comparison Table 1 and revised related work position the contribution as a comprehensive evaluation and improvement framework, replacing the earlier emphasis on VGBench's visual-geometry novelty.

T1.justification: The Plan-Execute and ReAct mathematical formulations remain equivalent apart from notation and explicit backbone bookkeeping. Neither version develops theorems or proofs. V2's standard fine-tuning description and MRA scoring instructions add method and evaluation documentation rather than substantive mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evaluation validity through annotation-error auditing, visual-dependence filtering, full-set manual verification, and explicit human/text-only controls, addressing weaknesses left open in v1. Detailed fine-tuning experiments, source-dependent generalization analysis, and quantified agent failures also deepen the evidence beyond headline accuracy. These gains outweigh the loss of source-by-source result tables. Some reporting inconsistencies remain: Appendix C.1 uses 48.72 as the starting point for an agent improvement, although Table 6 identifies that as the fine-tuned score and gives 42.97 for zero-shot.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpatialScore/SpatialAgent research project, and their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison. The redesigned benchmark and protocols limit direct score comparisons, rather than document comparability.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations, human and text-only controls, supervised fine-tuning results, SpatialAgent comparisons, and additional subset and failure analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of MLLMs and SpatialAgent on VGBench, SpatialScore, and SpatialScore-Hard, with additional source-dataset results in Appendix F.

C1.justification: The central benchmark, training-corpus, and training-free agent contributions remain unchanged, as do claims about persistent spatial-intelligence limitations. The abstract and conclusion update the reported evaluation count from 40 to 49 models, reflecting expanded supporting evidence rather than a new central claim.

C2.justification: Section 2.3 qualifies the earlier characterization of spatial fine-tuning by explicitly recognizing VST's substantial improvements. Appendix B.3 adds a practical feasibility explanation based on CPU offloading and single-A100 execution. The existing limitations concerning RGB inputs, training-data coverage, and tool reliability remain.

D1.justification: v3 discloses five curation volunteers, an intermediate pool of 8,793 samples, and selection criteria. Appendix B clarifies identical baseline prompts, OpenCV-assisted human evaluation, and GPU/CPU deployment details. The title page adds checkpoint and SpatialCorpus access links. These are documentation and access additions, without evidence of changed underlying training or agent procedures.

E1.justification: Both versions retain SpatialScore's 5,025 examples across 30 tasks and SpatialCorpus's 330,802 training examples across 16 tasks, with the same source datasets and modality types. Revised modality counts and additional prompting settings do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 substantially expands specialist comparisons with SpatialThinker-3B/7B, VST-3B/7B in SFT and RL variants, Spatial-MLLM-4B, and SpatialReasoner-8B: eight added configurations, with none removed. Table 3 also adds one-, two-, and four-shot Qwen3-VL comparisons for both model sizes.

E3.justification: v3 adds one-, two-, and four-shot evaluation using randomly selected, pre-allocated category examples, plus tool profiling with Qwen3-VL-8B under Plan-Execute. Table 5 revises single-/multi-image counts from 2,826/1,006 to 2,493/1,339; this does not establish dataset replacement or rerunning. Existing accuracy/MRA scoring, frame budgets, and fine-tuning settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 3 adds a focused analysis of performance with different numbers of in-context examples. Appendix B.3 and new Table 6 examine inference overhead and tool invocation frequency. Existing failure-rate analyses, subset comparisons, and qualitative case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B.1 newly specifies that the human baseline averages the scores of the already-described three PhD evaluators. This clarifies statistical aggregation without establishing additional evaluations. Fixed-seed and deterministic model evaluation practices remain unchanged, with no added confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: New Table 2 results make VST-3B-RL (48.04) and VST-7B-RL (52.47) their groups' leaders. Table 3 adds few-shot results, including four-shot scores of 46.59/49.00 for 4B/8B. Appendix B.3 newly reports 0.9/5.4/9.3 seconds per sample for base/Plan-Execute/ReAct and per-tool costs. This substantially expands reported findings; shared accuracy values and appendix subset results are unchanged.

M1.justification: The supervised fine-tuning procedure, Plan-Execute and ReAct workflows, and spatial toolbox remain unchanged. The appendix training settings, agent prompts, and tool specifications match. Few-shot prompting is added as a comparison setting, not a proposed method component.

P1.justification: There are localized additions to curation, evaluation, and efficiency explanations, along with cross-reference wording and affiliation edits. The section hierarchy, overall narrative, and most existing prose remain intact; there is no extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: Tables 2 and 3 expand to accommodate new comparisons, and a computational-overhead table is introduced as Table 6. Existing appendix Tables 6–7 become Tables 7–8 and relocate. Figures retain their content, with surrounding material reflowing within the same overall visual design.

R1.justification: Seven references are added: Cosmos, SpatialThinker, VersaViT, LAMRA, Satori-R1, SVQA-R1, and OmniStream. These modestly broaden the research context without restructuring the paper's positioning. Publication-venue updates for existing references do not represent additional cited works.

T1.justification: The mathematical problem formulation and agent equations (1–8) are unchanged, as is the appendix MRA scoring formula. No new assumptions, propositions, proofs, or derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens comparative evidence through specialist baselines and few-shot controls, appropriately qualifies its fine-tuning interpretation to acknowledge VST, and exposes inference costs in Appendix B.3. Clearer curation details and resource links also improve reproducibility. These are useful incremental gains; the benchmark, proposed methods, and retained experimental findings remain substantially unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpatialScore, SpatialCorpus, and SpatialAgent study. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding figures, tables, equations, and supplementary material can be matched despite pagination changes.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and additionally reports specialist-model evaluations, few-shot comparisons, and computational measurements in Appendix B.3.

before.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations, supervised fine-tuning and SpatialAgent experiments in Tables 2–3, with additional quantitative results and case studies in Appendix C.

C1.justification: The central dataset, benchmark, and multi-frame spatial-learning contributions remain intact. v2's introduction additionally claims comparability with specialized 3D perception models, scalability with trainable parameters, and preservation of general abilities. It also adds a first-time novelty claim for observing spatial emergence, extending the existing contribution framing.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning the importance of vision-encoder tuning, the proposed orthogonality of spatial and general capabilities, and depth/correspondence as more fundamental spatial tasks. SpatialRGPT's results motivate a new claim about failure of single-image supervision to transfer. The limitations now acknowledge extra-frame generalization evidence while retaining the need for training beyond pairs.

D1.justification: Table 7 newly discloses task-wise corpus counts, while Appendices H–L document configurations and sample counts for added experiments. Existing code listings, core hyperparameters, and hardware details remain. v2 removes v1's project-page link and Appendix B's pointer to complete templates; the PDFs do not establish whether actual resource availability changed.

E1.justification: v2 expands held-out evaluation to synthetic indoor views rendered from 3RScan, spatial and embodied reasoning in CVBench-3D and ERQA, and broader general VQA coverage through MMMU, MME, and MMVet. Appendix L also tests camera-direction prediction with additional intermediate images, extending evaluation beyond image pairs.

E2.justification: Tables 2 and 3 remove InternVL-13B and add SpatialRGPT to the MultiSPA and BLINK comparisons; 13B remains in other experiments. Appendix I additionally evaluates VGGT for camera-vector prediction, Depth Anything for depth comparison, and LoFTR for image matching, substantially broadening the comparator set.

E3.justification: The default training setup and MultiSPA scoring rules are retained. New protocols vary trainable components and full versus LoRA tuning, normalize scale for the VGGT comparison, test 1K correspondence examples with 50K auxiliary-task examples, compare 400K-example auxiliary-task additions, and insert 1–4 intermediate frames. These are additional experimental settings, not evidence that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's scaling, pooled multi-task, and Easy/Hard correspondence studies, v2 adds component-tuning ablations (Table 8), task-specific transfer analyses (Tables 12–13), a forgetting curve throughout training (Figure 6), and robustness to additional input frames (Table 14). These investigate previously untested sources of gains and failure concerns.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The statement about using different random seeds to sample image pairs is retained and does not constitute new experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The retained model's MultiSPA and BLINK averages remain 56.11 and 84.3. v2 adds extensive results, including a 66.72 fully tuned average in Table 8, 18.7/27.7 accuracy for 8B/26B on 3RScan, and scale-normalized VGGT-versus-ours scores of 86 versus 82 in Table 9. Figure 4 adds a full-tuning result near 72%; v1's reported 44% used a different tuning configuration, so this is not a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The data-generation algorithms, architecture, objectives, and default InternVL2-8B LoRA procedure remain unchanged. The original appendix algorithms and Listings 1–4 are retained. Newly evaluated component-unfreezing and full-fine-tuning configurations are experimental variants rather than new proposed algorithmic components.

P1.justification: There are localized rewrites of the abstract, introduction, related work, and scaling discussion, plus author/header edits. The appendix gains sections H–L and moves the limitations from H to M. Most existing prose, the main section sequence, algorithms, and dataset examples are retained.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the opening page, placing Figure 1 above a two-column abstract/introduction arrangement. Figure 4 is redrawn with a logarithmic data axis and explicit LoRA/full-tuning curves. Tables 7–14 and the forgetting plot are added, and existing tables are repositioned. The original appendix example figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including VLM-3R, Spatial-MLLM, OST-Bench, and the newly evaluated expert models and benchmarks. Flamingo, ShareGPT4V, and ShareGPT4o references disappear with shortened training-background discussion. Positioning expands toward specialist-model comparability and emergence novelty, while the principal distinction from single-image spatial methods and SAT remains.

T1.justification: The projection, visibility, overlap, and rotation definitions in Equations 1–8 retain their mathematical content. Section 3.3's explicit inequality restates the existing 20% relative L2-error criterion. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The expert comparisons, additional domain and benchmark evaluations, component/task ablations, and extra-frame tests substantially strengthen evidence for the central claims and address important gaps in v1's validation. Appendices H–L also clarify what drives performance. Removed resource pointers and some overbroad interpretations are drawbacks: for example, the introduction claims no degradation despite Table 11 showing MMVet falling from 62.0 to 58.1. These issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Multi-SpatialMLLM and MultiSPA. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison; retained material can be matched across reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds expert-model comparisons, additional benchmark evaluations, and training and robustness analyses in Appendices H–L.

before.justification: v1 reports original MultiSPA, BLINK, and general VQA evaluations, scaling and multi-task experiments, and robotics demonstrations in Section 4.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding contribution statement retain the same central claims: DTR uses KV-cache optimization to defend against multimodal jailbreaks while preserving utility and efficiency, with a claimed first application of this approach to multimodal safety. The added evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v3 develops substantial new interpretations about refusal directions being intrinsic and universal, visual reweighting protecting against textual attacks, robustness to RSS-targeting adversaries, and the necessity of dynamic rather than uniform scaling. The conclusion removes v1's reference-data limitation and adds combining DTR with decoding defenses as future work. Some new interpretations exceed their evidence, including the VLGuard metric confusion and inconsistent accuracy judgments in Table 14.

D1.justification: The replication link changes from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository, and v3 explicitly identifies the regularization norm. New experiments document reference-mixture counts, the adaptive perturbation budget, sample selection, and judge model. Core implementation disclosures, including AdamW, learning rate, iteration count, and H100 hardware, remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 adds VLGuard evaluation with unsafe-image/harmful-text and safe-image/harmful-text subsets. It also uses six additional reference corpora: Dolly-15K, GPT4All, Open-Orca/FLAN, StrongREJECT, JBB-Behaviors, and HarmBench. These substantially broaden the evaluated data sources and attack coverage while retaining the original benchmarks.

E2.justification: AdaShield, JailGuard, CoCA, and ShiftDC retain their original comparison membership. Appendix B.8 newly compares DTR against uniform visual-token scaling at four fixed values, but this additional comparator is evaluated through a single benign-image case study.

E3.justification: v3 adds Llama-4-Scout-17B evaluation, VLGuard subsets of 1,023 and 977 queries, and controlled reference-mixture and cross-category protocols. Appendix B.7 introduces RSS-minimizing PGD with an L-infinity budget of 16/255 on the first 50 HADES samples, using GPT-5.2 and a harmfulness score. These are substantial additional protocols; Appendix A's original defaults and benchmark selections remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test layer selection, learning-rate sensitivity, reference-source robustness, cross-category transfer, stronger defense-aware attacks, and uniform versus dynamic reweighting (Appendices B.2-B.5 and B.7-B.8). The original reference-count, optimization-step, lambda, eviction, and token-nulling analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 3.2 newly reports multiple independent trials of random reference sampling and describes their variance as minimal. It supplies no trial count, seeds, or numerical uncertainty, so this is additional reporting rather than evidence of an increased run count. Figure 3's shaded variability bands already appear in v1.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results are retained, including the relocated MME and lambda tables. Substantial new results include Llama-4-Scout HADES S+T+A ASR of 11.2% without DTR versus 8.4% with DTR, and adaptive-attack ASR of 68% versus 18% in the new 50-query setting. VLGuard, sensitivity, reference-transfer, and uniform-scaling results are also added; these are new evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The refusal-direction estimator, reversal safety-relevant shift, regularized token-weight optimization, clipping, early stopping, and token eviction remain unchanged, as does Algorithm 1. Specifying the regularizer's L2 norm in v3 Equation 8 clarifies the previously unspecified norm; it does not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The title changes, citations become numeric, and v3 adds subsection headings and acknowledgements, condenses some explanatory passages, and revises the conclusion. The appendix gains interleaved subsections, but the original narrative order and most existing prose remain recognizable; much of the expansion is new scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main document from single-column to two-column layout, extensively resizing and repositioning displays. Figure 5 changes from a two-by-two arrangement to one row, and eight tables plus a uniform-reweighting figure are added. The retained MME table also corrects category and total placement without changing its numerical values.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for the new model and reference datasets, plus COSMIC and cross-language refusal-direction research to support its universality discussion. The existing related-work organization and positioning of DTR relative to jailbreak defenses and KV-cache optimization remain largely intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and optimization formulation remain substantively equivalent. Splitting the mean-activation equation, renumbering equations, and explicitly identifying the L2 norm do not introduce new mathematical reasoning. The universality discussion cites other work and adds empirical interpretation, without a new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: The reference-transfer, sensitivity, and explicit adaptive-attack experiments address gaps in v1 and strengthen support for the unchanged method. The gains are limited by the small adaptive evaluation and reporting inconsistencies: Section 5.2 calls Table 9's 66.5%-to-7.4% refusal-heuristic change a harmfulness reduction, although harmfulness changes from 4.7% to 3.1%. Table 14 also labels a fire-extinguisher detail as a hallucination for uniform scaling but accurate for DTR. These weaknesses temper the otherwise useful expansion of evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DTR research, with matching core methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and layout.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds model evaluations, VLGuard results, reference-transfer studies, stronger adaptive attacks, and a uniform-reweighting comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack-success, benign-task performance, runtime, sensitivity, and token-reweighting experiments in Section 5 and Appendix B.

C1.justification: The introduction newly claims the first fixed-point convergence proof for a diffusion-based posterior optimization method and presents latent-space inference as an achieved contribution. These substantially extend v1's contribution scope, while the abstract's image-quality, noise-robustness, consistency, and speed claims remain largely unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 explains why residuals near zero are preferable to deviations in either direction, distinguishes asymptotic convergence assumptions from the practical finite schedule, and discusses latent data-consistency tradeoffs. It removes latent diffusion from future-work limitations. Appendix D additionally interprets existing confidence intervals as evidence of practical fixed-point uniqueness, an inference not made in v1.

D1.justification: v2 supplies latent model sources, Algorithm 2, and detailed latent hyperparameters in Tables 5–6. New Appendix I documents baseline configuration sources, official implementations, and the main comparison budgets: DDiff-1k throughout versus DAPS-1k for linear and DAPS-4k for nonlinear tasks. These budget disclosures do not establish changes to previously used settings.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate FFHQ and ImageNet at 256×256 on the same eight restoration tasks and retain the same measurement-noise scenarios. The new latent experiments cover seven existing tasks; they introduce a model configuration rather than new data or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated DMPlug, DCDP, DDRM, and RED-diff rows on task-specific subsets, alongside retained DAPS, DPS, and DiffPIR. New Table 3 compares LatentDDiff against LatentDAPS, PSLD on linear tasks, and ReSample. PnP-DM is discussed but is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: v2 adds a substantial latent-model evaluation configuration using unconditional LDM-VQ4 models, PIXEL-DC, and task-specific step-size and threshold settings. The existing 100-image, sigma=0.05 evaluation remains. Appendix H also changes the stated DDPM noise formula from alpha to cumulative alpha-bar; this documents a formula correction without establishing that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds a brief qualitative comparison of latent-space and pixel-space data consistency, reporting better quality and efficiency for PIXEL-DC without paired scores or timings. The original dual/noising ablation in Table 2, noise studies, runtime-quality curves, and supplementary qualitative cases are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals over 100 validation images, best-of-five phase-retrieval results, and fixed degradation seeds for selected tasks. Changed interval values are results changes. Appendix D adds an interpretation concerning independent initializations, but documents no new repeated-run design or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline results and the latent results in Table 3, and revises existing entries. In Table 1, DDiff's FFHQ phase-retrieval residual changes from 1.4690 to 0.0040, DAPS's ImageNet super-resolution residual from 0.2871 to 0.0047, and DPS's ImageNet Gaussian-deblurring PSNR from 23.07 to 21.07. These are reported revisions, not established performance gains from rerunning unchanged experiments.

M1.justification: v1 treats latent diffusion as future work. v2 introduces LatentDDiff in Section 3.3 and Appendix C, with encoder–decoder operations, latent denoising, re-encoding, and alternative LATENT-DC and PIXEL-DC updates in Algorithm 2. The original pixel-space Algorithm 1 is retained.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative order survive. v2 corrects terminology and cross-references, condenses Discussion into Conclusion, removes the generic Broader Impact statement, and organizes supplementary material into Appendices A–J. Much of the expansion is new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting of retained material.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with substantial resizing and relocation of figures and tables. Table 1 gains comparator rows, Table 3 adds latent results, and hyperparameter tables are restructured to include both model families. Existing supplementary image panels are retained and enlarged, becoming Figures 6–13.

R1.justification: The central ADMM-versus-HQS positioning is retained. v2 adds references to half-quadratic regularization, latent diffusion, DMPlug, and PnP-DM, and introduces a first-convergence-proof novelty claim. Previously cited latent methods now contextualize an implemented extension instead of future work; the surrounding related-work discussion remains largely intact.

T1.justification: New Appendix A introduces formal assumptions, six lemmas, and Theorem 1 establishing conditional asymptotic convergence, including vanishing and summable schedules and boundedness requirements. v1 contains update derivations and the DiffPIR equivalence but no convergence theorem. Appendix B also adds a formal posterior-expectation statement for the residual.

improvement.justification: Broader baseline comparisons, latent experiments, and implementation disclosures provide substantial benefits. However, new material introduces important ambiguities: Algorithm 2 uses the same dual variable in pixel-space subtraction and latent-space updates without defining a conversion; Appendix D infers initialization stability and practical uniqueness from confidence intervals over different images. Revised results also introduce an inconsistency: DAPS's FFHQ box-inpainting PSNR is 24.12 in Table 1 but 24.52 in Table 4. These reproducibility and evidential problems prevent a reliable judgment that the additions produce a net overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Dual Ascent Diffusion for Inverse Problems by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluated baselines and latent-diffusion experiments in Table 3.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-restoration experiments, baseline comparisons, noise-robustness and runtime studies, ablations, and appendix confidence intervals.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a semantically aligned MLLM-generated misinformation benchmark and an efficient AMD framework for detection, grounding and generalization. v2 adds numerical highlights to the abstract and contribution list, but these substantiate retained claims rather than introduce a different core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies dataset difficulty through size-controlled comparisons, explains limited transfer to untampered but mismatched COSMOS pairs, and discusses persistent FA&TF/TF failures and possible retrieval-based remedies (Appendices C, H and M). This substantially expands the interpretation beyond v1's brief celebrity-face scope limitation and general performance discussion.

D1.justification: Appendices D–E add full prompts, coordinate conventions, baseline adaptations, hardware, image preprocessing, batch size, optimizer, learning-rate schedule and training duration. Appendix L documents head-shot sourcing and filtering. v1 supplied mainly the backbone, frozen encoder and token count. Both versions still promise future code release.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands beyond MDSM and DGM4 to COSMOS, MiRAGe, DiFF and DiffFace, plus diffusion-based face editing, background modification and full-image generation (Appendices H–I). v2 also evaluates missing-modality and non-aligned inputs and introduces a human participant study.

E2.justification: Table 9 adds fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-3B and -7B comparisons on MDSM; v1 evaluated Qwen2.5-VL only zero-shot. This is a focused comparator addition. The original ViLT, HAMMER, HAMMER++, FKA-Owl and zero-shot comparator rows remain.

E3.justification: New designs include a 100-pair study with 15 volunteers, size-matched dataset comparisons including a 103k-sample Guardian subset, cross-dataset transfer, and two-epoch LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen models (Appendices A, C, G–J). Newly disclosed settings for the retained AMD experiments do not establish that their protocols changed.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and cross-MLLM analyses, v2 tests token length, knowledge-preservation strategies, TRP placement, modality removal and semantic alignment. It adds corpus analysis, diffusion robustness tests, token visualizations and concrete failure cases (Tables 5–8 and 11–15; Figures 5 and 11–14).

E5.justification: Appendix K.2 newly specifies averaging token representations over 100 samples per group, with three independent groups per manipulation class, to reduce sampling randomness. This is limited statistical aggregation for visualizations. Neither version reports training seeds, repeated-training variability, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results, but v2 adds extensive outcomes in Tables 5–15 and new figures. For example, Table 9 reports 72.00 average ACC for NYT-trained Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and Table 10 reports AMD's 54.08 average cross-dataset ACC. These are newly reported experiments, not improvements to the original scores.

M1.justification: AMD retains artifact tokens, frozen pre-perception encoding, manipulation-oriented reasoning, auxiliary losses, TRP and textual inference. The fuller prompts and dataset-construction descriptions document existing procedures rather than establish a changed method. Diffusion and non-alignment variants serve as experimental conditions.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the explanatory material: dataset construction is rewritten by manipulation category, related work is expanded, quantitative discussion is condensed, and experimental setup moves into a structured A–M appendix with a contents list. The method and conclusion remain largely verbatim.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is revised and placed before the abstract, Figure 2 is extensively redrawn, and Table 1 gains a dataset row and training-support column. New Figures 5–14 and Tables 5–15 add visualizations, comparisons and cases, substantially expanding the presentation beyond relocation or numerical edits.

R1.justification: Related work adds a focused comparison with MMFakeBench and elaborates FKA-Owl's task and computational limitations. Supporting references expand to diffusion benchmarks, corpus tools, visualization and celebrity resources. The principal positioning around semantically aligned, MLLM-driven misinformation remains intact.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation and Equations 1–10 are retained, including attention pooling, auxiliary objectives and TRP. The appendices add empirical analyses and metric explanations, without new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or substantive derivations.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked human validation, evaluation beyond MDSM/DGM4 and substantial reproduction details. v2 addresses these gaps with human evaluation, size and alignment controls, fine-tuned comparators, transfer tests, failure analysis and detailed prompts/settings. These additions substantially strengthen empirical scrutiny and reproducibility. Some new reporting is imprecise—for example, Appendix G calls Table 9's domain-average accuracies in-domain—and performance uncertainty remains unquantified, but these limitations do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MDSM dataset and AMD framework. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no separate appendix; v2 includes readable appendices A–M.

C1.justification: The introduction's quantitative empirical contribution shifts from standalone superiority on ten-task ImageNet-R to average integration gains across three datasets and both task splits. The central claims of geometry-aware exemplar-free regularization, quadratic Sylvester computation, and compatibility with existing CL methods remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds qualifications about averaging losing fine-grained variation and the computational cost of non-diagonal A. It removes v1's explicit warning that Inf-SSM+ violates orbit invariance and drops the CKD-based discussion of data-dependent need to regularize B. Algorithm 1 clarifies frozen previous-model parameters and updates. Conversely, v2 removes CUB-200 hyperparameter columns, L2P pool-size/prompt-length/top-k values, and the reservoir-sampling description. These documentation changes do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256, and CUB-200-2011, with class-incremental learning under exemplar-free and replay settings. Additional integrations use already represented datasets and tasks; Vim-tiny changes model configuration rather than dataset or task coverage.

For existing ImageNet-R LUCIR integrations, Appendix J changes the reported Inf-SSM coefficient from 10 to 500 for five tasks and from 1500 to 1000 for ten tasks. These are reported setting revisions, without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds evidence about information retained by different averaging axes (Table 5), practical CL latency (Table 3), and sensitivity to model size (Appendix H.5). It removes v1's CKD-over-tasks analysis and Figure 3, while retaining layerwise CKD, block-count ablations, and distance-computation simulations. The Inf-SSM+ comparison is retained and regrouped.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seeds 0, 10, and 100 and report classification results with standard deviations. The 10,000-iteration Monte Carlo studies and their correlation, p-value, and variability reporting are retained. Additional tables follow existing reporting practices; no new confidence-interval or significance-testing procedure is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds integration results on CIFAR-100 and Caltech-256, CLFD/UCL results, Vim-tiny scores, variance measurements, and CL latency measurements.
