The new 8.31% AA and 9.36% FM integration averages agree with the expanded Table 1.

M1.justification: Appendix D.5 corrects the computation for nearly identical states from cos(theta)=0 to cos(theta)=1. The core observability regularizer, channel averaging, and Gram-matrix computation remain unchanged. Inf-SSM+ is retained in Appendix H.4 rather than removed. The PDFs do not establish whether the computational correction changed the implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, SSM preliminaries, method motivation, related work, and experimental narrative undergo extensive rewriting. Integration results lead the revised evaluation; Inf-SSM+ moves to the appendix, limitations and conclusions are combined, and Appendix J gains structured subsections. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned into a multi-panel summary, Figure 2 moves from the appendix to the main text, and a new orbit illustration becomes Figure 3. The taskwise CKD figure is removed. Results tables are expanded, merged, relocated, and reformatted, including moving v1 Table 1 to v2 Table 6 and separating Inf-SSM+ results into Table 9.

R1.justification: v2 expands coverage of CL families and SSM applications, adding citations including UCL and CLFD. Appendix J.1 develops a substantial baseline-selection and exclusion rationale, positioning other Mamba CL approaches as scenario-specific future integration targets rather than direct comparators. Much of the earlier Mamba discussion is retained in Appendix F.2.

T1.justification: Appendix I replaces proofs restricted to equal principal angles with general multivariate expansions establishing local equivalence of three Grassmannian distances. Appendix C.2 corrects equality of observability matrices to equality of their spanned subspaces. Appendix D.5 also corrects the normalization denominator and the cosine value for matching states.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the integration claim by extending its evidence beyond ImageNet-R to all three main datasets and additional methods. It also repairs the restricted proofs in Appendix I, corrects the invariance statement, and replaces overstated integration averages with table-supported summaries. Lost tuning details and an overstrong interpretation of (A,C) sufficiency remain drawbacks, but the stronger validation and mathematical corrections provide a substantial overall quality improvement.

These substantially extend v1's masking, difficulty, city, and qualitative analyses. The original difficulty and city plots are retained as Figures A1–A2, not new experiments.

E6.justification: All shared numerical entries in Tables 2 and 3 remain unchanged. v3 adds the 7B results, training outcomes, and Tables A3–A7. For example, Table 4 reports 7B short/long accuracy increasing from 13.28%/7.12% to 26.22%/26.04% after fine-tuning. Table A5 shows English-alias improvements for every long-question comparison but declines in four of six short-question comparisons. Symbolic-input results use different conditions from visual evaluation.

Map Metadata is renamed Metro Data.

It explicitly contrasts ReasonMap with MapBench and V*Bench, adds geospatial benchmarks such as Geo-Bench, GeoReasoner, and GeoChain, and connects future work to localization, agentic vision, and embodied research. Earlier cited works are retained, including those with updated publication metadata.

T1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds a formal centered group-advantage definition and reward-weighted log-likelihood objective, Equations 1–2, for the new training baseline. v1 contains no corresponding training mathematics. The original scoring algorithms are retained, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's diagnostic value: symbolic-input and language controls test explanations that v1 largely discussed, scoring ablations examine metric sensitivity, and cross-city fine-tuning demonstrates use of the previously unused training partition. Added evaluation and annotation details also improve transparency. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including an overgeneralized English-language advantage despite mixed short-question results and inconsistent Doubao labels in Figure A3. The improvement rests on stronger validation and practical usefulness, rather than higher scores alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReasonMap benchmark despite the changed title. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding datasets, algorithms, tables, and relocated figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds fine-tuning experiments, symbolic-map evaluation, language substitutions, and scoring analyses. Table A7 separately identifies its OCRBench scores as collected from other works.

The three restoration tasks, 22-method benchmark and claim of inadequate clinical restoration quality remain.

Section 5.2 reinforces the existing restoration-versus-parsing mismatch using quantitative rankings. The domain-gap explanation and single-degradation restriction remain; revisions to v1 Appendix G's limitations cannot be checked.

D1.justification: v2 adds approximately 43,640 minutes of source-video duration and site-specific procedure/video-size information. Conversely, v1 provides an explicit repository URL and pretrained-weight/evaluation-code availability statement, while v2 only says that data and code are available without an access link. Core hardware and training hyperparameters remain documented identically.

E1.justification: v1 already covers gallbladder, bile duct, liver, pancreas and spleen procedures in Appendix B.3. v2 adds thoracoscopic lung, mediastinal and esophageal surgery and a second medical site, substantially broadening the represented population and imaging environments. Desmoking, defogging and desplashing remain the three restoration tasks.

E2.justification: The main 12 generic and 10 task-specific restoration methods, and the seven cross-dataset comparators, remain unchanged. Downstream parsing comparisons expand from the four restorers illustrated in v1 Figure 7 to all 12 generic methods in v2 Table 4, adding participation by methods such as MambaIRv2, Fourmer and SFHformer in that comparison.

The restoration metrics, 200,000-iteration budget, patch size, batch size and DesmokeData 761/200 split are retained.

E4.justification: v2 Table 4 substantially extends the previously qualitative downstream analysis by measuring whether restoration rankings translate into depth-estimation and parsing performance across 12 methods. Cross-dataset validation in Section 4.4 was already present in v1 Appendix E. Changes to v1's fine-grained analyses and Haze4K training-strategy ablation cannot be fully checked without v2's supplement.

E5.justification: The available benchmark results in both versions use point estimates without reported seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. However, v2's supplementary statistics are unavailable, including the counterpart to v1 Appendix B.3's patient-distribution summaries, preventing a reliable full-paper comparison of statistical reporting.

E6.justification: Table 3 replaces results across the enlarged dataset: the desmoking PSNR leader changes from AST at 18.630 to ConvIR at 19.432, and the desplashing leader from MambaIRv2 at 21.995 to X-Restormer at 22.317. These are results under different data conditions, not same-setting gains. v2 Table 4 also adds extensive depth and parsing measurements.

M1.justification: The documented procedure retains pre-degradation reference frames, PWC-Net optical-flow estimation, reference warping and the masked reconstruction loss in Equations 1-3. No new restoration architecture, loss or algorithmic component is introduced; the enlarged dataset and additional evaluations do not establish a method change.

Related work, downstream discussion and the conclusion are condensed or rewritten; cross-dataset validation moves from Appendix E into Section 4.4, and discussion and conclusion become separate sections. Much of the remaining prose and section sequence is retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explicit interpretation of the remaining trade-off: adversarial regularization can shift probability mass away from the clean manifold and reduce sample fidelity. It revises the gradient-component interpretation and explains sampling steps through attack strength versus collapse risk. The high-dimensional training limitation remains, while v1's misuse and safeguards discussion is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds GPU-hour estimates, per-epoch timing, explicit attack norms and AutoAttack components, and ImageNet preprocessing information. E4.justification: v1's five-setting gradient-weight ablation is replaced by four different configurations in v2 Table 6, changing the component controls and removing the classification-gradient-free case. v2 adds Figure 5, testing 1, 5, 10, and 20 adversarial sampling steps against performance, collapse, and runtime. The explicit perceptual-loss versus no-perceptual-loss comparison in v1 Table 3 disappears.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty across runs. Table 1 retains the same energy-difference mean and variance reporting; this describes sample distributions rather than experimental uncertainty.

E6.justification: Numerous results are replaced or added. Table 2's SADAJEM-based CIFAR-10 clean/PGD/AA results change from 92.28/66.12/64.76 to 90.39/68.76/66.30 under revised defaults; 66.30 AA already appeared for v1's perceptual-loss-free variant. Section 3.3 replaces perceptual-loss-based naturalness constraints with perturbation-set-constrained adversarial sampling and removes the LPIPS term. Default gradient weights change from (0.45, 0.05, 0.45) to (1, 1, 1). A perceptual-loss-free variant already appeared in v1, so this is a revision of the default procedure rather than an entirely new framework.

E3.justification: The supplement substantially extends testing procedures with surrogate transfer attacks, APGD-CE distortion bounds of 4/255–32/255, iteration counts of 1–50, and EOT-PGD. Section 8 also specifies random initialization for JEM despite the earlier informative-initialization description and retained captions; this revises the reported setting without establishing that experiments were rerun. Main training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Section 7 investigates gradient masking through attack-wise AutoAttack results, transfer attacks, distortion and iteration sweeps, and EOT-PGD. This adds a substantial robustness-validity analysis. The original gradient-weight and adversarial-sampling-step ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Table 2 changes from point estimates without run information to explicitly reporting three runs with seeds {1,2,3} and ± values for both proposed variants across both CIFAR datasets. Section 4.1 additionally specifies default seed 1. The uncertainty statistic is not defined, and the PDFs do not establish an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Tables 7–9 add a substantial body of attack-specific, transfer, and stress-test results; Section 8 adds EB-JDAT-JEM FID 39.43. Table 2 replaces earlier estimates with three-run summaries: CIFAR-10 AA changes from 64.61 to 64.78±0.23 for EB-JDAT-JEM++ and from 66.30 to 66.12±0.23 for EB-JDAT-SADAJEM. These are reporting-basis changes, not demonstrated performance gains or losses. Tables 1 and 3–6 retain their values.

M1.justification: The joint distribution, energy objectives, SGLD updates, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. The supplementary EB-JDAT-JEM result applies the existing framework rather than introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: The title changes from Bridging to Balancing, author affiliations and contact information are revised, and acknowledgements are added. Targeted abstract, related-work, and conclusion edits accompany moving limitations into the supplement and adding two supplementary sections; most existing prose and the method structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds supplementary Tables 7–9 and expands Table 2's display for uncertainty reporting. Existing graphics are retained, with figures and tables relocated; the ImageNet samples and comparative generation grids exchange Figure 3/4 numbering. The overall visual format remains similar.

R1.justification: v3 adds ten references, including gradient-obfuscation work and additional adversarial-training/EBM studies. Related Work now explicitly contrasts robust-classification regularization and JEAT's adversarial joint distribution with EB-JDAT's full joint distribution. This refines the existing positioning without replacing its central argument.

T1.justification: Equations 1–13 and their derivations are unchanged. Calling the existing formulation a conditional EBM adds characterization, not a new mathematical definition, assumption, or proof.

improvement.justification: The new multi-seed reporting and gradient-masking checks strengthen empirical support, while runtime-estimation disclosure and a code pointer improve reproducibility information. The gains remain limited: uncertainty notation and several new attack settings are unspecified, and Section 8's random-initialization account is not reconciled with the informative-initialization captions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EB-JDAT and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables. The complete documents were compared, including v3's supplementary material; v2 has no separate appendix.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds three-seed summaries, attack diagnostics, transfer-attack comparisons, and an additional generation result.

before.justification: v2 reports original classification, adversarial robustness, generation, and ablation results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and an ImageNet subset.

C2.justification: Section 3.4 adds the rationale that box-coordinate pretraining teaches object location and scale, with zero-size boxes maintaining input consistency during point fine-tuning. The result interpretations and limitations concerning marginal instance/panoptic gains and dependence on score ensembling are retained.

D1.justification: v2 explicitly documents four-coordinate box inputs, zero-padding of point coordinates and the box-pretraining-to-point-fine-tuning sequence. Hardware, optimizer, learning rate, crop sizes, training epochs and the code/model access statement remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The same segmentation tasks and dataset coverage are retained, including ADE20K, Cityscapes, COCO, COCO-Stuff-164K and Objects365 pretraining. Changing how box annotations are encoded does not introduce a new dataset or task.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in Tables 1–3 and the supplementary comparisons. In particular, the MAFT comparison with CLIP and DINOv2 remains in v1 Table 9 and v2 Table 6.

E3.justification: The reported preparation of Objects365 pretraining examples changes from within-box point sampling to direct box-coordinate inputs, with subsequent point fine-tuning specified in Section 3.4. Metrics, benchmark settings and Section 4.2 training budgets remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The point-count, point-selection, backbone and annotation ablations are retained as v2 Table 4a–d. The appendix upper-bound and prompting analyses and all qualitative examples are also unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or other uncertainty estimates for the experiments.

E6.justification: Reported numerical results are unchanged across Tables 1–3, the matched ablation tables and the appendix comparisons. Figures retain identical result imagery. No new result separately evaluates the revised box-input procedure.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 changes the reported box-pretraining procedure from sampling labeled points inside boxes to directly supplying [x,y,w,h] coordinates, followed by point fine-tuning using [x,y,0,0]. This is a localized input/training adaptation; the transformer classifier and geometric score fusion remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 revises the box-training paragraphs and replaces inconsistent central-point descriptions with highest-value-point or general point terminology. Appendix subsections become Sections 6–9, while most prose and the narrative sequence remain unchanged.

P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout, with extensive resizing and repositioning of figures and tables. v1 Tables 4–7 become four panels of v2 Table 4, and the supplementary tables move together onto a separate page. The six underlying figure images are unchanged.

R1.justification: The same 57 cited works and substantive research positioning are retained. Reference renumbering, expanded author names and bibliography formatting do not change the cited literature.

T1.justification: The token-concatenation and geometric-fusion equations retain the same mathematics. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs, and v2 adds no formal result, assumption or derivation; its coordinate-encoding revision concerns the training procedure.

improvement.justification: v2 improves clarity by aligning point-selection terminology with the highest-value rule already used in v1's implementation and ablation. It also makes the revised box-input and point-fine-tuning formats explicit. These are limited documentation gains: empirical evidence is unchanged, and no experiment compares the revised box-pretraining procedure with the earlier description.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ViT-P work and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures and supplementary material. v1 Appendix A.1–A.4 corresponds to v2 Sections 6–9; no material gap prevents comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains the original benchmark experiments, ablations, upper-bound analysis and mask-versus-point prompting comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original ViT-P segmentation experiments, ablations and appendix comparisons, including results on ADE20K, Cityscapes and COCO.

C1.justification: V3 narrows the novelty statement from demonstrating orthogonal transformations' effectiveness in FL generally to theoretical and empirical validation specifically in black-box FL. Efficiency and large-scale scalability become explicit headline claims. The central contributions concerning generalization, personalization, representation preservation, and external adaptation remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations concerning poor transfer of conventional personalized-FL methods to foundation models and efficiency from avoiding encoder backpropagation, including a backbone-independent computation claim. It removes the lower-dimensional projection and block-size-selection caveats and adds possible LLM/token-embedding applications. The central interpretation connecting orthogonality, feature preservation, and generalization remains.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies the scalability study's minimum 100 images per client and five test-client IDs, and supplies runtime and parameter-count information. However, it removes v1's exact initialization prompts, optimizer momentum, special random-initialization learning rates, block-search procedure, detailed CoCoOp configuration explanations, and dataset-level training-time ranges. This substantially changes reproducibility documentation, without establishing corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: Both evaluate FEMNIST, PACS, Office-Home, VLCS, and TerraIncognita, retaining the same cross-domain classification coverage and FEMNIST cross-device setting. Increasing participant counts extends an existing experiment rather than introducing a new dataset, task, or population.

E2.justification: V3 adds nonlinear FedAdapter comparisons and introduces PromptFL into the cross-device study. FedOT(-o), renamed FedLT, expands from the three-dataset condition-number comparison to the full benchmark suite, and local-only comparisons broaden. FedAVG is simply renamed FedOT(All Global). Detailed benchmark tables remove the random-initialization variant, although the separate initialization ablation remains.

E3.justification: V3 extends client-scaling evaluation to 1–75 participants; v1 describes 2–15 in its text and plots through 20 in Figure 5. It introduces round-averaged pseudo-gradient cosine similarity as an evaluation measure. Reported block settings change from 4 to 1 for VLCS and 16 to 4 for TerraIncognita. The base data splits and generalization, personalization, and comprehensive metrics remain.

E4.justification: V3 adds direct gradient-conflict analysis comparing orthogonal, unconstrained linear, and nonlinear adaptation (Table 2), expands the condition-number analysis from three datasets to five, and adds computational analysis. The existing scalability study is substantially extended. Initialization, degrees-of-freedom, global/local-component, and communication-frequency ablations already appear in v1.

E5.justification: V1 supplies benchmark point estimates without specifying repeated-run counts. V3 reports means and standard deviations across three named seeds (50, 77, 98) throughout the main and detailed benchmark tables, and specifies three seeds and 12 runs per dataset for gradient-conflict analysis. This establishes new uncertainty reporting, without establishing v1's original run count. No formal significance test is supplied.

E6.justification: Benchmark and ablation values change extensively. For example, Table 1 reports FEMNIST FedOT generalization as 94.89% in v1 versus 94.23 ± 0.84% in v3; these are revised reporting summaries, not an established same-setting decline. V3 adds gradient-similarity, runtime, and scalability results, including 71.18% for FedOT versus 65.30% for PromptFL at 75 clients. Some revised summaries conflict with appendix entries.

M1.justification: Both versions use a frozen black-box image encoder, a shared linear classifier, client-local orthogonal transformations parameterized through the Cayley transform, cross-entropy optimization, and server averaging. Block-diagonal transformations and random classifier initialization already exist in v1. The new comparison architectures do not change the proposed method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, and results discussion are extensively rewritten around black-box access and dual privacy. Scalability and efficiency receive dedicated subsections, and the supplement is reorganized with shortened background and implementation sections. The title, affiliation notes, and acknowledgments also change.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column main layout and substantially restructures Table 1 and the detailed appendix tables. It adds gradient-conflict, scalability, and runtime tables, removes the learning-framework comparison table, and moves the communication plot into the main text. Figure 5 changes from per-client improvement curves to absolute-accuracy comparisons among methods.

R1.justification: V3 substantially contracts the cited domain-adaptation, foundation-model, and personalized-FL literature, including removing BlackFed and the explicit black-box FL versus black-box foundation-FL taxonomy. Positioning shifts toward incompatibility of white-box adaptation with proprietary models and contrasts FedOT's gradient-based feature adaptation with ZooPFL's query-intensive optimization. These changes exceed bibliographic renumbering or venue updates.

T1.justification: The principal gradient-difference bound remains, but v1 Appendix E.3's prompt-learning extension, including Jacobian and Lipschitz-based reasoning, is removed. V3 corrects the false assertion that orthogonal-matrix eigenvalues must be ±1, replacing it with unit-modulus eigenvalues and a singular-value argument for condition number 1 (Appendix C.2). Separate degrees-of-freedom derivations are also omitted.

improvement.justification: V3 adds useful uncertainty reporting, mechanism controls, scalability comparisons, and a corrected eigenvalue argument. However, reproducibility details are lost and revised results introduce unresolved contradictions: Office-Home FedAKT(C) personalization is 73.49% in main Table 1, while Appendix Tables 13–14 average approximately 55.34%; the corresponding v1 tables agree at 27.24%. V3 also infers statistical significance from low standard deviations without a test. These issues leave the reliability of the expanded evidence, and therefore the net quality improvement, uncertain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FedOT research. Their main texts, appendices, tables, figures, and equations are available and readable, supporting a reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V3 reports original benchmark results, gradient-conflict measurements, ablations, scalability experiments, and runtime comparisons in Section 5 and Appendices E–F.

before.justification: V1 reports original five-dataset federated-learning experiments, component ablations, and communication-frequency and client-scaling studies in Section 5 and Appendices F–G.

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit central claim that clustered rewards in few-step generation produce weak learning signals and that structured self-refinement advantages address this problem. It more clearly presents MV-PG, MV-DPO and MV-RDL as baselines. The main contributions concerning multiview coordination, constrained optimization and preserved inference efficiency remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of zigzag refinement as filtering condition-misaligned features and producing more informative learning signals. Appendices F–G interpret the added experiments as evidence of scalability and broader backbone applicability. The existing first-step structural explanation, reward trade-off interpretation and approximate-inversion caveat remain.

D1.justification: v2 Table 3 documents hyperparameters for the added larger-training and SDXL configurations, and Appendix C expands the optimization-loop description. Conversely, it omits v1's RTX 4090 identification, 22–24-hour runtime, dedicated MV-ZigAL hyperparameter block and Table 1's 192-image averaging detail. The paper's code link remains the same.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the animal prompt set, MATE-3D's diverse 160 prompts and the retained qualitative prompt sets. v2 reuses MATE-3D for training and adds backbone configurations, but introduces no new dataset, generation task or test domain; those changes concern experimental settings.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 adds SPAD, Latent-NeRF and TextMesh to the MATE-3D comparison and removes its standalone MV-ZigAL rows. Table 2 adds the non-finetuned baseline and MV-ZigAL to the ablation comparison. Figures 8–11 substantially expand visual comparisons with competing methods; the MV-PG/MV-DPO/MV-RDL comparison remains.

E3.justification: v2 adds MATE-3D training for 100 epochs with larger batches and a lower learning rate, plus 16-step SDXL finetuning with LoRA rank 4. Table 2 specifies epoch-70 checkpoints for all finetuned variants, whereas v1 documents 190 epochs for MV-ZigAL and 70 for MVC-ZigAL. No held-out split is documented for the added MATE-3D training experiment.

E4.justification: Appendices F–G add analyses of training-scale effects and applicability to SDXL, including reward trajectories in Figure 7. Existing zigzag, weighted-sum, adaptive-threshold and adaptive-step-size ablations are retained. Figures 5–6 move from the appendices into the main text rather than introducing new ablations.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seed 42 and use the same seed for qualitative comparisons. Neither reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's additional result rows and training curves do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Table 1 and standard MVC-ZigAL benchmark scores remain unchanged. v2 adds HyperScore submetrics, comparator results, SDXL curves and larger-training results, including 8-step HyperScore 7.24 and ImageReward 0.865. MV-ZigAL's 8-step HyperScore is 6.95 in the new epoch-70 comparison versus 7.33 previously, not an established same-setting decline. Reported DreamFusion and Consistent3D scores also change from 4.15 to 4.13 and 4.21 to 4.08.

M1.justification: The central architecture, zigzag sampler and optimization objectives remain. However, Algorithm 1 changes the reported update order: v1 constructs mixed rewards before updating the Lagrange multiplier, whereas v2 uses the updated multiplier. v2 also specifies trajectory resampling within an inner optimization loop; these procedural revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and much of the method narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 separates baseline formulations from MVC-ZigAL, moves detailed T2I preliminaries into Appendix B, incorporates the constrained-objective derivation into the main text and moves adaptive-optimization analyses into the main ablation section.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, moves Figure 1 onto the opening page, restructures comparison and hyperparameter tables, and adds Figures 7–11. Existing adaptive-optimization plots move into the main text. v1's final five qualitative figures are retained as v2 Figures 12–16, rather than being new results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to constrained policy optimization, Latent-NeRF, TextMesh and constrained-RL diffusion alignment, while removing the original language-model DPO reference. Appendix A's positioning relative to multiview generation and alignment methods is largely retained. Publication updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: The Lagrangian formulation, advantage losses and inversion equations are retained, with v1 Appendix F largely incorporated into the main text. However, v2 Equation (2) assigns terminal reward at t=0 while defining actions as x_(t-1), unlike v1 Equation (8)'s consistent terminal transition. This introduces a limited formal indexing inconsistency rather than new theory.

improvement.justification: The added SPAD comparison, metric breakdowns, SDXL experiments and clearer organization provide useful gains. However, Table 4 labels evaluations out-of-distribution while including a model trained on the same MATE-3D prompts without a documented held-out split. Unlike v1's pseudocode, v2 Algorithm 1 averages joint rewards after zero-mean normalization, which would eliminate the stated constraint-feedback signal. These gains and new methodological reporting problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MVC-ZigAL research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and qualitative figures, support a reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds larger-training and SDXL finetuning experiments. Its original results are distinguishable from baseline results attributed to MATE-3D.

before.justification: v1 reports original finetuning experiments, quantitative comparisons, ablations and generated multiview images, including additional analyses in its appendices.

C1.justification: The broad claim of prior-free extrapolation from videos remains. However, v2 makes generalized higher-order dynamics beyond velocity-field models a central contribution and explicitly claims independence from geometric priors. It drops v1's categorical claim to be the first end-to-end general extrapolation method without manually defined physical priors.

C2.justification: v2 interprets performance through higher-order dynamics, shared-field efficiency, latent-state coherence, and the new training ablations. It replaces v1's emphasis on new-scene generalization and possible large-scale pretraining with a limitation concerning unseen changes in motion, such as breakage. v1's caution that rendering metrics can confound reconstruction quality with dynamics accuracy is also omitted.

D1.justification: Supplementary Section 7 specifies the 14-dimensional input, 2,048/4,096 sampled keypoints, 32 neighbors, latent dimensions, GELU activations, Adam optimizer, and detailed training stages. Network depths and widths are revised relative to v1 Appendix A.1. Conversely, v1's explicit code-availability statement and repository URL are removed; this establishes a disclosure loss, not that the repository became unavailable.

E1.justification: The Dynamic Object and Dynamic Indoor Scene datasets are retained. PanopticSports human-motion evaluation is removed, while Dynamic Multipart and FreeGave-GoPro add articulated-object motion and real-world human-object interactions. The appendix also adds a noisy 2D damped-oscillator experiment, extending coverage beyond video rendering.

E2.justification: On the retained synthetic benchmarks, v2 adds TRACE and FreeGave and removes 4D-GS from the quantitative comparisons. HexPlane, TiNeuVox, DeformGS, Grid4D, NVFi, and GaussianPrediction remain. These changes materially strengthen the velocity-field comparison and alter the comparator set independently of the added datasets.

E3.justification: Reported training budgets on the retained Object and Indoor datasets change from 50,000 and 60,000 iterations to 40,000, with a new dynamics warm-up between iterations 3,000 and 7,000. Their 75/25 temporal split is retained. v2 adds FPS evaluation and new ablation settings, including field-count sweeps and an A6000 exception to the otherwise RTX 4090 setup.

E4.justification: v1 Table 4 ablates latent space, Neural ODEs, and affine deformation. v2 substantially redesigns this analysis around factorized encoding, field count, ODE versus parameter-matched MLP, Rodrigues decoding, progressive training, and neighborhood rebuilding. Figure 3 adds latent-state analysis, and supplementary Section 6 adds a toy comparison of time-conditioned fitting against ODE extrapolation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests. Both primarily provide point estimates; the toy experiment's noisy inputs do not constitute uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: ParticleGS extrapolation PSNR changes from 27.558 to 38.067 for Falling Ball and from 33.568 to 32.679 for Factory (v1 Tables 1–2; v2 Tables 5–6). These are revised-model and training-setting results, not controlled version-to-version gains. The six retained baselines keep their shared-dataset scene scores. New benchmark, speed, and ablation results are added, while PanopticSports results disappear.

M1.justification: v2 replaces position-hash features and a max-pooled global state with Gaussian-attribute features and learnable-query attention over multiple dynamic fields. It revises the ODE architecture, replaces general affine/additive rotation updates with Rodrigues-based and quaternion updates, changes the stated loss weighting, and adds a separate dynamics warm-up. Periodic neighborhood rebuilding already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodology, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. The separate preliminaries are folded into the method formulation, and the appendix is reorganized into dedicated experimental, implementation, rotation-formula, visualization, and quantitative-results sections. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: v2 switches to a two-column layout, redraws the introductory and architecture figures, and reorganizes qualitative comparisons with marked locations and enlarged details. It adds latent-state and spiral plots. Main-text NVFi scene tables become dataset summaries, with scene-level results relocated to the appendix; table highlighting changes from colored cells to bold and underlining.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against velocity-field methods and approaches requiring structured geometry, adding discussion and citations for TRACE, FreeGave, NeuMA, VisionLaw, and neural constitutive-law learning. v1 mainly contrasts reconstruction methods, imposed physical constraints, and GaussianPrediction. This revises the novelty argument beyond reference renumbering or publication updates.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.2 adds the standard reduction of higher-order differential equations to an augmented first-order system, together with an explicit O(NG)-to-O(FG) evolution-complexity argument. These are bounded mathematical additions to v1's ODE formulation; no formal extrapolation or stability guarantee is established.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central extrapolation claim: TRACE/FreeGave comparisons, targeted factorization and training ablations, and speed measurements address important gaps in v1's comparative and component evidence. More explicit architecture and implementation descriptions improve transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of PanopticSports coverage, code-access disclosure, and some qualifications. The improvement rests on stronger validation and documentation, not on treating revised scores as controlled gains or accepting physical-law identification as proven.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ParticleGS and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The substantial architectural and experimental revisions can be reliably compared.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, rendering-speed measurements, latent-state visualizations, and a spiral-dynamics toy experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction and extrapolation experiments on synthetic datasets and PanopticSports, together with component ablations.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain monocular-video spatial reasoning, Spatial-Visual-View Fusion, scalable instruction data, and a temporal benchmark. V3 softens v1's explicit 'first 3D vision-language framework' contribution claim and extends the introduction's claims to OST-Bench generalization and competitiveness with ground-truth-depth models.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations connecting encoder choice to metric scale and temporal ordering, and discusses spatial gains versus non-spatial losses on OpenEQA and recovery through data mixing. Existing static-scene and reconstruction-quality limitations remain. Some new interpretations overreach: Table 7's caption claims improvement across all OST categories although counting and agent-information scores decline.

D1.justification: V3 newly specifies adherence to source-dataset train/test splits and explains mixed 2-, 3-, and 4-choice camera-direction questions and their chance baseline. It documents the 200k-plus-30k data-mixing recipe. Most implementation details, hardware, hyperparameters, preprocessing instructions, and the project link are retained; v1's explicit VSTI fine-tuning statement is omitted.

E1.justification: V3 expands beyond VSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench to ScanQA and SQA3D scene QA, OST-Bench online embodied reasoning, Video-MME, VQAv2, and OpenEQA. Training also includes ScanQA/SQA3D splits for their evaluations and an experiment incorporating general LLaVA-Video data. The original temporal benchmark remains based on static scenes.

E2.justification: V3 Table 1 adds Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Spatial-MLLM-4B, VG-LLM-4B, and a fine-tuned LLaVA-OneVision comparison. Gemini-2.5 Pro replaces Gemini-1.5 entries in Tables 1–2, while several smaller-model comparisons and VSI tiny-set/human rows are removed. New experiments introduce substantial additional comparator groups, including Video-3D LLM and GPT-4V.

E3.justification: New protocols include combined ScanQA/SQA3D training, evaluation on 4,675 validation and 3,519 test questions with language-generation and EM/EM-R metrics, zero-shot OpenEQA evaluation, and a controlled addition of 30k general videos. These expand the evaluation design; the original one-epoch recipe and VSTI train/test counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 adds 2D–2D and explicit-point fusion ablations, a CUT3R-versus-VGGT comparison, general-data mixing, and spatial/non-spatial transfer analysis on OpenEQA. These test architectural choices and capability tradeoffs absent from v1. Token-removal ablations remain, but most of their task-specific scores are omitted from the condensed Table 6.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The added experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: The headline VLM-3R averages remain 60.9 on VSI-Bench and 58.8 on VSTI-Bench. V3 adds extensive results, including ScanQA CIDEr 101.9, SQA3D EM 60.7, OST-Bench 42.9, and Video-MME 59.9 versus 62.1 with data mixing. Some old comparison and ablation entries disappear. V3 also introduces a prose/table inconsistency: 50.09 versus Table 6's retained 59.09 for removing view tokens.

M1.justification: The proposed model retains CUT3R spatial and camera tokens, cross-attention fusion with visual tokens, a two-layer projector, frozen encoders, and LoRA fine-tuning. The residual connection explicitly formulated in v3 Section 4.1 was already documented in v1 Appendix A.1. Alternative fusion and encoder configurations are evaluated as ablations.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, dataset explanations, and architecture narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed. Contributions are reorganized, experiments gain a broader benchmark structure, and Appendix C becomes three named analyses. Much of Appendices A–B remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 changes the document to two columns, redraws Figure 3, adds numerous comparison tables, and replaces the detailed component-ablation table with an average-only summary. Figure 2 loses its donut chart although its caption still refers to rings. The existing trajectory illustration and dataset-distribution tables are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V3 substantially updates positioning around Spatial-MLLM, VG-LLM, SpatialStack, and newer dynamic-scene work such as VLM4D and DynamicVerse. It develops a specific distinction between CUT3R's metric-scale representations and VGGT-based approaches, extending v1's emphasis on avoiding depth sensors and prebuilt maps.

T1.justification: The recurrent tokenization, cross-attention, residual fusion, and MRA definitions are unchanged in substance. V3's explicit residual equation restates v1 Appendix A.1. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new encoder discussion is qualitative interpretation.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for transfer, general-purpose capability retention, and the choice of fusion and geometry encoder through Tables 3–7 and D–F. Reporting non-spatial losses alongside spatial gains makes the applicability assessment more informative. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed token-ablation scores and localized reporting errors, including the view-token score inconsistency and overstated OST caption. The improvement comes from stronger validation and clearer tradeoffs, not higher retained headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VLM-3R and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C. The retained architecture, datasets, and results can be matched despite substantial rewriting and layout changes.

after.justification: V3 retains these original results and adds evaluations on additional benchmarks, fusion and geometry-encoder ablations, and a data-mixing experiment.

before.justification: V1 reports original VLM-3R evaluations on VSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, together with component ablations in Tables 1–3.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list redefine the temporal-modeling contribution from latent-feature flow to explicit scene-point motion estimation. Conversely, the named Step-1V dataset-construction model becomes an unspecified in-house LLM, and release statements change to future tense; actual online availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same stated 80-story, 1,317-shot benchmark with 344 characters, 509 references, ten visual styles, bilingual prompts, and a 20-story Lite subset. Additional generators and qualitative examples use retained story-visualization coverage; they do not establish new datasets, domains, or task requirements.

E2.justification: Tables 2 and S4 add evaluated comparisons with OmniGen2, CharaConsist, QwenImageEdit-2509, Gemini-2.5, Gemini-3.0 Pro, Seedream-4.0, and Sora2, including Sora2 reference-image and text-only variants. OmniGen2 was cited but not evaluated in v3. Earlier comparators remain after matching renamings and table relocations.

E3.justification: v4 introduces full/Lite Qwen evaluation, revised copy-paste scoring, and a Sora2 protocol using TransNetV2, manual shot matching, and exclusion of failed generations. These materially expand evaluation procedures without establishing that earlier generation experiments were rerun. Section 4.1 also changes the Lite nonhuman-character count from 4 to 43, contradicting the retained full-set count of 19; an actual dataset change cannot be inferred.

E4.justification: New Appendices H.6–H.7 investigate GPT-4.1 scoring repeatability and agreement between GPT-4.1 and Qwen3-VL. Expanded failure illustrations and the new Story 01 comparison add qualitative cases. The earlier CLIP/VinaBench case study and reference-selection sensitivity analysis are retained, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v4 first reports 3–5 independent rescoring runs on five stories and three methods, with means and standard deviations, including Scene Score 2.82 ± 0.03 and Individual Action 2.40 ± 0.08. It also specifies Qwen seed 42. This adds targeted uncertainty reporting; the existing human-study design remains, and increased generation-run counts are not established.

E6.justification: Numerous existing scores change beyond rescaling: Table 2's GPT-4o Cross-CIDS changes from 0.589 after normalization to 0.420, and full-set UNO OCCM changes from 89.8 to 74.2. v4 also adds seven methods, Qwen results, and evaluator-validation outcomes. These are revised or newly reported results, not demonstrated performance changes under identical evaluation conditions.

M1.justification: The overall benchmark pipeline remains, but copy-paste scoring changes from v3's similarity-gap measure to a temperature-scaled softmax over reference similarities in v4 Appendix L. Qwen3-VL becomes an alternative prompt-alignment evaluator. Expanded descriptions of structured prompting and CIDS matching do not independently establish further procedural changes.

P1.justification: v4 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, metric explanations, and discussion, replacing several prose descriptions with staged procedures. Detailed insights move into a new Appendix B, and appendix organization expands. Terminology is standardized from prompt adherence to prompt alignment and from global/single-character action to interaction/individual action.

P2.justification: The overview is replaced while v3 Figure 1 reappears as v4 Figure S2. v4 adds dataset visualizations, expands failure and storyboard displays, and redraws metric diagrams. Tables 2 and S4 gain backbone information, input-mode symbols, and explicit alignment submetrics; a Qwen table and revised polar charts further change the presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially revises the discussion toward unified multimodal generation, native multi-shot video, and cinematic evaluation, adding works such as USO, HoloCine, ShotAdapter, ShotBench, and Video-Bench. Earlier citations including StoryBooth, DreamRunner, and DropletVideo disappear. These changes exceed citation renumbering or bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Appendix L introduces the bespoke softmax CopyRate definition, normalized reference features, and temperature parameter, extending beyond v3's verbal similarity-gap description. OCCM's stated smoothing constant changes from e^-6 to 10^-6. The added CIDS averaging formula largely restates existing computation; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: Compared with v3, v4 adds useful model comparisons, evaluator-repeatability evidence, and a reproducible Qwen option. However, new reporting conflicts undermine central evidence: Appendix B gives GPT-4o OCCM as 93.5 while Tables 2/S4 give 69.33, and the Lite copy-paste baseline scores 1.000 in Table 2 but 0.550 in Table S4. The PDFs do not reconcile these results and interpretations, preventing a reliable judgment that the substantial additions produce a net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ViStoryBench. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, references, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renamed content.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and reports additional model evaluations, repeated evaluator scoring, and GPT–Qwen agreement analyses.

before.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations, a human study, metric correlations, qualitative comparisons, and reference-image sensitivity results.

Totals cover reported usage only; unknown or launched attempts without usage may still have consumed tokens. Finalized known pre-launch failures are counted as not launched.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: a diverse reference-based story benchmark, twelve evaluation metrics, human validation, and broad model comparisons. The abstract is shortened without substantively changing these claims.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendices A–B retain the same interpretations, consistency–diversity trade-offs, applicability boundaries, and limitations. Minor wording changes do not introduce new scientific explanations or qualifications.

D1.justification: v5 revises the stated scoring-model identity and adds explicit Gemini-3-Pro provenance notes to Tables 2 and S4. However, Appendix H still identifies GPT-4.1. Prompts, method adaptations, hardware/runtime information, and code/data access links otherwise remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same 80-story benchmark and 20-story Lite subset, with unchanged styles, languages, references, and task coverage. Table S5's revised title mentions both datasets, but both Full and Lite results were already present in v4.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark tables and case studies retain the same comparison methods and variants. Gemini-3.0 Pro was already evaluated as a generator in v4; its new role as evaluator does not add a generation baseline.

E3.justification: The reported primary judge changes from GPT-4.1 to Gemini-3-Pro across the four prompt-alignment submetrics in Tables 2 and S4, substantially revising a central scoring protocol. Table 2 also removes SEED-Story's ranking exclusion and includes its scores in rank highlighting. Dataset splits and generation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The Lite-versus-Full analysis, qualitative cases, reference-selection analysis, evaluator stability study, and GPT/Qwen correlation analysis are retained. No new analysis validates the replacement Gemini evaluator.

E5.justification: Both retain the same fixed-seed disclosures, human-rating procedures, and Appendix H.6 study using 3–5 evaluation runs over five stories and three methods. Its GPT-4.1 means and standard deviations remain unchanged; Gemini-specific uncertainty reporting is not added.

E6.justification: Prompt-alignment results throughout Tables 2 and S4 are replaced. For example, Table 2's full-set OmniGen2 average changes from 3.10 to 2.49; on Lite, GPT-4o moves above Gemini-2.5, with averages 3.34 versus 3.09 instead of 3.505 versus 3.567. These reflect different reported judges, not comparable generator performance gains or losses. Non-alignment metrics and Table S5's Qwen scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 and Figure 5 replace GPT-4.1 with Gemini-3-Pro as the prompt-alignment scoring component. The four-part rubric, aggregation, dataset-construction procedure, and other metric pipelines remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v5 condenses the abstract and captions, reorders the prompt-alignment descriptions, standardizes some Scene/Shot/CI/IA terminology, and adds acknowledgements. The main narrative and appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: Figures and tables are retained, with limited resizing and relocation, revised captions and labels, updated ranking highlights, and a Gemini logo replacing GPT in Figure 5. The main text is compacted and running headers/page numbers are removed; there is no substantial visual redesign.

R1.justification: Eleven references are added, including LogiStory, MUSE, StoryMem, and 2KCharacters-10KStories, mainly through expanded citation groups. The surrounding research positioning remains substantially unchanged; FilMaster's expanded bibliographic entry represents the same previously cited work.

T1.justification: The task formulation, metric definitions, OCCM equation, copy-paste formula, and mathematical explanations in the appendices are unchanged. Renaming alignment sub-scores does not change their definitions.

improvement.justification: v4's stated primary judge matched the GPT-4.1 validation in Appendix H. v5 replaces the judge and scores but leaves Appendix H attributing Table S4 to GPT-4.1 and retains its GPT-specific stability and correlation evidence. This introduces a reproducibility and validation inconsistency. Clearer labels and updated references provide limited benefits, but the PDFs supply no Gemini-specific validation establishing an offsetting improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ViStoryBench and contain readable main text, tables, figures, equations, and appendices A–M. Content can be matched reliably despite pagination and layout changes.

after.justification: v5 retains these original empirical studies and reports revised prompt-alignment scores in Tables 2 and S4.

before.justification: v4 reports original model evaluations in Table 2 and appendix tables, a human study in Table S7, and metric-validation analyses.

token_usage.accounting_note: Input totals include cached input; output totals include reasoning output. These subsets are not added again. Totals cover reported usage only; unknown or launched attempts without usage may still have consumed tokens. Finalized known pre-launch failures are counted as not launched.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain SpookyBench and the approximately 98% human versus 0% VLM recognition gap. v2 removes v1's abstract claim that training on low-spatial-SNR data causes temporal understanding to degrade faster than human perception. Its conclusion emphasizes additional evidence for the largely retained architectural explanation.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the interpretation of failure: semantic judging addresses the string-matching explanation, training-size experiments address insufficient data, and augmentation distinguishes extracting temporal cues from recognizing cues presented spatially. Appendix H attributes concrete responses to timestamp hallucination, prompt echoing, pattern collapse, and language-prior scene fabrication. These extend v1's more general architectural discussion, although the causal conclusions remain stronger than the controls alone establish.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial implementation information: LlamaFactory use, judge inputs, classifier backbones, 64-frame clips at 256×256 resolution, optimizers, learning rates, batch sizes, and RTX PRO 6000 hardware. It also describes generation of additional training videos and a fixed test set for the size sweep. The project access route remains unchanged. Conflicting classifier split and epoch descriptions limit reproducibility despite the added detail.

E1.justification: The principal coverage remains the 451-video synthetic benchmark; v1's 156 Object Images and 28 Shapes are consolidated into 184 Images, rather than establishing removal of shape content. v2 adds an auxiliary foreground-presence classification task with noise-only negatives and an evaluation scenario using explicit motion-boundary inputs. These extend coverage within the existing synthetic domain.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds evaluated Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and Gemini 2.5 Pro rows to v1 Table 2's comparator set. The fine-tuning study changes from Qwen2.5-VL-7B to InternVL2.5-8B and Qwen2-VL-7B. New foreground-detection comparisons evaluate VJEPA-2 and DINOv3 against chance, with an additional Qwen3-VL-8B result reported in Appendix D.

E3.justification: Fine-tuning changes from 400 videos for five epochs in v1 Appendix B to 30-epoch experiments with 100, 400, and 1,100 training videos in v2. The human FPS study changes from 60 videos, 15 per category, to 120 videos, 40 per regrouped category. v2 also adds manual and GPT-4o semantic scoring, revises CoT prompts, and introduces binary-classification protocols. Its conflicting split and training-budget descriptions leave the exact binary-classifier settings unresolved.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing fine-tuning, FPS, and motion-coherence analyses, v2 adds training-size sweeps, foreground-presence controls, motion-boundary augmentation, semantic-scoring checks, and concrete failure-response case studies. SNR-threshold analysis expands from text to images and dynamic scenes. Most earlier motion-coherence examples are retained, but the Shapes example panel is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same general mean-plus/minus reporting for benchmark, human, and SNR summaries. No new seed counts, repeated-run information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are documented. Changed summary values and sample sizes belong to results and evaluation design.

E6.justification: v2 Table 5 newly reports 51.54% overall accuracy for Qwen2-VL-7B and 59.10% for GPT-4o with motion-boundary augmentation; these are new input conditions, not improved raw-video scores. It adds near-chance foreground-detection results, zero-accuracy training-size results, and image/dynamic-scene thresholds of 6.0/9.0 dB. Human FPS and regrouped Image summaries also change under revised samples or aggregation. The original raw-video VLM results remain 0%.

M1.justification: The benchmark-generation procedures in Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. v2 adds a diagnostic inference adaptation: Farneback motion-boundary overlays are fed to Qwen2-VL-7B and GPT-4o (Section 4.5), whereas v1 used motion-boundary overlays for analysis and visualization.

P1.justification: v2 extensively condenses and rewrites the introduction and related work, removes the separate contribution bullets, merges related-work subsections, and renames Methods to SpookyBench. Architectural implications move from Section 3.3.3 to Section 5.1, while FPS and fine-tuning receive main-text sections. The appendix is reorganized into a separately titled supplement with contents, sections A–I, and its own references.

P2.justification: v2 relocates the main benchmark table, redraws the SNR plot with three category curves, and restructures category tables and the distribution chart. It adds classifier training curves, augmentation and training-size tables, a judging flowchart, and response panels. The supplement switches to a single-column layout with enlarged retained illustrations; v1's Shapes panel is removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused positioning around common-fate perception and Tangemann et al.'s random-dot segmentation work, motion-controlled diffusion, and an ARC-AGI analogy. References for new models, Farneback flow, VLMEvalKit, and LlamaFactory are also added. The central positioning against spatial shortcuts in temporal-video benchmarks remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The four SNR definitions and the underlying exact-match accuracy calculation are retained. Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs, and v2's explanation of the binary chance-loss baseline does not introduce a new derivation or formal result.

improvement.justification: v2 improves the paper's diagnostic support: semantic judging checks whether exact matching caused the zero scores, and motion-boundary augmentation quantifies recognition once temporal cues are exposed spatially. These address weaknesses in v1 beyond merely adding more benchmark rows. However, the new classifier reporting gives inconsistent 80/20 versus 90/10 splits and unreconciled 30-, 80-, and 100-epoch accounts. These problems limit reproducibility and confidence in the architectural interpretation, making the net improvement limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SpookyBench research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison. Reporting inconsistencies in v2 affect particular findings, but do not prevent matching the work across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark and human results and adds semantic judging, foreground-detection experiments, training-size comparisons, and motion-boundary augmentation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original VLM evaluations, a six-participant human study, SNR analyses, and appendix experiments on fine-tuning, frame rates, and motion coherence.

token_usage.accounting_note: Input totals include cached input; output totals include reasoning output. These subsets are not added again. C1.justification: v2 explicitly claims the first single-stage video LLM reasoning with frame references and foregrounds synthetic-to-real transfer. The claim of leading VIDEO-MME, MVBENCH, and VSI-BENCH narrows to the latter two, with VIDEO-MME now second-best. The central contribution remains efficient, temporally grounded CoF reasoning.

C2.justification: The limitations shift from untested architectures beyond InternVL to fixed-FPS compatibility and unresolved adaptation to dynamic-frame-rate models such as Qwen2.5-VL. v2 more strongly interprets synthetic-data results as task transfer across distributions. It retains the general data-overlap caveat but removes v1's specific note about InternVL2.5 pretraining on CLEVRER.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies uniform sampling of 30 inference frames regardless of video duration. Appendix A.3 adds Phi's indexed image-token explanation and fine-tuning details. Existing InternVL hardware, learning rate, batch size, epoch count, and the code-link destination remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions train on VIDEOESPRESSO and CLEVRER and evaluate on VSI-BENCH, VIDEO-MME, MVBENCH, VIDHAL, EVENTHALLUSION, and NEXTQA. NEXTQA already appeared in v1 Appendix B. The Phi experiments reuse existing benchmark coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Tables 4-8 add Phi-3.5-Vision-4B with standard and CoT prompting as comparators for its CoF variant. The existing InternVL, external video-LLM, M-LLM, and Video-of-Thought comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: v2 extends evaluation to the Phi-3.5-Vision-4B configuration and introduces an across-benchmark average in Table 1. Existing benchmark splits, individual metrics, and InternVL training budgets remain unchanged. The newly stated 30-frame inference sampling is additional documentation, not an established change to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds an explicit test of whether CoF generalizes beyond InternVL using Phi-3.5-Vision. It removes the CoF-4B frame-reference distribution and its 68.7% reference-use finding from Figure 7, retaining the 8B analysis. Existing data-source ablations, prompting comparisons, and qualitative examples largely remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The results continue to use point estimates.

E6.justification: CoF-InternVL3-8B's reported VIDEO-MME and MVBENCH scores change from 75.3 and 90.4 in v1 Table 2 to 73.7 and 77.1 in v2 Table 1, with revised appendix breakdowns. VIDEO-MME leadership consequently changes. v2 also adds Phi results throughout Tables 4-8. These are substantial reporting changes; the PDFs do not establish why the earlier scores were revised.

M1.justification: The data-generation pipeline, frame-index reasoning, and CoF fine-tuning procedure remain unchanged. Phi-3.5-Vision is an additional application of the existing procedure; no new CoF component, objective, or algorithmic adaptation is specified.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory framing, related-work taxonomy, method motivation, and synthetic-data discussion are extensively rewritten. Main comparisons precede ablations, additional analyses become Section 5, and the previously supplementary video-CoT comparison moves into the main text.

P2.justification: The paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, moves Figure 1 before the abstract, relocates the full data-distribution figure to the appendix, and redisplays its combined-data pie in the main text. Tables gain average and Phi entries, and Figure 7 loses its 4B panel. Figure 1 is redrawn with an accuracy axis inconsistent with the tabulated scores.

R1.justification: v2 sharpens the single-stage versus multi-stage positioning and adds references to Phi-3, Flexible Frame Selection, VidHalluc, and VideoTree. References to BGE-M3 and Grounding DINO are removed with the corresponding detailed discussion. These are limited changes around the retained comparison with prior video-reasoning methods.

T1.justification: The MRA definition and threshold set in Appendix A.2 are unchanged. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions, proofs, or formal derivations beyond the retained metric description.

improvement.justification: Phi evaluation and clearer inference and applicability documentation strengthen v2. However, new reporting inconsistencies affect central comparisons: Tables 4 and 7 give 74.3 and 72.5 for the same InternVL3 CoT MVBENCH baseline; Table 2 reports a 7.8-point gain although 73.7 minus 66.5 is 7.2; and Figure 1's revised accuracy axis contradicts the tables. These regressions coexist with useful additions, preventing a confident judgment of net overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Chain-of-Frames research and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A-C. Content can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original CoF evaluations and adds experiments with Phi-3.5-Vision-4B, including aggregate and task-level results in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original CoF model evaluations, training-data and prompting ablations, and frame-reference analyses in Section 4 and Appendix B.
