C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same principal contributions: CNP neurodynamic analysis, training-free interpretable decision maps without post-processing, and state-of-the-art results on four datasets. The claimed average improvement over baseline CNP remains 5.73%. Removing 'generalizable' from the conclusion does not withdraw the generalization claim repeated elsewhere.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations that the tested radius and iteration settings are universal, SML benefits noisy inputs, and the C++ runtime satisfies real-time MFIF requirements. The low-contrast-edge explanation is retained but attached to the SSIM shortfall instead of PSNR, following the changed comparator set. The noisy-input explanation lacks its referenced appendix evidence.

D1.justification: v3 explicitly states that comparators use official code and weights and reports an implemented C++ version where v1 only suggested a future port. It supplies image dimensions for the energy estimate. Hardware and the project-code link remain unchanged; appendix-only parameter configuration details are unavailable.

E1.justification: The documented fusion coverage remains Lytro, MFFW, MFI-WHU, and Real-MFF, with the same respective counts of 20, 13, 120, and 710 image pairs. v3 newly references downstream salient-object detection and noisy-input evaluation, but the cited Appendices C.2 and C.4 are absent, preventing verification of added task or scenario coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1-2 and Figures 5-6 replace ZMFF and MGDN with CCF and Mask-DiFuser, retaining seven other fusion comparators. This is a bounded revision of the comparison set. v3 also mentions an LIF comparison, but its results are assigned to missing Appendix C.3 and cannot be verified.

E3.justification: Section 5.3 extends the coupling-radius sweep from {2, 4, 8, 16, 32} to include zero. v3 adds C++ runtime evaluation and an energy estimate for 520-by-520 Lytro images. The main dataset counts, six fusion metrics, hardware assignments, selected radius of 16, and 110 iterations remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 7 adds a zero-radius control to the existing neighborhood sensitivity analysis. The neurodynamic and SML ablations and Lytro failure-case study remain. v3 claims an additional noisy-input analysis in Appendix C.4, but its evidence is unavailable and cannot substantiate a broader robustness expansion.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures. Figure 7 already contains shaded bands in v1; v3 retains this presentation without adding an explanation of their statistical meaning.

E6.justification: All 24 ND-CNPFuse scores in Table 1 remain unchanged, while comparator rows and rankings change: the MFFW exception shifts from PSNR to SSIM. Table 2 adds 0.18 seconds for C++ alongside the retained 0.41 seconds for MATLAB; Section 5.2 adds 1.12e-5 J per pair. Table 3 revises percentage gains, including FMIw from 17.09% to 17.29%, and Table 4 changes without-SML PSNR from 26.987 to 26.983.

M1.justification: The available method description retains SML preprocessing, coupled-neuron iteration, neighborhood aggregation of spike counts, decision-map comparison, and pixelwise fusion. Time reindexing and the C++ implementation do not establish an algorithm change. Detailed parameter rules referred to Appendix A.2 cannot be compared.

P1.justification: v3 locally streamlines related work, proof explanations, and experimental discussion while retaining the same section sequence and narrative. It replaces the third-generation-network description with biological inspiration wording, adds two authors, and revises affiliations and an acknowledgement identifier. These are limited editorial changes.

P2.justification: Figures 3-4 are redrawn, Figures 5-6 update and reorder comparator panels, and Figure 7 extends its radius axis to zero. Table 1 consolidates method labels and adds publication tags; Table 2 displays dual implementation runtimes. The eight figures, four tables, and overall two-column layout are retained.

R1.justification: Related work adds explicit diffusion-model coverage and correctly groups the already-cited Mask-DiFuser there. Six references are added, covering CCF, VDMUFusion, Text-DiFuse, nonlinear spiking P-system fusion, SpikingJelly, and energy calculation. The central novelty positioning remains unchanged; bibliographic updates to existing works are not new citations.

T1.justification: Section 3 corrects the synaptic-input definition from K(i) using Pkl(t-1) to K(n) using Pkl(n). Corollary 1 changes its bound from strict to non-strict inequality. The linear-decay relation is explicitly identified as an approximation. The four theorems and principal continuous-firing threshold remain; appendix derivations are unavailable.

improvement.justification: v3 modestly improves clarity and evidential support through corrected mathematical statements, an explicit approximation, a zero-radius control, and reported C++ timing replacing v1's speculative efficiency claim. These gains are limited: fusion scores are unchanged, comparator replacement removes MGDN's stronger MFFW PSNR result, and missing appendices prevent crediting the claimed downstream and noise evaluations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ND-CNPFuse, and their main text, equations, figures, and tables are readable. However, both end after the references on page 10 and omit the cited appendices A-C. This prevents verification of appendix-only derivations, configurations, and experiments, including newly referenced evaluations in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original fusion evaluations and ablations, updates evaluated comparators, and reports additional C++ timing and an energy estimate.

before.justification: v1 reports original four-dataset fusion evaluations, runtime measurements, neuron simulations, parameter sensitivity experiments, and ablations in Tables 1-4 and Figures 2 and 5-8.

token_usage.accounting_note: Input totals include cached input; output totals include reasoning output. These subsets are not added again. Totals cover reported usage only; unknown or launched attempts without usage may still have consumed tokens. Finalized known pre-launch failures are counted as not launched.

C1.justification: The abstract extends the headline state-of-the-art claim from CheXpert Plus to MIMIC-CXR, and the contribution summary explicitly emphasizes recall. The central claims of novel GRPO/DPO integration, factual rewards and highly data-efficient training remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for GRPO+SFT failure, interpretations of expert-label and commercial-model comparisons, and discussion of micro-F1 versus recall. Appendix C argues that low ROUGE-L reflects wording differences rather than clinical errors and interprets individual cases. The original limitations concerning scale, non-verifiable rewards and diagnostic attributes remain in the condensed conclusion.

D1.justification: Appendix A and Table 6 newly disclose the learning rate of 2.5e-7 and hyperparameter search ranges; Algorithm 1 adds pseudocode. Hardware, software, batch/group sizes, mixing settings and length-aware variants were already documented in v1 and are retained or relocated. These disclosures do not establish changed training settings.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates the proposed method only on CheXpert Plus. v2 adds separate training and evaluation on MIMIC-CXR, previously mentioned only as background, substantially broadening dataset coverage within chest X-ray report generation.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in CheXpert Plus Tables 1–2 are retained. New comparisons introduce methods including CXR-RePaiR, HERGen and MCA-RG in Table 3, MedRAT and other methods in Table 7, GPT-4.1 and GPT-5 Thinking in Table 5, and a GRPO+SFT control in Table 4.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluation on 200 studies from 200 patients using three radiologists' majority-vote labels. Commercial-model comparisons use matched images and prompts, with GPT-5 set to medium reasoning. Supplementary evaluations introduce micro-averaged metrics and case-level ROUGE-L. The original CheXpert Plus macro-averaging protocol is retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds an ablation replacing DPO with SFT, checks whether gains persist against expert labels, and presents three qualitative cases with extracted facts, diagnostic discrepancies and ROUGE-L scores. The original component, training-size and training-dynamics analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experimental results. The additional evaluations do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the five original ablation rows retain their scores, including CheXpert Plus F1 of 0.341. v2 newly reports MIMIC-CXR macro F1 of 0.357 and micro F1 of 0.481, expert-label F1 of 0.288 versus GPT-5's 0.301, and GRPO+SFT F1 of 0.106. D1.justification: v5 adds an explicit project-page link on the title page. The supplied PDFs do not establish what code or data is available there. Algorithm 1, prompts, and other implementation disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MS COCO captioning and word localization, MMVP visual question answering, and RePOPE hallucination attribution. Appendix examples are retained; changing their description from object-level to word-level does not introduce a different task.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains LLaVA-CAM and IGOS++ (w/ GNC). Tables 2–3 retain these methods plus TAM. Newly added citations do not introduce evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The same four model configurations, evaluation metrics, sensitive-token threshold of 0.2, and hallucination-correction procedures are reported. Appendix captioning and RePOPE prompts are unchanged, with no revised experimental settings identified.

E4.justification: Tables 4–5 retain the same objective-component ablation and subregion-count comparison using 36, 50, and 64 regions. The hallucination case studies and additional qualitative analyses in Appendix 9 are also retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same point-estimate reporting. Neither reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–5 match, including EAGLE's Qwen2.5-VL 7B captioning insertion/deletion scores of 0.7006/0.4597. Qualitative results are retained. Adding the seconds unit to the existing 15.4 timing entry does not change its value.

M1.justification: SLICO partitioning, the insight-plus-necessity objective, greedy search, saliency updates, and modality-influence calculation remain unchanged. Equations 1–5 and appendix Algorithm 1 retain the same procedures; deleting the optimality remark does not change the algorithm.

P1.justification: Editorial changes include simplified affiliations, added acknowledgements, correction of 'Token poisons' to 'Token positions,' and consistent word-level terminology in the appendix. The main prose and section sequence are largely retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 moves before the abstract, Figure 2 is slightly rearranged and moves earlier, and Tables 1 and 3 are relocated. Figures 12–14 receive terminology corrections in their captions. Existing displays are preserved, with no new experimental figures or table structures.

R1.justification: v5 adds citations to CamEdit, Disentangle to Fuse, and DeFacto, and removes the Edmonds reference associated with the deleted optimality remark. The substantive positioning against existing attribution methods remains unchanged.

T1.justification: v5 deletes v3's Remark 4, which asserts a reduction to monotone submodular maximization, a tight (1 - 1/e) greedy approximation, and essential optimality unless P = NP. This withdraws the stated approximation and optimality guarantee without replacement, although the mathematical definitions and complexity analysis remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Removing Remark 4's unsupported optimality guarantee resolves its conflict with Section 3.2's admission that the objective may not be submodular. Terminology corrections and the project-page pointer provide smaller clarity and access benefits. The improvement is limited because no replacement theoretical guarantee, new validation, or substantial implementation detail is supplied.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EAGLE and contain readable main text, equations, five tables, and complete appendices. Relocated displays and renamed appendix captions can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v5 retains these original experimental results, including the benchmark comparisons, ablations, and appendix examples.

before.justification: v3 reports original attribution evaluations, hallucination-correction experiments, and ablations in Tables 1–5, with additional qualitative results in the appendix.

C1.justification: v1 principally claims preliminary viability despite an ImageNet accuracy gap. v2 presents two-stage alignment as a central contribution and claims competitive performance across a broad benchmark, retaining 90–98% mean dataset-wise relative RGB accuracy while providing substantial loading-speed benefits. This materially broadens the central effectiveness and efficiency claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications about offline fitting cost, dependence on the RGB teacher, sensitivity to distribution shifts, and alignment using non-pruned FP16 splats. Its appendix interprets reconstructed-RGB experiments as evidence about compression-limited performance and architectural studies as evidence for a token bottleneck. These extend v1's discussion of the accuracy gap, weak scratch training, and omitted quantization.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents preprocessing iterations and batch sizes, estimated fitting GPU-hours, normalization statistics, Fourier frequencies, Perceiver dimensions and heads, and forward-pass pseudocode (Tables 3–4 and Section 11.2). These substantially improve implementation specificity without establishing that every newly disclosed setting changed. Code release remains prospective, with v2 expanding the promised release to the full preprocessing and CLIP pipeline.

E1.justification: Training retains the 12.8M DataComp dataset, but evaluation expands far beyond ImageNet-1K to fine-grained recognition, medical and satellite imagery, rendered-text sentiment, synthetic spatial tasks, and shifted ImageNet/ObjectNet inputs. v2 describes 38 datasets, although Table 5 contains 37 dataset rows; the substantial coverage expansion is clear despite that discrepancy.

E2.justification: v2 adds 98-token RGB comparisons without fine-tuning and with one or five fine-tuning epochs (Table 7), plus rendered-RGB, grid/convolutional-stem, and point-transformer comparisons (Figures 18–20). The ViT-L/16 comparator plotted in v1 Figure 7 is absent from the corresponding v2 studies. These change the evaluated comparator set, beyond extending existing models to more datasets.

E3.justification: The reported GS training budget changes from six adaptation epochs to two distillation epochs followed by five CLIP epochs. v2 adds explicit RGB token-merging/fine-tuning controls, cross-dataset absolute and dataset-wise relative accuracy summaries, load/decode timing on batches of 256, and pruning sweeps over 100 images per configuration. These are substantive protocol additions, while the main RGB training recipe remains largely retained.

E4.justification: v1 mainly examines initialization, qualitative pruning, splat/token budgets, and training from scratch. v2 adds quantitative pruning sensitivity and convergence analyses, plus controlled studies of distillation order and losses, normalization, learning rates, text freezing, alternative stems, point transformers, reconstructed RGB inputs, and direct Gaussian tokenization (Sections 9 and 11.5–11.6). These test substantially more explanations for performance and optimization behavior.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 4 newly uses KDE summaries to estimate empirical distributions of pruning and PSNR outcomes across configurations. This adds descriptive statistical estimation, rather than repeated-training uncertainty. Neither version reports seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its classification results.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive dataset-level scores, timing results, and ablation findings. For example, Table 5 reports 16.87% ImageNet top-1 for GS-1600 with 196 tokens under the revised training procedure; this is not a same-protocol gain over v1's reported 13–15% range. The earlier top-5 summary is absent. Initialization PSNR examples also change alongside the illustrated image, whereas Figure 2 retains the original 90.3× fitting-speed result.

M1.justification: v1 directly adapts an RGB-initialized GS encoder through CLIP training. v2 introduces a preceding vision-only distillation stage matching normalized RGB and GS CLS embeddings, followed by CLIP adaptation with optional text-side unfreezing (Section 5.2). Its stem also changes from the gated, z-score/global-mean design in v1 Figure 5 to the simpler normalization and projection path in v2 Figure 1d and Algorithm 1.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the presentation: it adds the GaussianVision name, condenses preliminaries, moves CLIP background from Section 3.3 to appendix Section 8.1, rewrites the alignment section around setup/training/protocol/results, and separates Discussion from Conclusion. The structured appendix further reorganizes technical explanations and analyses; this exceeds a simple content extension or renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 redraws and combines the overview and GS architecture into a first-page Figure 1, replaces the qualitative pruning display with quantitative plots and new examples, and replaces the ImageNet-only result display with a broad benchmark chart. It adds substantial comparative tables, profiling displays, and ablation panels throughout the appendix. These are extensive visual and layout changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: The main positioning against pixel-based tokenization, INRs, GaussianImage, and earlier Gaussian recognition methods is retained. v2 adds references and discussion for CLIP Benchmark, VTAB, and contrastive representation distillation, principally supporting its expanded evaluation and loss studies rather than redefining its relationship to prior research.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.4 newly specifies the exact batch-averaged reconstruction-plus-L1 objective, weighted absolute-RGB luminance score, and retained-splat index set, which v1 leaves verbally specified. This is a limited addition of mathematical definitions. The Gaussian reconstruction equation is unchanged, and neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's narrow validation and limited support for its design choices through broader evaluation, token-matched RGB controls, and targeted distillation and architecture ablations. Detailed preprocessing and model specifications also improve reproducibility. Reporting defects remain: 38 datasets are claimed but 37 are tabulated, and Table 3's speedup column matches batch-time ratios rather than throughput speedups. These weaken particular summaries but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and technical transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with v2 adding the GaussianVision name and substantially extending the study. Text, equations, figures, and tables are readable. v1 ends with references; v2 includes an accessible appendix in Sections 8–11.

after.justification: v2 reports original cross-dataset classification results, profiling measurements, pruning studies, and extensive architecture and training ablations, including appendix results.

before.justification: v1 reports original CUDA speed measurements, initialization and pruning experiments, and zero-shot ImageNet results for its Gaussian-splat encoders.

C1.justification: The abstract, three stated contributions, and conclusion retain the same core claims: an interpretable two-stage diffusion framework, competitive or state-of-the-art performance, and data-efficient real-world transfer.

C2.justification: v2 adds an argument that direct motion prediction simplifies learning relative to RGB-video prediction and interprets inference overhead as a worthwhile accuracy–speed tradeoff. It removes v1's explanation that the strongest real-world results use a VPP-based variant for matched comparison. Most benchmark interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 removes Appendix C's complete DAWN* recipe, including VPP initialization, RGB-plus-motion conditioning, the shared action expert, and one-step denoising, despite retaining its results. It also omits CALVIN's specified 10-action replanning interval. Conversely, it adds bimanual data-collection and task details, changes the project-page address, and mentions a supplementary video index. General training hardware and hyperparameters remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds a locally collected Galaxea R1 Lite dataset with 150 demonstrations and eight plush-toy/pot tasks, illustrated through qualitative motion predictions (Supplement Section 2.3.2, Table 7, Figure 10). This extends existing bimanual coverage with a new tabletop scenario; the original simulation, xArm, DROID, and Galaxea Open-World coverage remains.

E2.justification: MoDE is added to both CALVIN comparisons, with average lengths of 3.39 without external robotic data and 4.01 with external data (Tables 1–2). The other external comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds average inference time per action chunk, measured in milliseconds, to the real-world evaluation. Existing CALVIN evaluation sequences and step limits, xArm trial counts, and the 300-episode bimanual MSE evaluation remain unchanged. CALVIN evaluation details move to the supplement.

E4.justification: The CALVIN representation, pretraining, gripper-view, and diffusion-step ablations are unchanged (v1 Table 5; v2 Table 6). v2 adds an efficiency analysis and qualitative cases involving basket placement and coordinated plush-toy/pot manipulation. The existing CALVIN and Galaxea examples are retained or redisplayed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical tests. The new runtime averages do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds MoDE results, qualitative cases, and runtimes of 112.77, 571.89, 190.55, and 319.82 ms for Enhanced DP, pi0, VPP, and DAWN. Table 4 removes the original DAWN row, including apple results of 12 successful lifts and 10 placements, while retaining DAWN*'s 19/19 under DAWN. This does not establish a same-setting improvement. Other quantitative results remain unchanged apart from rounding.

M1.justification: The main architecture, motion representation, losses, and inference equations are unchanged. However, v1 defines a VPP-based DAWN* variant with RGB-plus-motion conditioning, VPP's action expert, and one denoising step. v2 removes that description while retaining its scores under DAWN, leaving uncertain whether the real-world procedure changed or only its labeling and documentation.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work are extensively rewritten, experimental descriptions are compressed, and CALVIN evaluation details move into the supplement. The appendix is reorganized around dataset descriptions and qualitative results, replacing the DAWN Variants section. Much of the method and conclusion remains textually stable.

P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout, with extensive figure and table relocation and resizing. v2 adds a framework-comparison diagram, a task-definition table, and qualitative displays, and adds a runtime column to Table 4. The original Galaxea figure is shortened in the main text and reproduced fully in the supplement.

R1.justification: The research positioning is substantially recast around sparse trajectories, future-RGB prediction, and VLAs. The detailed LangToMo comparison is removed, while SuSIE and HAMSTER discussions and a MoDE citation are added. Earlier discussions and citations, including DVD, 3D-VLA, and Octo, disappear. These changes extend beyond citation formatting.

T1.justification: The pixel-motion definitions, three-channel encoding, and denoising equations (1)–(3) are unchanged. Neither version adds or removes substantive theoretical assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: The MoDE comparisons, runtime measurements, and new bimanual examples provide useful additions. However, v2 Table 4 presents v1's DAWN* scores as DAWN while removing the original DAWN results and the appendix explaining the variant's substantially different implementation. This reduces the traceability and reproducibility of an important real-world claim. That loss outweighs the limited additional evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DAWN research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and reused material.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and additionally reports inference timings and qualitative predictions on a newly collected bimanual dataset.

before.justification: v1 reports original CALVIN and MetaWorld experiments, real-world xArm trials, bimanual action-prediction results, and ablations.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion broaden the work from demonstrated linear restoration/MRI reconstruction to a unified framework with demonstrated linear and nonlinear applications. Nonlinear implementation was explicitly future work in v1. The proximal-prior interpretation, few-NFE efficiency, and first MRI-trained CM claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 removes the LSUN-only limitation and nonlinear-future-work discussion as coverage expands. It adds interpretations of comparable visual quality to diffusion-PnP methods, robustness to hyperparameter perturbations, and phase-retrieval ambiguity. Its new MRI analysis qualifies momentum as especially useful at low NFEs and not the primary performance driver, replacing v1's emphasis on momentum dominance in its LSUN ablation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, explicit noise/penalty/momentum schedules, coefficient values for CelebA-HQ and MRI in Table 3, nonlinear implementation instructions, additional baseline tuning details, and training losses and budgets. v1 largely described empirical tuning and referenced external implementations. Conversely, v1's explicit [0,1] input-normalization statement is no longer stated.

E1.justification: v2 adds CelebA-HQ training and evaluation and evaluates JPEG restoration, nonlinear deblurring, and coded-mask phase retrieval on both natural-image datasets. LSUN Bedroom's original linear restoration tasks and fastMRI PD/PD-FS reconstruction remain.

E2.justification: Linear natural-image comparisons add DiffPIR, DPnP, and PnP-DM. The new nonlinear comparisons evaluate DPS, ΠGDM, and DPnP. MRI comparisons now include quantitative and visual CM4IR results alongside DPS and DDS; v1 only described CM4IR's failure without corresponding comparative entries.

E3.justification: The reported MRI CM distillation budget changes from 7M iterations in v1 Appendix D.1 to 700k in v2 Supplement C; this establishes a revised stated setting, without establishing retraining. New protocols include CelebA-HQ training/evaluation splits, JPEG quality factor 5, eight-NFE phase retrieval, MRI momentum controls at 4/10/20 NFEs, and randomized hyperparameter perturbations up to 25%.

E4.justification: v2 adds an MRI study testing whether momentum benefits diminish with increasing NFEs and a CelebA-HQ deblurring hyperparameter-sensitivity study (Supplement D.1–D.2). The four-way component ablation and noise/NFE sweep move from LSUN Bedroom experiments to CelebA-HQ experiments, replacing their evidence rather than merely relocating it.

E5.justification: Both versions use averaged reconstruction metrics and retain plus/minus reporting for MRI. Neither introduces seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new randomized sensitivity study changes experimental design without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive CelebA-HQ, nonlinear-task, baseline, and sensitivity results while revising retained entries. For example, four-NFE LSUN deblurring changes from 28.10/0.237 to 27.49/0.285 PSNR/LPIPS, and MRI PD R=4 PnP-CM mean PSNR changes from 32.69 to 35.57. These are revised reported results, not established controlled performance gains. Original two-NFE comparator entries and LSUN ablation/sweep results are removed or replaced.

M1.justification: v2 implements nonlinear data-fidelity optimization, including a differentiable JPEG surrogate, whereas v1 left nonlinear implementation to future work. Supplement B.1 also adds phase-retrieval output disambiguation and specifies median-filter initialization for inpainting, contrasting with v1's explicit zero-initialization/no-heuristics description. The ADMM-CM core remains; the explicit CM noise-scale parameter mainly formalizes separately tuned noise levels already mentioned in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, related-work discussion, acceleration narrative, and results discussion are substantially rewritten. v2 introduces separate Final Algorithm and Ablation Studies subsections, removes the standalone Discussion section, and reorganizes the appendices into experimental details, training details, and further results. These changes extend beyond renaming and renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws the introductory overview, and merges the original natural-image and MRI tables into an expanded multipart Table 1. It adds nonlinear comparisons, a sensitivity plot, and CelebA-HQ image grids. Retained LSUN and MRI grids are expanded with comparator columns and rearranged; new hyperparameter and momentum tables further change the presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 replaces the Schrödinger-bridge discussion of I2SB/CDDB with substantive positioning against diffusion-based PnP approaches, including newly cited work by Graikos, Park, Wu, and Xu/Chi. v2 also expands nonlinear-imaging references and more explicitly positions noise and momentum as established acceleration techniques, including momentum-ADMM prior work.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 removes v1's specialized empirical ODE, dx/dt = -t sϕ, and instead describes sampling through the general drift/diffusion probability-flow equation. This is a limited mathematical-formulation revision. Theorem 1, its Lipschitz and summable-noise assumptions, and Appendix A's convergence argument remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility: it addresses v1's acknowledged narrow natural-image coverage and untested nonlinear extension, adds relevant diffusion-PnP comparisons, and documents tuning with sensitivity evidence and explicit coefficients. These gains outweigh the loss of some original LSUN analyses. Important gaps remain: Table 3 omits LSUN coefficients, and broad superiority wording is not supported uniformly across Table 1's metrics.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PnP-CM research, with matching authors, core algorithm, and convergence theorem. The main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction experiments on LSUN Bedroom, CelebA-HQ, and fastMRI, including nonlinear tasks and additional ablation and sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LSUN Bedroom and fastMRI reconstruction experiments, component ablations, and noise/NFE analyses in Tables 1–4 and the appendices.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the claims of training-free, parameter-free, model-agnostic paneling, broad benchmark improvements, and further gains through fine-tuning. Additional commercial-model evidence supports these existing claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies missing temporal encoding as a limitation affecting ordering questions and explains the task-dependent tradeoffs of index and timestamp overlays. It also expands discussion of native long-video models. The central spatial-versus-temporal tradeoff interpretation remains.

D1.justification: v1 promises code upon acceptance; v2 states that code is available and supplies a project link. v2 also identifies Leonardo at CINECA as a computing resource. Conversely, some dataset counts, including TimeScope's 1500/450-video counts, disappear. Core implementation and fine-tuning settings remain documented.

E1.justification: Both versions use VideoMME, TimeScope, MLVU, MF2, and VNBench, with LLaVA-Video-178K for fine-tuning. The new question-type breakdowns and qualitative examples concern retained benchmark coverage; commercial models do not introduce new datasets or tasks.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds baseline-versus-panel comparisons for models labeled GPT-4o-mini-2025-04-14 and GPT-4.1-2025-04-14 on VideoMME. Existing open-model comparators and the low-res pooling baseline are retained. The cited Qwen2.5 default result was already discussed in v1.

E3.justification: v2 adds commercial-model evaluation configurations using 8 and 32 input frames and a controlled comparison of unencoded, frame-index, and timestamp panels with 32-frame Qwen2.5 on MLVU. Retained experiments preserve their stated metrics, sampling defaults, context sizes, and fine-tuning budget.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends diagnostic analysis through an MLVU question-type breakdown, targeted temporal-encoding ablations, reported overfitting when fine-tuning pooled representations, and two additional qualitative cases. These investigate failure conditions and possible remedies beyond the retained duration, context-size, panel-grid, threshold, and prompt ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates for its experimental results.

E6.justification: New result families extend evidence to commercial models and ordering failures. Added Table 1 rows report baseline/paneled VideoMME accuracies of 51.1/53.6 and 72.5/73.6. New Tables 5–6 report question-type outcomes and ordering accuracy of 48.6 without explicit encoding versus 50.6 with either encoding variant. Retained Tables 1–4 and the relocated prompt table preserve their numerical results.

M1.justification: Supplementary Section 8 introduces optional panels-F and panels-T variants that overlay frame indices or timestamps. These alter the visual inputs. The default dynamic sampling, panel construction, and fine-tuning objective remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 edits paragraphs and captions, retitles experimental subsections, condenses the main dataset description, and organizes supplementary content into numbered sections. The dedicated reproducibility statement is removed and acknowledgments are added. Much of the original narrative and section sequence remains.

P2.justification: The document changes from one-column to two-column formatting throughout. Figures 3–4 switch from side-by-side to vertically stacked plots, and tables and illustrations are resized and relocated. Table 1 gains a commercial-model block; two tables and two qualitative figures are added. The original prompt table becomes Table 7.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including GPT-4, MovieChat, SlowFast-LLaVA, Visual Context Window Extension, and An Image Grid Can Be Worth a Video. Related work more explicitly distinguishes frame-level from token-level processing and contrasts its video-model and fine-tuning contributions with earlier composite-image approaches.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 corrects the panel-construction condition from gamma C >= D to gamma C < D, resolving its contradiction with the unchanged sampling rule in Equation 1. The remaining mathematical formulation and training objective are retained; no proofs are added.

improvement.justification: The added failure analysis and temporal-encoding experiments clarify applicability limits, while commercial-model comparisons, the corrected paneling condition, and reported code access strengthen the paper. These gains are tempered by an unexplained inconsistency: v2 reports plain-panel MLVU accuracy as 64.9 in Table 1 but 63.4 in Table 6 under the same stated model and frame count. Overall, the evidence supports a limited quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Video Panels for Long Video Understanding. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite extensive layout changes.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds commercial-model evaluations, question-type analyses, and temporal-encoding experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original paneling evaluations across five benchmarks, fine-tuning experiments, ablations, and qualitative examples.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a multi-source dataset with structured descriptions. v2 increases the claimed resource size and broadens the benchmark contribution to diffusion and autoregression. It also replaces v1's introduction claim of consistent improvements from progressively adding sources with a narrower statement about supporting diversity and detail.

C2.justification: Section 10 extends the single-source overfitting and multi-source generalization interpretation to autoregressive models. The introduction adds an argument connecting part-level object generation and scene generation through enriched bounding boxes. Existing explanations of diffusion results and the limitation concerning language-model annotation noise remain.

D1.justification: Sections 8.2–8.3 substantially expand implementation disclosure, specifying 120-object padding, coordinate ordering, orientation encoding, BERT conditioning, attribute embeddings, diffusion learning-rate decay, and autoregressive training details. These disclosures do not establish changes to the existing diffusion procedure. The abstract also newly promises dataset and code release upon acceptance, without establishing actual availability.

E1.justification: The three data sources, 26 scene categories, and bedroom/dining-room/living-room evaluation coverage remain unchanged. Although v2 enlarges Inf3DLayout, Section 8.1 explicitly retains the original 15,080-scene experimental subset. No new task, domain, or test scenario is evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds AR-M3DLayout to the comparison alongside the retained diffusion model, DiffuScene, and InstructScene. The external comparator set, including its participation in the qualitative comparison and user study, is unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported diffusion optimizer changes from AdamW in v1 Appendix A.1 to Adam in v2 Section 8.3; the PDFs do not establish that experiments were rerun. v2 also introduces autoregressive training settings and timing metrics. Existing splits, 1,500 test prompts, and user-study design remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends supplementary analysis with source-specific autoregressive ablations (Table 5), computational-efficiency comparisons (Table 4), and five additional prompt-adherence examples (Figure 11). The earlier diffusion ablations are retained in Table 5, not removed.

E5.justification: Figure 6 retains the same user-study means and error bars, without newly explaining their statistical meaning. Model results remain point estimates; neither version supplies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Reported dataset totals increase from 15,080 layouts and 258,413 objects to 21,367 and 433,842, with revised distribution statistics. New results include AR-M3DLayout's Inf3DLayout FID of 57.90 and CLIP-Score of 0.2026, three autoregressive ablation rows, and timing measurements. Existing diffusion, external-baseline, and user-study results are unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 adds an autoregressive Transformer encoder alongside the diffusion generator. It predicts objects sequentially from text and preceding objects, uses start/end tokens, and minimizes object-parameter negative log-likelihood (Sections 4.3 and 8.2). This is a distinct generation procedure.

P1.justification: The unified Benchmark section becomes separate Indoor Scene Generation and Experiments sections. Appendix A is reorganized into a supplement with an overview and dedicated implementation, visualization, ablation, and retrieval sections; references move behind supplementary text. Motivation and model explanations are also expanded.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout, substantially resizing figures and tables. The original Table 3 is split between benchmark and supplementary ablation tables. v2 adds a timing table and autoregressive/prompt-adherence figures, while retaining and relocating earlier visual material.

R1.justification: v2 adds AutoPartGen, OmniPart, X-Part, and CoPart, with an introduction paragraph positioning layouts as a bridge between part-level object generation and scene generation. The existing indoor-dataset and scene-synthesis related-work discussion is largely retained.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4.3 adds the autoregressive conditional-likelihood factorization and its negative-log-likelihood training formulation. The diffusion reverse distribution and noise-prediction objective are retained. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: The autoregressive benchmark and source ablations broaden evidence for the dataset's utility, while Section 8 substantially improves implementation disclosure. These gains support a limited net improvement: the enlarged corpus is not experimentally evaluated, timing results lack hardware and measurement controls, and the optimizer revision is not reconciled with unchanged diffusion scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe M3DLayout and retain matching dataset construction and benchmark material. Text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, allowing additions to be distinguished from relocations.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds autoregressive-model results, source ablations, and generation-time measurements in Tables 3–5.

before.justification: v1 reports original diffusion-model experiments and source ablations in Table 3, generated layouts, and a 42-participant perceptual study in Figure 6.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the 21,367-layout multi-source dataset, the detailed Inf3DLayout subset, and diffusion/autoregressive benchmarks demonstrating richer, text-controllable layouts. Additional validation supports these retained claims without redefining their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the added audits as supporting dataset quality and explains that shape codes are omitted because Matterport scans lack complete object shapes. It also removes v2's conclusion warning that language-model-generated descriptions may contain noise. Existing explanations of generation performance and generalization remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 specifies the axis-aligned IoU calculation and explicitly documents training without shape-code embeddings. R1.justification: Related work adds SANA-Video, Compact Attention, SpargeAttn, trainable sparse attention, sliding tile attention, and an Open-Sora reference. Positioning shifts toward lightweight conversion and all-token attention, replacing explicit superiority statements over Efficient-vDiT and M4V with broader comparisons.

T1.justification: The attention equations, feature-map construction, loss definitions, and knapsack formulation retain their mathematical substance. Dimension notation and equation formatting are simplified; no new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears.

improvement.justification: Mobile measurements provide practical support for the central efficiency argument beyond v1's FLOPs comparisons, and newer baselines and moderated novelty claims improve positioning. The gain is limited by block-level rather than end-to-end timing, unexplained VBench score revisions, and inconsistencies between the new VBench-2.0 summary and retained appendix.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Attention Surgery work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions.

after.justification: v3 retains original generation experiments and the human study, and additionally reports mobile latency and memory-traffic measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original VBench and VBench-2.0 evaluations, component ablations, generated-video examples, and a human study comprising 562 paired comparisons.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on high-quality, efficient transparent generation through a shared-latent VAE and curated data. v3 redefines the central contribution as shifting alpha distributions while preserving RGB generation, explicitly claiming stable and spatially controllable transparency. These new mechanism and capability claims appear throughout the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 attributes transparency holes to RGB–alpha entanglement and explains why preserving RGB capability can retain unwanted backgrounds without mean sampling. It adds qualifications about weak control at small mean shifts and red bias at large shifts. v1's broader discussion of remaining unnatural content, background debris and inaccurate masks is no longer retained as a limitations assessment.

D1.justification: v3 specifies the Wan2.1-T2V-14B backbone, its I2V counterpart, and a typical mean-shift strength of 0.05. It omits v1's 272 × 272, 17-frame crop specification, caption-language/manual-refinement details and testing-prompt instructions. Common adapter ranks, batch sizes and the project link remain. These omissions establish documentation changes, not changes to the underlying preprocessing.

E1.justification: The underlying matting datasets and Internet-data domains remain. However, v3 adds mask-conditioned generation with controllable subject position and size, and trains Wan2.1-I2V-14B for image-and-text-conditioned animation (Section 4.4; Figures 9–10). These extend v1's text-to-video task requirements. Changes in training sample counts are settings changes, not new dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates TransPixeler's open and closed versions. v3 retains both and adds LayerFlow (Single) and LayerDiffuse + AnimateDiff to the comparisons in Figure 5 and Tables 1–2. Figure 6 additionally evaluates Wan + MatAnyone, introducing a generation-plus-matting alternative.

E3.justification: v3 introduces white-background evaluation with VBench and GPT-4o metrics, user-ranking evaluation, and PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS reconstruction tests. Reported VAE/DiT training budgets change from 60,000/1,500 to 75,000/1,750 iterations. The generation-training collection changes from 437 to 429 samples: images increase from 20 to 43, Internet-effects videos decrease from 116 to 85, and matting videos remain 301.

E4.justification: v1 provides illustrative failures but no component ablations. v3 adds reconstruction ablations for rendering and the bidirectional loss (Table 3), generation ablations for that loss and mean sampling (Figure 7), mean-shift sensitivity tests (Figure 8), and mask-geometry tests (Figure 9). The earlier astronaut and explosion failure examples are not retained.

E5.justification: Neither PDF reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. v3's new scores and average user rankings are point estimates; they do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds the first quantitative comparison, user-ranking and reconstruction tables. Examples include text alignment 4.00 and aesthetics 0.649 in Table 1, transparency/overall ranks 1.23/1.11 in Table 2, and full-model RGB/alpha PSNR 41.47/42.22 in Table 3. Qualitative comparisons are replaced and control/animation findings added. These are newly reported results, not matched v1-to-v3 gains; the 128-second versus 32-minute timing comparison remains.

M1.justification: v3 adds a transparency-aware bidirectional diffusion loss using a frozen DiT during VAE training, beyond v1's reconstruction objectives. It also introduces alpha-derived Gaussian ellipse masks that shift noise means during training and inference, enabling spatial transparency control. These change the objectives and generation procedure while retaining the shared-latent VAE and LoRA/DoRA framework.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method narrative and conclusion. It creates a separate Related Work section, consolidates dataset discussion, compresses the reconstruction-loss exposition, and reorganizes experiments around comparisons, ablations and applications instead of v1's extended results gallery and limitations section.

P2.justification: The single-column presentation becomes a two-column layout. Framework diagrams are redrawn to include the new components, the detailed feature-merge diagram disappears, and several dataset illustrations are consolidated into Figure 4. Long comparison galleries are replaced by compact comparison panels, three quantitative tables, and new ablation, control and animation figures.

R1.justification: v3 substantially repositions the work around distribution separation, criticizing prior methods for entangling RGB and alpha rather than primarily emphasizing quality and efficiency. It connects its sampler to BBDM, TKG-DM, ShiftDDPMs and Shifted Diffusion, and expands the comparison and evaluation literature with MatAnyone, VBench and OpenS2V.

T1.justification: v3 introduces mathematical definitions for the signed transparency mask and bidirectional loss, conditional Gaussian noise, and covariance-based ellipse construction (Equations 1–3 and 12–19). No theorems or proofs are added. Equation 13 also writes the velocity target as Z_t minus shifted noise, unlike v1's noise minus Z; this is inconsistent with the stated interpolation.

improvement.justification: v1's superiority claims rely mainly on selected visual examples and timing. v3 substantially strengthens their support through broader comparisons and component ablations, especially Table 3 and Figure 7. Material weaknesses remain: study sizes and uncertainty are unspecified, reproducibility details disappear, and Equation 13 is inconsistent. Table 2's transparency ranks also total 14 rather than the 15 expected for complete untied five-method rankings, without explanation. These issues limit confidence, but the controlled analyses provide a substantial net improvement in experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Wan-based RGB-A video-generation project despite retitling and substantial revisions. All pages, figures, tables and equations support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix; v3 references separate supplementary material that is not included.

after.justification: v3 reports original quantitative comparisons, user rankings and reconstruction ablations in Tables 1–3, alongside transparency-control and image-to-video demonstrations.

before.justification: v1 reports original generated-video comparisons, inference timings and failure examples in Sections 3.2–3.4 and Figures 10–20.

C1.justification: Both abstracts, contribution lists, and conclusions retain the same central claims: adaptive global–regional coupling through SAA, monthly expert routing through TMoE, and superior performance across four forecasting tasks. The additional experiments support these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds an accuracy–parameter tradeoff supporting twelve experts and identifies the 24-expert configuration as computationally prohibitive. It also interprets Gaussian routing relative to one-hot routing and characterizes distance-metric effects as limited, with Great Circle performing best. These are bounded additions to the existing mechanism explanations.

D1.justification: V2 specifies Xavier-uniform initialization for the spatial-prior ablation and reports parameter counts for expert configurations. Its dataset and training summary largely relocates existing information. However, the missing referenced appendix prevents determining whether v1's normalization instructions, reconstruction loss, frozen-backbone training details, and code-access disclosure were retained or revised, leaving the overall extent uncertain.

E1.justification: The documented coverage remains ERA5 global forecasting, Eastern Asian regional forecasting, Typhoons Ewiniar and Yinxing, and long-range and ensemble forecasting. V2's additional ablations and extended typhoon horizon do not establish a new dataset, domain, or task.

E2.justification: The typhoon comparison expands substantially from ECMWF alone in v1 Figures 9 and 11 to operational and learned forecasting methods. V2 Figure 9 adds FourCastNet, FengWu, and Pangu-Weather to both track comparisons; its Yinxing error plot includes ECMWF, FengWu, and Pangu. Comparator membership in the retained main global and ensemble comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: The quantitative Yinxing evaluation extends from four days in v1 Appendix Figure 11 to five days in v2 Figure 9c. New ablation protocols vary expert count and temporal allocation, Gaussian versus one-hot embeddings, and spatial-distance choice. The training period, AdamW learning rate, batch size, epochs, and GPU count summarized in v2 already appear in v1's appendix.

E4.justification: V2 Tables 4–5 substantially extend the original component-removal ablations by testing temporal granularity and expert count, Gaussian versus one-hot routing, and Manhattan versus Euclidean versus Great Circle initialization. These analyses are absent from v1, including its appendix, and directly examine design choices behind both proposed modules.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports training-seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained ensemble evaluation uses the same ten initial conditions; no change in statistical reporting practice is documented.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial ablation and typhoon-comparison results. Table 2 replaces the regional RMSE row, including 0.0493 to 0.0478 at six hours and 0.4945 to 0.4921 at ten days; Table 5 associates these with Manhattan and Great Circle configurations. Figure 9 reports five-day Yinxing mean errors of 96.5 km for STCast versus 160.0 km for Pangu. These are not directly comparable to v1's four-day averages. Tables 1 and 3 remain numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: SAA replaces the coordinate-based distance described as Manhattan in v1 with latitude/longitude expressions described as Great Circle in v2 Section 3.2. This changes spatial-prior initialization within the retained framework. The alternating attention architecture described in v2 already appears in v1's appendix, so it is not a new component.

P1.justification: The shared main text receives localized rewriting, numbered sections and cross-references, terminology corrections, and reordered experimental discussion. Dataset/training information and the backbone overview move from v1's appendix into the main text. Most of the abstract, introduction, related-work narrative, and conclusion remains closely matched.

P2.justification: V2 adds two ablation tables and revises Figure 9, replacing the three MSL panels with a Yinxing error curve and expanding the track legends and comparisons. Table captions, headers, and placement are reformatted, while most existing diagrams and plots are retained. Presentation changes within the unavailable v2 appendix cannot be checked.

R1.justification: V2 adds Prithvi WxC to regional-weather positioning and cites Efficient Attention for the attention formulation. Several appendix-associated references, including KARINA and WeatherBench 2, are absent from its bibliography. The main positioning against OneForecast and earlier MoE weather models remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The spatial-distance definition changes from v1 Equation 1 to the latitude/longitude expressions in v2 Equations 1–3. V2 Equation 5 also explicitly formulates the previously described and diagrammed efficient attention operation. The Gaussian routing mathematics is retained, and no new theorem or proof is presented.

improvement.justification: The new ablations provide useful evidence for central design choices, and the expanded typhoon comparisons strengthen evaluation beyond ECMWF. However, v2's referenced appendix is absent, preventing verification of the detailed method, reproducibility information, and supplementary validation available in v1. These demonstrated benefits and unresolved material-completeness issues prevent a reliable paper-level judgment of net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe STCast and their included pages are readable. However, v1 contains an appendix on PDF pages 11–47, whereas v2 ends with references on page 11 despite repeatedly referring to an appendix. The shared main text supports reliable comparison, but appendix-level changes remain partly unresolved.

after.justification: V2 retains original forecasting experiments and reports additional expert-routing and distance-metric ablations, plus expanded typhoon comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original STCast forecasting results, component ablations, ensemble experiments, and typhoon analyses in the main text and appendix.

C2.justification: Both retain the same explanations involving adaptive boundaries and monthly expert specialization, along with the accuracy-versus-parameter tradeoff supporting 12 experts. No substantive limitation or applicability qualification is added.

D1.justification: v3 adds an explicit STCast code-repository link at the end of the abstract; v2 has no such link. Training and hardware disclosures remain unchanged. The PDFs establish the added access information but do not establish the repository's contents or usability.

E1.justification: Both use ERA5 for global and Eastern Asia regional forecasting, evaluate the 2024 Ewiniar and Yinxing typhoons, and retain the same long-range and ensemble forecasting scenarios.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged across the reported comparisons. Tables 1 and 3 retain Pangu, Graphcast, Fuxi and OneForecast; regional comparisons retain Direct Train and OneForecast, and Figures 5 and 9 retain their respective comparator sets.

E3.justification: The reported training period, variable counts, 100-epoch budget, batch size 16, forecast horizons and evaluation metrics are unchanged. Ensemble evaluation still uses the same 10 initial conditions described in Section 4.2.

E4.justification: Both retain the component ablations in Table 2, expert-count and embedding comparisons in Table 4, distance-metric comparisons in Table 5, and spatial-error and 100-day forecast visualizations in Figures 6–8.

E5.justification: Ensemble sampling and averaging descriptions are unchanged. Neither version adds training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or other statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The numerical tables, plotted curves and qualitative forecast maps are unchanged. For example, Table 1 reports STCast's 10-day RMSE/ACC as 0.5763/0.4715 in both, and Figure 9 reports the same 96.5 km average Yinxing track error.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same STCast architecture, Spatial-Aligned Attention, Gaussian month-conditioned Temporal Mixture-of-Experts, and Perlin-noise ensemble procedure.

P1.justification: v3 makes a small abstract edit, updates the author/contact line to identify corresponding authors, and adds Section 6, Acknowledgements. The scientific narrative and existing section organization remain unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 removes printed page numbers, adjusts the first-page text layout, and reflows the bibliography around the new acknowledgements. Figures 1–9 and Tables 1–5 retain their displays, captions and placement.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion and all 52 bibliography entries are unchanged. Positioning relative to OneForecast and earlier mixture-of-experts forecasting methods is retained.

T1.justification: The task definitions and mathematical formulations in Section 3, including distance, attention and Gaussian-routing equations (1)–(7), are unchanged. No theorem, proof or derivation is added.

improvement.justification: The explicit code-access pointer and new funding acknowledgements modestly improve documentation and transparency. Scientific methods, evidence and analyses remain unchanged. The referenced appendix is still absent, and code usability cannot be established from the supplied PDFs, so the supported improvement is limited.

A1.justification: Both are readable 11-page versions of the same STCast paper, with corresponding text, equations, figures and tables. However, both reference an Appendix containing additional details and experiments that neither supplied PDF includes. The judgments below cover the supplied material.

after.justification: v3 retains these original forecasting experiments and ablation results, including numerical evaluations of STCast.

before.justification: v2 reports original global and regional forecasting experiments, typhoon predictions, ensemble results and ablations in Section 4, Tables 1–5 and Figures 5–9.

C1.justification: The benchmark contributions and headline accuracy claims remain unchanged. However, the introduction broadens the bottleneck hypothesis from fixed-token encoder compression to visual representations and multimodal alignment, while the new concluding limitations qualify generalization to natural-image benchmarks.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive discussion of artistic abstraction, texture-versus-shape bias, and limits on transfer to natural images. Appendix B also newly attributes difficulty to image/question content rather than domain shift. Its claim that Figure 9 proves this attribution exceeds what the uncontrolled per-image distributions establish.

D1.justification: New Appendix I/Table 4 supplies creators, titles, dates, and source links for all 150 artworks. Appendix A documents the complexity assessor, prompt, and sampling parameters; Appendix H adds complexity_win_rate database information and the PyArrow distribution format. These substantially expand provenance and reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 150 artworks and 2,720 questions across six task categories, with the same stated OCR languages. The new appendix analyses reuse these images; the domain-shift discussion adds no natural-image evaluation.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains all 37 models and both chance baselines. Comparator membership in the blind, resolution, and prompting experiments is also unchanged. Qwen3.5-27B serves as the new complexity assessor, not an added VQA comparator.

E3.justification: v3 adds counting RMSE and per-model normalized OCR edit-distance reporting to Table 1. Appendix A introduces an auxiliary pairwise complexity-scoring protocol, and Appendix B aggregates accuracy by image. The original VQA splits, preprocessing, decoding policy, and resolution/prompting settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix A measures relative image complexity across all 150 images, including extremes and a score distribution. New Appendix B examines per-image accuracy for DeepSeek VL2, InternVL3 8B, and o3 to investigate domain shift. These substantially expand dataset validation beyond the retained error, resolution, prompting, and embedding analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The counting-tolerance mean-and-standard-deviation display is retained. The new parenthesized table values are error metrics, and the complexity scorer's sampling settings do not establish repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds error-magnitude results for all 37 models, including o3 counting RMSE of 4.0 and OCR edit distance of 0.24, plus complexity win rates and three per-image accuracy distributions. All matched accuracy entries in the main, blind, and CoT tables are unchanged; the expansion supplies additional findings rather than performance gains.

M1.justification: The benchmark's collection and annotation procedure, question formats, answer extraction, and paired-answer scoring remain unchanged. The new Qwen3.5 complexity scoring characterizes the existing dataset without revising the VQA procedure.

P1.justification: The main six-section narrative and most prose remain intact. v3 locally rewrites the motivation and benchmark comparisons, shortens datasheet questions, and replaces the numbered appendix subsections with named supplementary sections and an overview.

P2.justification: v3 replaces the single-column format with a two-column layout, adds an artwork collage and new diagnostic figures, expands the main table, and adds the artwork catalogue. It also separates the counting panels, redraws existing plots, and relocates the unchanged blind-results table to the supplement.

R1.justification: v3 adds explicit distinctions from prior art-VQA work, including VISCOUNTH and Garcia et al., extends the discussion to DocVQA and SlideVQA, and cites literature on complexity and perceptual biases. These broaden the supporting context while retaining the central positioning around knowledge-free perception in dense scenes.

T1.justification: Appendix A newly defines an image's complexity score as its empirical win rate across pairwise comparisons. This is a limited new quantitative definition; no theorem, proof, or formal performance guarantee is added.

improvement.justification: v3 improves auditability through complete artwork provenance, documented complexity scoring, and per-model error magnitudes, while explicitly acknowledging the art-domain limitation absent from v1. The gains are tempered by the unvalidated complexity assessor and Figure 9's unsupported claim to rule out domain shift. Overall, the documentation and diagnostic additions provide a clear but limited improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VisualOverload and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Retained content can be reliably matched across the substantial formatting changes and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds image-complexity measurements, per-image accuracy distributions, and per-model error metrics.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 37 VLMs, blind evaluations, error analyses, and appendix experiments on resolution and chain-of-thought prompting.

C1.justification: v3 broadens the headline claims to superiority over dedicated moderation tools and generalization across external safety benchmarks. Its contribution list replaces v1's explicit first-formalization contribution with a systematic vulnerability and component-analysis contribution. The MMDS dataset and joint user/assistant moderation contributions remain central.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of image-driven risk, dialogue progression, and MCTS effectiveness. It qualifies late-turn trends because samples become sparse, retains rationales chiefly for interpretability despite modest performance effects, and distinguishes augmentation benefits on targeted scenarios from ordinary MMDS performance. New limitations address long-context computational cost and false positives, supported by WildChat results.

D1.justification: The expanded appendix supplies generation, annotation, moderation, attacker, and evaluator prompts; detailed policy specifications; image-resolution thresholds and CLIP configuration; three-expert annotation procedures; and role-specific rationale-generation instructions. v3 also adds a project-page link, although Appendix F still describes data/model release as planned. These disclosures substantially exceed v1's training and MCTS settings.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates moderation on MMDS and its policy-relaxation subset. v3 adds MM-SafetyBench, VLGuard-Test, ActorAttack, SafeDialBench (English), and benign WildChat dialogues, extending evaluation to single-turn multimodal and external text-only multi-turn settings. Appendix D.4 also adds human-crafted multimodal dialogues.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds InternVL3.5-38B, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, Gemini-2.5-Pro, OpenAI Moderation, and Llama Guard-4-12B. Additional comparisons introduce LlavaGuard, Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B, their combined OR baseline, and linear search against MCTS. These are evaluated comparators, beyond additions to related-work citations.

E3.justification: v3 introduces rationale retraining/inference ablations, paired image-removal tests with regenerated target responses, and four 100-sample augmentation evaluations. Existing MMDS splits and principal training settings remain unchanged. The reported malicious-intent count changes from 350 to 348, and the attack target changes from Claude-3.5-Sonnet to Claude-3.7-Sonnet without establishing reruns. Policy adaptation now uses FPR instead of safe-class recall.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's policy-adaptation and per-dimension analyses, v3 adds rationale ablation, leave-one-out augmentation ablations, image-removal and dialogue-length analyses, MCTS-versus-linear search, safeguard-combination analysis, generated-image quality assessment, and a human-versus-synthetic generalization check. Figures 17–19 also add comparative case studies.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run summaries, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v3 acknowledges that sparse late-turn observations have high variance, but does not introduce an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: LLaVAShield's MMDS F1 remains 95.71%/92.24%, and Table 2 is unchanged. Table 1 revises Qwen2.5-VL-72B F1 from 33.50%/27.03% to 33.33%/28.00%. Substantial new results include 97.62% average MM-SafetyBench recall, 15/16 human-crafted attacks detected, and extensive ablation results. The policy-test FPR values merely re-express v1's safe-recall outcomes.

M1.justification: The LLaVA-OV-7B model, supervised objective, structured outputs, and core MCTS procedure remain intact. One explicit procedural revision concerns augmentation: v1 Section 3.4 says policy relaxation is not used independently, whereas v3 Appendix A.3.2 describes both independent and combined use. Expanded rationale-generation details otherwise do not establish that the original model was changed or retrained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related work are substantially rewritten, with the introduction organized around three risk characteristics. Detailed MCTS and dataset explanations move into a much broader appendix structure. Main-text method sections are consolidated, discussion is reorganized, and MMRT-MCTS is generally renamed MMRT.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 gains explicit risk annotations; the taxonomy is recolored and relocated, with a new main-text summary and intent-distribution plot. Test distributions are reorganized across appendix displays, and numerous experimental tables, component plots, prompt panels, and case-study figures are added. The old policy-adaptation table becomes prose.

R1.justification: Related work expands from multi-turn attacks and VLM moderation to broader black-box search, visual jailbreaks, industrial moderation, and newer safeguards. v3 explicitly credits IDEATOR as inspiration and acknowledges Llama Guard-4's multi-image/multi-turn capabilities, refining the claimed gap. This materially changes research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The conditional-generation objective and MCTS selection and reward mathematics are retained under revised notation and placement. Added dialogue-state notation, standard cosine similarity, and an average-score metric do not introduce substantive theoretical reasoning. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence relied mainly on MMDS and lacked component ablations and direct comparisons with dedicated safeguards. v3 substantially addresses these weaknesses through external benchmarks, stronger comparator coverage, controlled analyses, and extensive reproducibility details. New benign-dialogue results expose a meaningful false-positive tradeoff, acknowledged in the limitations. Although uncertainty remains unquantified and some rollout pseudocode is inconsistent, the empirical support and transparency improve substantially.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LLaVAShield, MMDS, and the same MCTS-based red-teaming framework. Their main text and complete appendices are readable, including figures and prompt templates inspected visually, and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds external benchmark evaluations, ablations, image and dialogue-turn analyses, and human-crafted dialogue results.

before.justification: v1 reports original MMDS moderation experiments, policy-adaptation tests, and red-teaming attack success rates in Tables 1–4.

C2.justification: The new 'Unified vs. Specialized' discussion attributes stability under unified training to adaptive routing that reduces domain conflicts, and interprets gains on MulSen-AD and BraTS as benefits for data-scarce infrared and complex multimodal inputs. P1.justification: There are localized introduction rewrites, method-description clarifications, author-affiliation and contribution-label edits, and a short new appendix comparison section. The main section sequence and most explanatory prose are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a document-wide visual redesign with institutional branding, a boxed full-width abstract, colored headings, running headers, and extensive figure/table relocation and resizing. Figure 5 is restyled, a training-control table is added, Table 3 is additionally displayed with CCL, and the efficiency table gains a FLOPs column. Existing appendix qualitative panels are retained.

The introduction also refines its characterization of earlier approaches toward fixed modality combinations rather than universally single-class models. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UniMMAD. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds specialized-versus-unified training comparisons and results against CCL.

before.justification: v1 reports original anomaly-detection results, component ablations, continual-learning experiments, and efficiency measurements, with additional results in the appendix.
