The eyeballing advantage is specified against GPT-5. The central paradigm, benchmark, few-shot learning, and self-consistency contributions remain.

C2.justification: V2 introduces a five-ability hierarchy and a rationale connecting visual text learning with language reasoning. Its visual-puzzle interpretation emphasizes competitiveness with Claude on symmetry rather than shape-drawing tasks. The strong characterization of temporal consistency as a confidence proxy is removed, while the prompt-rewriter hypothesis and closed-model limitation remain.

D1.justification: V2 documents the mini-set composition and changes the benchmark access link from the fnlp namespace to OpenMOSS-Team. Conversely, it omits the exact ARC-AGI-2 prompt and detailed palette-based grid extraction procedure, and removes the official-result markers for AIME25 and GPQA comparators. Most other prompts and generation parameters are retained or relocated.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same eyeballing puzzles, visual puzzles, ARC-AGI-2, three maze geometries, and text-centric benchmarks. V2's 750-sample mini set draws from the existing 4,149-sample benchmark. Renamed task groupings and additional model evaluations do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Tables 7–8 substantially expand comparisons with Veo 3.1, MiniMax Hailuo 2.3, Seedance 1.0 Pro, MOVA, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B, five image generators, and Qwen3-VL variants. Image comparators include Nano Banana Pro, Seedream 4.5, GPT Image 1.5, BAGEL, and Qwen-Image-Edit-2511. V2 also adds Grok 4 to the ARC-AGI-2 comparison and VLM comparisons on mazes.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a separate 750-sample evaluation subset comprising 500 vision-centric and 250 text-centric samples. Table 1 switches text-centric summaries from last-frame to audio accuracy, and visual-puzzle aggregation changes from color/shape groups to symmetry/gradient/compositionality. Joint video/audio correctness metrics are dropped. The stated Perpendicular VLM prompt is corrected; unchanged scores do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds qualitative multimodal-question cases from MathVista, MMMU, and MMBench. Visual-puzzle subgroup analysis shifts from output type to reasoning type. The principal few-shot, self-consistency, numerical-perturbation, prompt-rewriting, and reasoning-error analyses remain substantially unchanged.

E5.justification: The stated Avg@4 AIME reporting and five-attempt self-consistency voting are retained. V2 adds no seed reporting, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests; its new comparison tables continue reporting point accuracies.

E6.justification: Tables 7–8 add extensive mini-set results, including vision-centric averages of 31.6% for Sora-2, 27.7% for Veo 3.1, and 29.8% for Nano Banana Pro. All 13 retained text-benchmark rows are unchanged, but reported overall last-frame/audio averages change from 56.3/73.6 to 57.0/67.8. V2 also corrects the ARC summary to match v1 Table 4, reports new subgroup aggregates, and removes joint-modality result entries. These changes do not establish same-setting Sora-2 performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed video-generation reasoning approach, inputs and outputs, and existing few-shot and self-consistency procedures remain unchanged. Additional evaluated models are comparators; no new architecture, training objective, or proposed algorithmic component is introduced.

P1.justification: The main evaluation and analysis sections are extensively condensed and rewritten around reasoning capabilities. Detailed protocols and results move into reorganized appendices, and prompts are consolidated into Appendix F. Terminology, affiliations, and correspondence information are also revised.

P2.justification: V2 adds bar-chart presentations of retained eyeballing and visual-puzzle results while moving their detailed tables to the appendix. Numerous overview and case figures are redrawn or rearranged; new mini-set tables and multimodal examples are added. Reasoning examples move into the main text, the category-distribution chart moves to the appendix, and joint-modality table columns disappear.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for new comparators and visual text learning, including DeepSeek-OCR and See the Text. Section 4 now explicitly acknowledges quantitative evaluations in earlier video-reasoning work and presents this benchmark as complementary, while adding a first-systematic-comparison claim concerning Thinking with Images. The overall research positioning remains similar.

T1.justification: The visual-puzzle deviation definitions and equations remain equivalent, including RGB distance and binarized shape mismatch. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs; the new reasoning hierarchy is conceptual rather than mathematical.

improvement.justification: V1's broad paradigm claims relied chiefly on Sora-2 versus three VLMs. V2 Tables 7–8 add comparisons with other video generators and direct image-generation alternatives on a common mini set, substantially strengthening assessment of where video reasoning is competitive. Corrected summary inconsistencies and clearer organization also help. Removed joint-modality statistics and ARC implementation details reduce transparency, but the expanded comparative evidence addresses a substantial weakness and supports a clear overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Thinking with Video and VideoThinkBench, with directly matchable tasks, experiments, and analyses. The complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, and equations, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical studies and adds comparisons involving additional video generators, image generators, and vision-language models in Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original Sora-2 benchmark results, few-shot and self-consistency experiments, reasoning-process analyses, and a Wan2.5 prompt-rewriting ablation.

C1.justification: The introduction's first contribution qualifies v1's categorical claim that decoupled regression 'ignores' relationships and 'leads' to violations as 'often overlooks' and 'can result' in violations. The principal SPAN, training-stability, plug-and-play, and inference-cost claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendices F–H add targeted explanations involving MGIoU's structural constraints and gradients, interpret HTL as an amplifier of geometric-loss benefits, and argue that projection alignment and depth-bias supervision mutually regularize one another. These extend the existing mechanism account, although the depth comparison does not isolate projection alignment from HTL.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page pointer, explicitly documents region-loss aggregation, and supplies batch-one timing information on an RTX 3090, including the 42 ms MonoDGP baseline. Existing training details are retained. The PDFs alone do not establish what resources the project page provides.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate KITTI cars, pedestrians, and cyclists and Waymo vehicles, including the same noise-perturbation scenarios. The added comparisons and depth diagnostics use retained coverage rather than introducing another dataset, task, or environment.

E2.justification: Previously discussed geometric approaches become evaluated alternatives: Table 8 compares MonoDGP augmented with Deep3DBox, Shift R-CNN, or SPAN. Tables 9–10 additionally introduce L1 corner loss, exact 3D IoU, and linear scheduling as comparison choices, substantially expanding the alternatives tested against SPAN's design.

E3.justification: Existing dataset splits, training budgets, hyperparameters, and AP protocols remain unchanged. New experiments introduce batch-one inference timing, depth MAE for 0–20 m, 20–40 m, and beyond 40 m, and loss/schedule substitution controls. Detailed settings for the linear schedule and geometric-strategy integrations are not supplied.

E4.justification: New Appendices F–H test why MGIoU is preferable to alternative corner losses, separate geometric-loss benefits from scheduling using additional controls, and examine depth errors by distance. These substantially extend the original component, weight, and noise ablations, which are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state that validation results average five independent runs. v2 adds no new seed information, run-to-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Figure 6's annotation-deviation statistics are also unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 1–7 are numerically unchanged, but Tables 8–11 substantially expand the reported outcomes. Newly evaluated Deep3DBox and Shift R-CNN augmentations score 21.53 and 22.85 moderate AP3D; L1 and exact-IoU corner losses score 22.68 and 22.75 versus MGIoU's retained 22.89. Linear scheduling scores 22.95. New depth results show far-range MAE of 1.55 m for MonoDGP versus 1.50 m with projection alignment plus HTL, alongside a near-range worsening. These are additional comparisons, not improvements between versions under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: SPAN retains its MGIoU spatial alignment, 2D GIoU projection alignment, and Hierarchical Task Learning procedure. The alternative losses and linear schedule are experimental controls, not replacements for the proposed method. Formula clarifications do not establish an implementation change.

P1.justification: The main narrative is largely retained, with limited contribution and training-stage wording edits, notation clarifications, and correspondence-header changes. Four appendix sections are inserted, and the existing qualitative-results section moves from Appendix E to I.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 8–11 and rearranges existing tables and figures, including reducing the Waymo table to accommodate additional displays. The seven existing figures retain their visual content, and the established table structures largely remain intact.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds three references concerning feature aggregation, RT-DETR, and RT-DETRv4. Appendix E further develops the distinction between SPAN's differentiable optimization and the already-cited Deep3DBox and Shift R-CNN approaches. The overall research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Appendix B, Equation 21 newly defines the aggregate region loss as a sum of per-feature-map Dice losses; v1 specifies only the individual terms. The projection proof and HTL derivation remain unchanged. Other equation edits clarify equivalent indexing and interval notation.

improvement.justification: Tables 8–11 provide useful missing comparisons and controls for geometric strategies, MGIoU, and scheduling, strengthening the evidence behind SPAN's design choices. The improvement is limited by sparse implementation details for the new comparisons and by Table 11 changing projection alignment and HTL together, weakening causal attribution. The original method and benchmark results remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present the same SPAN research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds geometric-strategy comparisons, loss and scheduling controls, timing measurements, and depth-error analysis in Tables 8–11.

before.justification: v1 reports original KITTI and Waymo detection results, component and loss-weight ablations, noise-robustness experiments, and qualitative comparisons.

V1's claims of consistently outperforming alternatives across the board are qualified in v2 as superior overall robustness and superiority in most noise settings. The contribution statement also shifts emphasis from partially labeled or unlabeled learning toward noisy supervision.

C2.justification: V2 extends the prior-ability limitation to Qwen2-VL-2B, explains that unknown label correctness favors a unified schedule over subset-specific assignments, and interprets preprocessing controls as supporting intrinsic GRPO noise tolerance. It also introduces a contamination-based rationale for MMBench-GUI evaluation. The main exploration/exploitation explanation is retained.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code repository address, the InternVL training framework, KL coefficients of 0.04 for GUI grounding and zero for classification, and further benchmark implementation details. Appendix B states that detection shares classification settings. These are additional disclosures; the original hardware, training-time estimates, and most hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 adds OS-World-G evaluation, MMBench-GUI L2 evaluation and training, and GSM8K text-based mathematical reasoning. These substantially broaden the evaluated environments and tasks. ScreenSpot, Pets37, ScreenSpot-Pro, and COCO detection were already present in v1; relocating the detection experiment does not add coverage.

E2.justification: The comparison methods remain the base model, standard GRPO, entropy minimization, entropy maximization, and the retained Figure 1 reward baselines. New benchmarks largely reuse these comparators. Coordinate-format and resizing variants are preprocessing controls rather than new competing methods.

E3.justification: V2 adds InternVL-3.5-2B and Qwen2.5-3B configurations, four-rollout preprocessing controls, and MMBench-GUI training with 500 training/test samples each, switching at step 400 and evaluating at step 500. ScreenSpot-Pro sampling changes in the description from 150 total samples to 150 per category. Its retained scores do not establish that evaluation was rerun under that revised setting.

E4.justification: V2 adds absolute-versus-relative coordinate and image-resizing robustness tests under fully noisy supervision, expands OOD analyses, and introduces MMBench-GUI in-domain experiments explicitly motivated by contamination concerns. Model-family analysis also extends to InternVL. The original switching-point, stage-order, and noisy-data-scaling ablations remain.

E5.justification: Figure 3(b) adds shaded bands around training-accuracy curves; v1 shows only lines in that panel. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or seeds, and v2 does not define the new bands. Thus the visual uncertainty reporting changes without establishing additional runs or a particular statistical estimator.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results, including MMBench-GUI OOD accuracy of 60.6% versus 57.0% for GRPO on clean training data, but GSM8K clean-data accuracy of 79.6% versus GRPO's 81.4%. Existing Table 1 values remain unchanged. Table 2 corrects Qwen2.5-VL-3B GRPO at 50% noise from 76.0% to 76.2%, and Figure 3(b) changes the plotted accuracy trajectories.

M1.justification: The two-stage entropy strategy and Algorithm 1 are retained, but the specified GRPO loss changes: Eqs. (2)–(3) acquire negative signs, and Eq. (3) revises response aggregation. This is a limited correction to the documented optimization objective; the PDFs do not establish that the training implementation changed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodology explanations, and experimental discussion undergo extensive editing. Discussions move inside the experiments section, model comparisons move into main results, and limitations move to a reorganized, lettered appendix. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: Tables 2 and 5 expand, a new main-text OOD table and several appendix tables appear, and Algorithm 1 moves to the supplement. Figure 3 is redrawn with revised labels, legends, and shaded accuracy bands; Figures 1–2 also receive labeling changes. Existing detection and ablation tables are retained with revised placement and formatting.

R1.justification: V2 adds eight references covering new datasets, model families, and related RLVR work. Section 2.2 reframes annotation-free learning around noisy annotations and revises how external and internal reward sources are characterized. The principal external-signal, internal-signal, and entropy-based positioning remains intact.

T1.justification: Eqs. (2)–(3) correct the GRPO loss/gradient signs, replace response-index averaging with an explicit group sum, and introduce response-specific lengths. These are limited mathematical revisions. The entropy definitions and piecewise schedule remain, and no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The broader evaluations and preprocessing controls make the empirical evidence more informative, including revealing failures on new tasks. Corrected equations, several corrected numerical summaries, and added implementation information improve assessability. However, the ScreenSpot-Pro sample-size revision remains unreconciled, Figure 3's new bands are undefined, and the new OOD superiority discussion overstates Table 5. These shortcomings limit the overall benefit despite the substantial expansion.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds model, benchmark, preprocessing, and text-reasoning experiments, including results in Appendix D.

before.justification: V1 reports original training and evaluation results for GUI grounding, fine-grained classification, and open-vocabulary object detection, together with ablations and out-of-distribution evaluations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's four contributions and discussion retain the same scientific claims: developmental visual diets improve robustness, produce biologically aligned patterns and benefit standard SSL through CombDiet. New analyses interpret convergence as evidence against early-stopping effects and distinguish partial replacement by warped views from failure of single-view warping. v2 also qualifies some superiority statements, including changing the appendix's mCE advantage from all baselines to most cases.

D1.justification: The abstract replaces a promised future release with stated code, data and model availability and supplies a GitHub hyperlink. Section 4.2 clarifies that REV reverses stage-duration allocation as well as progression order. Existing optimizer, hardware and temperature-schedule disclosures remain unchanged; the PDFs alone do not verify repository contents.

E2.justification: v2 adds PAPN and MADAug as evaluated curriculum-learning comparators for SimCLR-ResNet on CO3D-10 in Table S6. Existing diet-order controls, Non-Smooth, SHF and standard SSL comparisons are retained; the additional comparison is confined to one configuration.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated CO3D test sampling from two random frames per video to two frames at the training interval. New ablations vary stage durations at fixed total epochs, warm-up proportions, temporal stride and real-versus-warped frame pairing. The stated sampling revision does not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Section S2 tests stage-duration schedules, 30%/50%/70% warm-up ratios, halved/doubled temporal stride and two geometric-warping pairing alternatives. Section S5 adds convergence curves investigating whether the advantage persists after training stabilizes. These substantially expand checks of schedule sensitivity, temporal information and training sufficiency beyond v1's existing controls.

E5.justification: Table 1 and v1 Table S2, now Table S5, change from point estimates to mean ± SEM across three runs. New Table S8 reports mCE t-tests against STD. Figures 3 and S1 already reported three-run standard errors in v1, so this is an expansion of uncertainty reporting, without evidence establishing an increase in run counts.

E6.justification: Central tables and recognition plots contain revised results, alongside new ablation, comparator and TOYS outcomes. For example, Table 1's SimCLR-ViT CombDiet SAY accuracy changes from 55.1 to 54.5 ± 0.3. The CO3D-10-C SimCLR-ViT mCE ranking changes from CombDiet beating STD, 67.6 versus 68.6, to STD leading, 67.8 versus 68.0. Revised sampling and aggregation limit interpretation as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The color and acuity curricula, adjacent-frame temporal objective, SimCLR/DINO adaptations and 30%/70% CombDiet phases remain unchanged. New schedule and pairing variants are experimental controls, not replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most prose are retained, with localized wording edits, corrected table references, changed author order/contact information and an acknowledgement. R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for PAPN, MADAug, synthetic-object datasets, Lu et al.'s developmental visual-diet work and attention-related future directions. T1.justification: The blending expression, curriculum definitions and metric definitions remain substantively unchanged. Neither version presents theoretical propositions or proofs that are added or revised in v2.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's point-estimate tables and narrower diagnostic evidence, v2 provides uncertainty estimates, targeted ablations, convergence checks and explicit applicability limits. C1.justification: The G2U, IPR, and PhysCode contributions and scaling/generalization claims remain. The headline performance claim strengthens from matching GPT-5 overall and surpassing it on Curiosity to surpassing GPT-5 overall.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations concerning latent representations filtering visual distractions, in-domain encoder training, codebook capacity, and structural versus mechanical transfer. It also identifies new failure boundaries involving rapid collisions, visual clutter, and multiple simultaneous threats, extending v1's limitations concerning games and short-horizon imagination.

D1.justification: Sections 9–10 supply recording and preprocessing procedures, baseline adaptations and prompts, architecture specifications, training budgets, sampling settings, and router calibration details largely absent from v1. Examples include 500k PhysCode training steps and eight action candidates. These disclosures do not themselves establish changed experiments. V3 also supplies project/demo access information.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same reported coverage: 863 retro, 134 HTML/Canvas, and three commercial games, evaluated through Survival, Curiosity, and Utility. The supplementary analyses partition or inspect this existing coverage rather than establish an additional dataset or task family.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Qwen3-VL-8B without IPR while retaining the existing comparator families. Table 3 adds VLM + GRPO and VLM + BC + GRPO controls. The Qwen3-VL-A30B label in v1 corresponds to the retained Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B comparator.

E3.justification: Table 2 changes reporting to random-zero/human-one normalization across objectives, replaces higher-is-better normalized ranks with lower-is-better average ranks, and adds an overall rank. Supplementary experiments introduce codebook sweeps, encoder configurations, and value-prediction evaluation. Section 10.5 inconsistently specifies 20 and 50 held-out games, so an actual split-size change cannot be established.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained PhysCode tests and scaling analysis, v3 adds GRPO controls, latent-versus-pixel value prediction, codebook-size sensitivity, encoder-pretraining comparisons, representation visualizations, and factor-wise transfer analysis. Section 12 and Figures 14–24 add extensive success and failure case studies, including IPR's difficulties with simultaneous threats.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Additional averaged results and qualitative claims of significant differences do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2 substantially changes scores and rankings: IPR's Survival/Curiosity/Utility means change from 0.589/7.874/0.178 to 0.252/1.173/0.493. These are revised results under changed reporting, not directly comparable performance gains. New GRPO rows, Tables 4–6, and supplementary analyses add further findings; Table 1 and the scaling curve remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Supplementary Section 10.1 adds an auxiliary temporal head predicting feature changes, a training component absent from v1's method description. The central PhysCode, latent world model, Qwen3-VL-8B, GRPO, and rollout-based action-selection pipeline remains unchanged; most other supplementary specifications are implementation disclosures.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, developing a longer argument across control, reinforcement learning, VLMs, and world models. Supplementary Sections 8–12 introduce a structured explanatory treatment of positioning, benchmark construction, implementation, analyses, and cases, although much of the main method text remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redesigned and its failure-case panel becomes Figure 3. Table 2 gains revised headers, group coloring, and an overall-rank column. V3 adds word clouds, benchmark and recording-tool illustrations, representation and transfer plots, three ablation tables, and extensive case-study sequences. Existing pipeline and scaling figures are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: The expanded introduction and supplementary discussion substantially broaden research positioning, including comparisons with Genie-2/3, SIMA/SIMA-2, Lumine, CombatVLA, and pi-star-0.6. They develop IPR's relationship to latent world models and generalist agents around shared physical and causal invariants, beyond v1's shorter discussion.

T1.justification: The core POMDP formalization and main method equations are retained. Section 9.3 adds a specific power-of-ten definition of the survival reference horizon, and Section 11.2 defines code usage through a 0.1% assignment threshold. These are limited formal definitions; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The added GRPO controls in Table 3 better separate prediction benefits from optimizer choice, while supplementary ablations, implementation details, and explicit failure cases strengthen evidence and transparency. The net improvement is limited by unreconciled metric descriptions across Table 2 and Sections 5.1/9.3, and the conflicting 20-versus-50-game specification in Section 10.5.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IPR-1 and contain readable text, equations, tables, and figures. The supplied v1 ends after its references; v3 includes supplementary Sections 8–12, which were included in this comparison.

after.justification: V3 reports original gameplay experiments and adds GRPO controls, value-prediction and representation ablations, transfer analyses, and qualitative case studies.

before.justification: Sections 5.2–5.5 report original PhysCode validation, comparative gameplay results, zero-shot scaling, and component ablations.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about NTK-guided selection, approximately halved training time, reconstruction quality, and adaptability. The additional appendix evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 interprets super-resolution as recovering missing high-frequency information, the FFHQ experiment as supporting transfer of the NTK mechanism across scales, and the timing measurement as demonstrating negligible overhead. Section 9 also overstates quality superiority over Stand.: Table 9 favors Stand. on all three quality metrics at 1,000 iterations.

D1.justification: Section 11 newly discloses matrix-free computation through a VJP followed by a JVP, together with the model, image resolution, and hardware used for profiling. v2 also adds a project-page link. These clarify implementation and access information; retained experiments' implementation settings otherwise remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds DIV2K super-resolution, requiring reconstruction at coordinates beyond the low-resolution training input, and 1024×1024 FFHQ image fitting. These extend task and data-population coverage beyond the retained Kodak/DIV2K fitting, LibriSpeech audio, and Stanford 3D shape experiments.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the corresponding original experiments, including EVOS variants and Expansive Supervision settings. The new experiments use existing comparators Stand., INT, and EVOS; no new comparison method is introduced.

E3.justification: Section 9 adds a protocol that downsamples 512×512 images to 256×256, trains on the low-resolution input, and evaluates high-resolution reconstruction at 1,000 iterations and time to 20 dB. Section 10 evaluates FFHQ at 1,000 iterations and time to 30 dB. Previously reported evaluation settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 11 adds a focused overhead analysis addressing the cost of NTK scoring: 3.2 ms, or 3.6% of total selection, for a specified Kodak/SIREN/GPU configuration. Existing network-size, architecture, hyperparameter, and sampling ablations in Tables 3–5 and 8 are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional results and timing measurements remain point estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 remain numerically unchanged, while Tables 9–10 and Figures 9–10 add results for previously unevaluated settings. For super-resolution, NINT reaches 20 dB in 7.91 s versus Stand.'s 8.63 s, but has lower 1,000-iteration PSNR: 24.266 versus 24.390. On FFHQ, time to 30 dB is 97.32 versus 141.53 s. Section 11 adds scoring-cost measurements, and Section 7.2 corrects the Unif. CHD example to 5.958×10^-3, matching the unchanged Table 7.

M1.justification: Section 3, Algorithm 1, and the hybrid sampling schedule retain the same scoring and training procedure. Section 11 newly explains computing the existing NTK-gradient product using VJP/JVP operations; it does not establish a change to the underlying method.

P1.justification: v2 appends Sections 9–11, adds acknowledgments and a corresponding-author designation, and makes a small numerical prose correction. The existing narrative, terminology, and section sequence are otherwise substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 9–10 and Figures 9–10 while retaining Tables 1–8 and Figures 1–8. Figure 2 and Algorithm 1 are rearranged within page 4, with additional spacing and pagination changes but no extensive visual redesign.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds Nonparametric Teaching for Attention Learners, listed as reference 77 in v2, to the nonparametric teaching context. The remaining research positioning is retained; shifted reference numbers do not represent additional works or baselines.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, Equations 1–8, and training-dynamics assumptions are retained. Section 11's identity J(Jᵀg)=Kg explains evaluation of the existing NTK product without adding a substantive theoretical result, proof, or assumption.

improvement.justification: Section 11 improves practical assessability by explaining matrix-free NTK computation and measuring its overhead; the super-resolution and FFHQ experiments broaden empirical support. These gains are tempered by Section 9's overstated quality claim: Table 9 favors Stand. on all three fixed-iteration quality metrics, although NINT reaches the target faster. The net improvement is useful but limited.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original super-resolution, FFHQ image fitting, and NTK timing results in Sections 9–11.

before.justification: v1 reports original image, audio, and 3D shape fitting experiments and ablations in Sections 4 and 6–8, including Tables 1–8.

C1.justification: The abstract and three stated contributions retain the same central claims: systematic analysis of visual thinking, capacity-dependent token economy, and a training-free controller improving accuracy and efficiency across six benchmarks. The added transfer evidence supports the existing generality claim rather than introducing a new contribution.

C2.justification: v3 restricts the token-economy interpretation to differing vision stacks under a fixed LLM family and adds a limitation for closed-source models without log-probability access. It removes the interpretation that phrase patterns reflect intrinsic LLM behavior rather than dataset artifacts, and adds explanations about insertion disrupting semantic continuity and branching alone failing to restore grounding.

D1.justification: v3 newly specifies use of one official InternVL reasoning prompt without averaging alternative prompts, clarifies that tabled baselines use Thinking variants of the same checkpoints, and explicitly states the log-probability access requirement. Conversely, it removes the MathVista-mini, MathVision-full and MathVerse-mini subset identifiers without establishing that the evaluated subsets changed.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate MMMU val, MMBench, MMStar, MathVista, MathVision and MathVerse. The new InternVL evaluations reuse retained tasks and datasets; they extend model configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Original Thinking, DEER, DeepConf and REFRAIN remain unchanged in Table 3. Section 4.5 additionally compares the proposed controller against periodic lookback insertion and uncertainty-only branching as ablation controls.

E3.justification: v3 reports an additional fairness control truncating Thinking to the same 16,384-token cap as Instruct, while retaining the original 32,768-token Thinking setting. It also introduces periodic-insertion settings n=1–5, a branching-only control and controller evaluations on InternVL3.5-Think at 4B and 8B.

E4.justification: v3 adds targeted tests of adaptive versus periodic insertion, branching without lookback prompts, budget matching and controller transfer across model families. Existing category, capacity, token-use and visual-sensitivity analyses remain. The explicit observation of similar phrase-alignment patterns across five additional datasets is removed.

E5.justification: The supplied material retains ten sampled paths per item, variation of random seeds, and identical standard-deviation bands and boxplots. No changed run counts, uncertainty-estimation procedures, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: Numerical entries in all four tables and the seven figure images are unchanged. v3 adds periodic-insertion scores, qualitative budget-matching and branching-only findings, and InternVL MMMU/MMStar gains of +1.5/+1.2 at 4B and +3.3/+3.1 at 8B. Section 4.1 replaces the 89% phrase-alignment result with unquantified 'high alignment' and removes the cross-dataset alignment finding.

M1.justification: Sections 4.1–4.3 retain the same visual perplexity probe, offline phrase mining, uncertainty-triggered lookback insertion and optional branch selection by visual helpfulness. Added implementation explanations and ablation variants do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized grammatical and terminology corrections, shortens parts of the introduction, reduces related work from three subsections to two, and adds acknowledgements. The main section sequence and most explanatory prose remain intact.

P2.justification: All seven figures and four tables are retained. The failure example moves from v1 Figure 4 on page 4 to v3 Figure 2 on page 3, and Figure 7 moves from page 7 to page 6. Table 4 is enlarged and its caption completed; equations and surrounding text are also reformatted.

R1.justification: v3 removes the 'Reasoning in LLMs' subsection and associated discussion and citations on overthinking, faithfulness, hallucination cues and distribution shifts, including MME-CoT. The main positioning around visual reasoning and adaptive decoding remains. Consolidation and metadata corrections for retained references are bibliographic editing rather than new research positioning.

T1.justification: The perplexity definition, visual-content and presence contrasts, insertion rule and branch-scoring equation are mathematically unchanged. Moving the perplexity formula inline, renumbering equations and replacing the injection symbol with the established lookback symbol are presentation changes.

improvement.justification: The added controls, InternVL transfer results and clearer applicability limits are useful, but their evidential benefit is uncertain. The new ablation claims periodic insertion is consistently worse although its InternVL score of 60.4 exceeds the reported 59.2 for the proposed method. Its Qwen reference scores, 59.3/61.6, match Table 3's Design column rather than overall 67.0/69.7, without explaining different settings. Missing supplementary details and removed subset identifiers further prevent a reliable judgment that these additions outweigh the reporting problems.

M1.justification: GMLG, dual-modality thresholding, calibration, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix B adds CUDA implementation details without establishing a change to the proposed method.

improvement.justification: v2 improves implementation transparency through the code link and router-kernel details, and corrects Section 6.5's contradiction with Figure 8. C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims about unified pairwise/higher-order alignment, Bird-MML, retrieval, classification, and robustness. The four-modality experiment supports an existing generalization claim. The new abstract release statement changes access information rather than the scientific contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix B.1 newly interprets lambda sensitivity as requiring little tuning and identifies principled lambda selection as future work. Appendix E interprets the artificial four-modality experiment as scalability evidence while acknowledging weak VB100 audio. Section 5.2 removes an explicit inference about avoiding redundant correlations and improving stability across runs.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-and-dataset release statement with a repository address absent from v1. It also describes construction of the new grayscale/low-resolution RGB inputs. Existing Appendix A architecture, optimization, and preprocessing details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds a four-modality input scenario by splitting vision into full-resolution grayscale and low-resolution RGB alongside audio and text, evaluated on SSW60 and VB100. All original datasets and tasks, including appendix CUB200 evaluation, are retained; no new data source is evaluated.

E2.justification: Corresponding existing experiments retain the same CLIP/Tri-CLIP, Symile, GRAM, and TRIANGLE comparators. The new four-modality experiment reuses pairwise CLIP rather than introducing a different comparison method.

E3.justification: The added four-modality experiment introduces grayscale/low-resolution RGB preprocessing and evaluates additional input combinations, including three-input fusion. Previously reported splits, training budgets, metrics, and single-frame/multi-frame bird protocols remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish reruns of those experiments.

E4.justification: New Table 7 expands lambda analysis to accuracy and both retrieval modes at 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8, while retaining the earlier Pareto-selected results as Table 8. Appendix E adds a preliminary test of effectiveness with four modalities. Existing masking, noise, XOR dimensionality, and modality-overlap analyses remain.

E5.justification: New Table 7 supplies standard deviations for aggregate retrieval results previously reported without uncertainty. For example, MUStARD at lambda 0.5 changes from mean-only 45.29/62.56 in v1 Table 7 to 45.3±2.6/62.6±3.1. Existing five-run statements are unchanged; no increase in runs is documented.

E6.justification: Table 2 materially revises aggregate comparisons: UR-FUNNY 1-to-1 ConFu/Tri-CLIP changes from 8.7/6.5 to 7.4/8.1, reversing their reported ranking; MUStARD 2-to-1 ConFu/TRIANGLE changes from 50.0/29.4 to 62.6/50.2. These are corrected averages of unchanged directional scores, not measured performance gains. New Tables 7 and 11 also add sensitivity and four-modality results, substantially expanding the revised result content.

M1.justification: The encoder/fusion design and weighted pairwise-plus-fused InfoNCE objective remain unchanged. The arbitrary-modality objective tested in v2 was already defined in v1 Appendix E; its new evaluation does not introduce a new method.

P1.justification: v2 condenses introductory and experimental prose, adds a brief methodological explanation and acknowledgments, corrects author/affiliation text, and converts Section 6 subsection headings to run-in headings. The overall narrative and section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 7 and 11, retaining earlier appendix Tables 7–9 as Tables 8–10. Several figures receive clearer rendering or revised line, grid, legend, and title formatting; figures and tables move within the document. The author block and introductory question display also change, while the two-column design remains.

R1.justification: Both versions cite the same 48 works and retain the same research positioning. The added Section 3.3 sentence elaborates the existing contrast between loss-level factorization and joint alignment objectives; reference differences are citation-location changes.

T1.justification: The total-correlation decomposition, InfoNCE bounds, and general subset/retrieval objectives in Appendix E are retained. Equation 6 changes fused-subset notation without changing its mathematics. No new proof, assumption, or derivation accompanies the four-modality experiment.

improvement.justification: Correcting Table 2's inconsistent averages improves the reliability of reported comparisons. The added sensitivity table, aggregate uncertainty estimates, preliminary four-modality evidence, and resource address improve empirical support and reproducibility information. These gains are limited: most results and the method remain unchanged, and Table 11 shows mixed fusion benefits in an artificial scenario, so its broad scalability interpretation warrants restraint.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ConFu research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices A–E are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and additionally reports a broader lambda sensitivity comparison and four-modality classification experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original XOR experiments, multimodal retrieval and classification results, and appendix analyses of masking, noise, embedding dimensionality, and few-shot adaptation.

P2.justification: The added URL and text edits produce small layout shifts, including figure positioning and spacing around Table 5; References begins on page 8 instead of page 9. All five figures and five tables retain their content, captions and display structures.

improvement.justification: The added Magma comparison in Section 2 modestly improves research positioning by explaining the distinction from another tracking-based approach. Methods and experimental evidence are unchanged. The project URL provides an access pointer, but removal of the broader release pledge and unverified resource availability limit any claimed reproducibility benefit.

The introduction's new accuracy measurements support the existing reference-quality claim without redefining the core contributions.

C2.justification: The introduction newly explains why image-space and cross-illumination evaluation are particularly suitable for appearance consistency, with geometry providing a metric anchor. Section 4 interprets checkpoint errors as consistent with standard UAV photogrammetry. The main implicit-versus-explicit interpretation and proposed future extensions remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The supplement newly specifies NVIDIA A800 GPUs with 80 GB memory, PyTorch 2.4.1, CUDA 11.8, COLMAP 3.7, and released artifacts; the title page adds a project-page address. Flight altitude and reference anchoring are also newly documented. Conversely, the shortened sunlight description omits some explicit timestamp, coordinate-convention, and alignment explanations from v1.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same 18-scene inventory and outdoor reconstruction/relighting tasks. However, v2's purported remaining-six-scene results include Roof, City2, and City, which lack mappings to that inventory, while Industrial repeats an existing name. The PDFs do not reliably establish whether these are aliases, changed scene coverage, or simply newly reported results for retained coverage.

E2.justification: Both evaluate NeRF-W, NeRF-OSR, GS-W, WildGaussians, and LumiGauss. W-GS and LumiGS in v1 correspond to the expanded names in v2; supplementary GaussianWild corresponds to GS-W. No additional comparator is introduced.

E3.justification: v2 introduces checkpoint-based geometric evaluation across 18 scenes, using approximately 10 checkpoints per scene and vertical/planimetric error measurements. It also revises the reported capture orientation from 'nadir or oblique' to nadir only. The existing A/B evaluation, image metrics, and tabulated training times remain unchanged; these revisions do not establish that baseline experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 4, Table 6, and Figure 4 add a focused analysis checking the metric accuracy of the geometric references against surveyed checkpoints. This addresses reference quality without introducing a broader ablation, sensitivity, or robustness study.

E5.justification: Both versions mention fixed random seeds in Section 6.2 without reporting repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new checkpoint averages are geometric-error point estimates, not an uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: All 180 image-metric entries in v1 Tables 4–5 match v2 Tables 3–4. v2 adds 90 entries in Tables 7–8, new qualitative results, and average vertical/planimetric errors of 10.31/11.83 cm. Grove2's reported area changes from 32,120 to 21,505 square meters. New Table 8 reports Industrial2 PSNR of 24.80 for WildGaussians versus 20.03 for LumiGauss. Ambiguous supplementary scene identities prevent treating these additions as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The RTK-constrained reconstruction pipeline, frame sampling, filtering, sunlight calculation, and paired lighting-transfer procedure remain substantively unchanged. Newly described ground-control anchoring and checkpoint validation do not establish a revised reconstruction algorithm or baseline model.

P1.justification: Sections 2, 4, and 5 undergo substantial condensation and rewriting, the introduction expands and recasts its contribution bullets, and a supplementary overview and reproducibility section are added. Much of the exposition changes despite retaining the main section sequence. Authorship, affiliations, and baseline terminology also receive edits.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displays with a checkpoint-validation diagram, additional point clouds, two multi-time galleries, another baseline-comparison figure, and three new tables. Existing tables are relocated, and main qualitative panels are revised, including the Road examples and the Town time label changing from 12:33 to 12:13.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds LightCity and positions it as a synthetic urban multi-illumination dataset lacking real-world variability. The broader positioning remains intact. Other bibliography changes mainly update metadata for already cited works.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 retain the same RTK-regularized bundle-adjustment objective, grouped reprojection term, sunlight-vector construction, and coordinate transformation. No substantive mathematical definition, assumption, derivation, theorem, or proof is added or revised.

improvement.justification: Table 6 supplies previously missing quantitative validation of geometric-reference accuracy, while the supplement and project address improve reproducibility documentation and access to reported evidence. These are useful gains beyond the unchanged main benchmark scores. However, inconsistent supplementary scene names obstruct verification of the claimed full-scene coverage, and the retained blanket claim of explicit-method superiority is not qualified by the additional counterexamples. The net improvement is therefore limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UAVLight and contain readable text, equations, tables, and figures supporting comparison. It adds direct-trajectory zero-shot Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct and Gemini-3-Pro, plus supervised fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-4B-Instruct, introducing both zero-shot and trained alternatives to the dedicated trajectory encoder.

E3.justification: Existing splits, MCQ construction, and CamFormer settings remain unchanged. New protocols include evaluating rendered trajectory videos or textual 9D sequences, fine-tuning baselines on DynPose-100K, and analyzing the most similar 1% of trajectory pairs from 5,000 Ego-Exo4D validation samples.

E4.justification: Supplementary Section 3.1 adds a targeted semantic-disentanglement analysis testing whether geometrically similar trajectories remain similar after encoding and whether this separation corresponds to activity labels. E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added similarity and label-agreement percentages are point estimates, without a new uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Table 4 adds accuracies of 21.5% for Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, 24.7% for Gemini-3-Pro, 23.1% for SFT Qwen3-VL-4B, and 25.7% for SFT Qwen3-4B-Instruct; CamFormer remains at 36.2% and 46.3%. Supplementary Section 3.1 adds 1.61% similarity-pair retention and 65.8% versus 7.6% activity-label agreement. Existing results are unchanged.

P2.justification: Table 4 gains four rows, main-text caption titles receive stronger typographic emphasis, and supplementary figures and tables are rearranged around expanded text. Existing plots and illustrations are retained; no new numbered figure or table is introduced.

improvement.justification: The direct-trajectory baselines in Table 4 and quantitative geometry-versus-semantics analysis provide useful support beyond v1's narrower comparisons and qualitative embedding illustration. improvement.justification: v2 adds attribution for GPU support and makes associated presentation updates. The methods, empirical evidence, technical documentation, claims, and limitations—including the appendices—are unchanged, establishing no meaningful overall quality gain or loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain the same BulletTime research work, with readable text, equations, tables, figures, and supplementary Appendices A–D. All content can be matched reliably across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and results, including the quantitative comparisons, ablations, and appendix analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic and real-world video-generation experiments, conditioning ablations, and baseline fine-tuning results in Tables 1–5 and D.1, alongside qualitative results.

C1.justification: Both versions retain the same main contributions: dual-field feed-forward/VLM planning, a unified object/scene benchmark, and strong reconstruction accuracy and efficiency under sparse-view budgets. The revised conclusion reiterates the existing view-efficiency claim.

C2.justification: V2 removes the blanket all-settings superiority statement and the unqualified component-removal performance-drop explanation. The retained Table 3 still shows single-object PSNR of 32.15 for Uniform versus 31.59 for AREA3D. New discussion interprets runtime scaling and attributes increased cost at finer voxel resolutions to spatial discretization.

D1.justification: V2 removes the promised-code sentence and repository address from v1's abstract. It adds voxel-size settings and total execution times for the scalability study. Supplementary prompts, coefficients and decay parameters remain unchanged; actual code availability cannot be established from these PDFs.

E1.justification: Both versions use four Replica rooms and four OmniObject3D tabletop configurations: single-object, five-object and two seven-object arrangements. The runtime sweeps vary computational settings without adding datasets, domains or tasks.

E2.justification: Corresponding tables and figures retain their comparator sets, including FisherRF for scene-level reconstruction and AIR-Embodied for object-level reconstruction. Newly cited related works are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: New Table 5 introduces runtime evaluation across view budgets T=5-40 at voxel size 0.5, and voxel sizes 0.5-0.2 at fixed F=25. Existing reconstruction budgets, PGSR representation and PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.5 adds a computational scalability analysis testing runtime sensitivity to view budget and voxel resolution. The component ablation, global-initial-weight ablation and qualitative comparisons are retained, including v1 Table 7 becoming v2 Table 8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added runtime measurements also use point values without statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Existing reconstruction scores, plotted trends and supplementary ablation values are unchanged. Table 5 adds runtimes increasing from 134.9 to 139.2 seconds across T=5-40 at voxel size 0.5, and from 138 to 207 seconds as voxel size decreases from 0.5 to 0.2 at F=25.

M1.justification: The reported VGGT/VLM dual-field method, visibility masks, greedy selection and uncertainty decay remain unchanged. Sentences explaining utility bounds and non-maximum suppression are shortened, but these operations remain in Algorithm 1.

P1.justification: The abstract and several related-work, method, baseline and results passages receive limited rewriting or shortening. Acknowledgements gain funding information and become Section 6, shifting supplementary section numbers. The overall narrative and organization remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the two-part runtime Table 5, adjusts table formatting and page flow, and corrects Figure 5's caption from a PSNR-versus-frames description to novel-view synthesis results. Existing plots and qualitative comparisons are retained; supplementary tables are renumbered.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to GLEAM, NextBestPath and Move to Understand a 3D Scene within existing related-work discussions. The overall positioning relative to geometric, neural-field and VLM planning approaches remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The budgeted selection formulation, back-projection, confidence objective, semantic modulation, frustum decay and additive uncertainty equations are mathematically unchanged. No new assumptions, derivations or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 supplies previously absent computational scaling measurements, softens overly broad performance interpretations and corrects Figure 5's misleading caption. These improve support and clarity, although the timings lack hardware and repeated-run details, and the promised-code link is lost. With the method and reconstruction evidence unchanged, the net improvement is limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AREA3D and contain readable main text and five-page supplementary material. Methods, equations, tables and visualizations can be matched reliably despite renumbering and layout changes.

after.justification: V2 retains those original reconstruction experiments and ablations, and adds measured wall-clock runtimes in Table 5.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction experiments on Replica and OmniObject3D, including baseline comparisons, component ablations and supplementary global-initial-weight experiments.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: compositional 4D reconstruction through separately learned spatial and temporal attention, without compositional 4D training data, and strong performance on the constituent reconstruction tasks.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability and limitation discussions. It describes degradation with increasing object count, qualifies the camera restriction for dynamic-only scenes, interprets low mesh overlap as evidence of implicit physical plausibility, and attributes weaker synthetic-scene scores to accumulated object-placement errors. These extend v1’s discussion of occlusion, physical causality, and fixed cameras.

D1.justification: The abstract changes code availability from a promised release to reported availability at the same repository. Supplementary Section I adds synthetic-data construction, normalization, asset-transformation, GLB-export, metadata, and rendering details; Section D mentions additional fine-tuning for 16 parts. Existing training hyperparameters and hardware disclosures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained benchmarks and generated-video examples, v2 evaluates a newly constructed synthetic compositional 4D dataset with reference static and dynamic geometry (Supplementary Sections I–J). Section F also adds a moving-camera scenario involving dynamic objects, extending the previously fixed-camera evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Supplementary Section H adds an evaluated optimization-based comparator, Shape of Motion (SOM), for compositional reconstruction. The original MIDI, PartCrafter, TripoSG, V2M4, GVFD, L4GM, and internal-ablation comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Existing training and evaluation settings are retained. New protocols include separate static-scene and dynamic-object scoring on synthetic compositions, averaging dynamic scores within samples before averaging across samples, and measuring mesh-intersection IoU across eight videos. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: The original embedding, diffusion-forcing, and attention-mixing ablations remain unchanged. v2 adds targeted checks of physical interpenetration and qualitative moving-camera and interaction cases in Supplementary Sections F–G; these provide limited additional robustness evidence.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing mean-score and user-preference reporting is retained; the new metric aggregation rules concern evaluation design rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the existing Panoptic and user-study values are unchanged. v2 adds synthetic static CD/F-score of 0.293/0.418 and dynamic scores of 0.284/0.434 (Table 4), interaction IoU of 0.0096, and SOM CD of 11.30 cm alongside COM4D’s retained 7.42 cm. New object-count statistics and qualitative examples also expand the reported findings.

M1.justification: Attention Parsing, Attention Mixing, the 21-block DiT, diffusion forcing, losses, and inference procedure remain unchanged. The new statement about supporting 16 parts with additional fine-tuning does not document an architectural or algorithmic revision.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains nearly verbatim, with small wording edits and an added pointer to synthetic evaluation. The supplement inserts new topical sections around retained material, but does not extensively rewrite or reorganize the existing argument.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 13–18 and Table 4 for moving-camera, interaction, SOM, and synthetic-scene evidence. Earlier Figures 13–16 are retained as Figures 19–22 and reflowed across the appendix. These additions and relocations substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The bibliography retains the same 99 works and the main related-work discussion is unchanged. New Supplementary Section H specifically contrasts COM4D’s learned generative priors with the already-cited SOM’s incomplete or noisy reconstructions under occlusion.

T1.justification: The formal problem formulation, attention equations, and training losses, including supplementary Equations 4–5, are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, derivation, or substantive mathematical definition is introduced.

improvement.justification: The synthetic component-level evaluation and SOM comparison strengthen evidence for the central compositional task beyond v1’s attention-mixing comparisons, while the placement-error and applicability discussions clarify limitations. The gains remain limited by the unspecified synthetic test-set size, sparse SOM evaluation details, and narrow physical-plausibility and moving-camera checks.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds synthetic-scene evaluation, mesh-interpenetration measurements, a Shape of Motion comparison, and qualitative tests.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction benchmarks, component ablations, a user-preference study, and CMU Panoptic evaluations.

E5.justification: Neither version supplies explicit seed counts, repeated-run estimates, confidence intervals or significance tests. The retained reward curves use the same presentation, and Table 4 introduces no additional uncertainty-reporting practice.

P1.justification: v2 makes limited grammar, punctuation and citation-formatting edits, adds a technique-contributor footnote and acknowledgments, and inserts the short other-baselines paragraph. The section sequence and overall narrative remain substantially the same.

However, the new integrations lack implementation and training details, while changed references create dataset and baseline provenance mismatches. The limited documentation makes the value of the added evidence difficult to weigh against the loss of traceability, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ParaUni study, with readable text, equations, algorithms, figures and tables supporting reliable comparison. Both end with references; neither includes an appendix or the supplementary material repeatedly cited in Sections 3–4. These assessments cover all supplied pages.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds results for applying ParaUni to Janus-Pro and BLIP-3o in Table 4.

before.justification: v1 reports original ParaUni benchmark results, component ablations, layer analyses and reward-training curves, including Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–5 and 9.

C2.justification: Section 4.5 reframes expert inversion from an ability to transfer physical attributes to evidence of distinct learned priors, with explicit attribute control presented as future potential. The main limitations paragraph survives, but appendix explanations of weaker dynamics annotations and dependence on VLM supervision disappear.

The code-release promise also disappears. v2 retains references to supplementary details without including them.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 retain the same comparator membership, including WISA, VideoREPA, the backbone models, and the additional generators in Table 1. Newly cited PhysHPO and PISA are not evaluated. The omitted Figure 13 supplies further examples of existing comparisons.

E3.justification: The retained benchmark protocol still uses 600 prompts, the 180-prompt HARD subset, and the same metrics. Supplementary procedures disappear: PCA using 100 unseen prompts per phenomenon and a human annotation audit using 100 videos per phenomenon with four accuracy categories. No changed settings or reruns are established for retained experiments.

E4.justification: v2 omits Appendix B’s full-category semantic PCA, human validation of VLM annotations, comparison of short and elaborate annotation prompts, and qualitative SEB/REB ablations. These remove substantive checks of expert behavior and supervision quality, although the main ablation tables and expert visualizations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, run-to-run variability, or significance tests. The omitted annotation-accuracy percentages are point results rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 are numerically unchanged. v2 correctly attributes the 19.7% Joint improvement to CogVideoX, whose score rises from 22.3 to 26.7. However, substantial supplementary results disappear, including annotation accuracy of 76.9% overall, category accuracies of 63.1%, 87.7%, and 80.0%, inference overheads of 20.3% and 11.5%, and additional PCA and qualitative findings.

M1.justification: The SEB/PB/REB architecture, routing procedures, physical alignment strategy, and training objectives remain unchanged. Loss of appendix implementation details does not establish a change to the underlying method.

P1.justification: Retained sections preserve their order and mostly their wording. Local edits affect the introduction, Figure 1 caption, and expert-inversion discussion; equal-contribution markings and an acknowledgment are added, contact text is removed, and the project link moves. The appendix block is omitted without substantial reorganization of the main narrative.

P2.justification: Figures 9–14 disappear, removing the PCA plot, annotation prompts and accuracy chart, qualitative ablation, and example galleries. Figures 1–2 receive labeling and diagram edits. Figure 4 moves and replaces one displayed video frame while retaining its heatmaps. The four main tables retain their structure.

R1.justification: The introduction adds PhysHPO, PISA, and Lin et al.’s physics-cognition survey, and sharpens the distinction between internalizing priors during training and explicit guidance during inference. The broader related-work organization and positioning against global physical guidance remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations and objectives in Equations 1–6 remain unchanged. Neither version presents theorems or proofs; omitted attention-extraction details concern implementation rather than revised mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects the 19.7% gain attribution, updates related work, and tempers the attribute-control interpretation. These useful refinements are outweighed by omission of the detailed implementation recipe and distinctive validation of annotation quality and expert behavior. The supplied later PDF substantially weakens reproducibility and supporting evidence while still directing readers to absent supplementary material.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of ProPhy, with matching architecture, equations, and main experiments. v1 includes Appendices A–D and Figures 9–14; the supplied v2 ends at the references and omits that material. This omission is directly observable, not an extraction gap.

after.justification: Tables 1–4 retain original benchmark results and ablations, with qualitative experiments and expert analyses in Figures 5–8.

before.justification: Tables 1–4 report original VideoPhy2 and VBench experiments and ablations. Appendix B additionally reports router analyses and a human assessment of annotation accuracy.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions and conclusion broaden the work from efficient 3D layout estimation to 3D scene understanding encompassing layout and object detection on synthetic and real-world data. The introduction adds a 5.14-fold detection-speedup claim alongside the retained 5.09-fold layout claim. The central MTP, filtering and parameter-efficiency contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving MTP regularization, inter-head agreement as a confidence-learning signal, and layout-token redundancy versus detection-token structure. It also discusses limited SceneCAD training data and explicitly identifies incomplete point clouds and non-Manhattan layouts as failure conditions. These substantially extend v1's discussion of softmax reliability and decoding tradeoffs.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the default CGD threshold of 0.90, teacher-forcing confidence-label construction, residual projection-block diagrams, detection annotation generation, task-specific training schedules and ASE split-file names. Existing optimizer, learning-rate, batch-size and layout-training details move to Appendix B largely unchanged. The split-file references do not themselves supply their contents.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates layout estimation on synthetic ASE and Structured3D. v2 adds real-world SceneCAD and evaluates 3D object detection on both ASE and SceneCAD. ASE detection covers cabinet, chair, table, sofa and bed, substantially broadening both task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: The existing SceneScript, SceneScript+MTP, RoomFormer, ProductThre and SoftmaxThre comparisons are retained. Table S4 adds the ground-truth-supervised confidence variant CGD, GT as a comparator. Extending existing baselines to detection and SceneCAD does not itself change their membership; TR3D supplies annotations rather than serving as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Existing layout protocols are retained. New detection experiments introduce an ASE 19k/1k train/test split, generated bounding-box annotations, and F1 evaluation at 0.25 and 0.50 IoU. Appendix B specifies detection training budgets and SceneCAD fine-tuning. Additional experiments vary head counts and thresholds and compare 60- versus 90-epoch SceneScript training.

E4.justification: The original ablations remain as Table 4. Tables S1-S5 add 12/16-head tests, scoring-threshold sweeps, confidence-supervision tolerance tests, ground-truth versus first-head supervision, and a longer-training baseline control. New analyses examine classwise and detection token-score distributions and show failures on incomplete point clouds and non-Manhattan scenes. The Structured3D visualization is relocated, not newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new confidence-score distributions and discussion of model uncertainty concern token predictions, not uncertainty estimation for experimental performance.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1-2 and v1 Table 3, now Table 4, retain their numbers. New results include SceneCAD layout SSD at 0.556 F1 and 42 ms versus SceneScript at 0.556 and 108 ms, and ASE detection SSD at 0.829 F1@0.50 and 104 ms versus 0.823 and 535 ms. Supplementary tables add sensitivity and control outcomes. Table S2 inconsistently reports 16.10 M parameters for ProductThre/SoftmaxThre versus 15.05 M in retained Table 4.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the reported projection sub-block architecture from two ReLU activations to one, consistent with v2 Figure S7. This is a limited architecture-description revision; the PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed or the description was corrected. MTP, SSD, CGD, their losses and head sharing otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The title and selected introductory and concluding passages are revised around scene understanding. Experiments are separated into layout and detection sections, while layout-related work and training details move to the supplement. Most existing method and results prose remains closely matched, so the editorial reworking is limited despite substantial new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with new benchmark and ablation tables, distribution plots, failure examples, and training and architecture diagrams. v1 Figure 6 moves to Figure S1, and Figures 7-8 become Figures 6-7. Existing displays also undergo placement, caption and styling adjustments; these relocations are distinct from the new visual content.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for MMDetection3D, TR3D and AdamW to support annotation generation and training details. The existing literature and first-use-of-MTP positioning are retained. The layout-estimation related-work subsection moves from Section 2.2 to Appendix C without a substantive change in its research positioning.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(5), the numerical-token consistency criterion and the training objectives remain unchanged. Appendix B.1 and Figure S6 explain the existing confidence-label construction with explicit head indices. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for applicability beyond synthetic layout estimation through real-world SceneCAD and object-detection experiments. Sensitivity tests, confidence-supervision comparisons, a longer-training control, failure cases and implementation details make the method better supported and more assessable. Limitations remain: ASE detection uses generated annotations, Table S2 conflicts with Table 4 on parameter counts, and Section 4.4 combines a CGD speedup with an SSD accuracy gain for SceneCAD. These reporting problems qualify some claims but do not outweigh the substantial validation and transparency gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Fast SceneScript by the same authors, with matching core methods and experiments. All supplied text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes supplementary Sections A-D.

before.justification: Tables 1-3 report original layout-estimation experiments on ASE and Structured3D, including models trained by this work and component ablations.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly clarifies independence from the actual capture and inference ISPs, interprets the new results as supporting image-specific editing and limited lambda sensitivity, and identifies failures under extreme low light or unfamiliar illumination such as green LEDs. These concrete failure conditions replace v1's closing future-work discussion.

D1.justification: v2 quantifies training overhead at approximately 15% and newly specifies an ASN-neighborhood threshold of L1 <= 0.05. v1 mentions both overhead and neighborhood restriction without these values. The new L1 specification conflicts with the Euclidean wording retained in Section 3.2, leaving the precise norm ambiguous.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates the Samsung S24 Ultra dataset. v2 additionally evaluates NUS data from Samsung NX2000, Olympus E-PL6, and Sony SLT-A57 cameras in Section S4. Section 4.4 also adds manual, image-specific edits, substantially broadening camera coverage and editing scenarios.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain CAM, RAW Diffusion, UNet, and the CIE XYZ Net cyclic-loss comparison. The latter moves from Table S4 to S6. New experiments reuse existing comparison methods without introducing a new competing reconstruction method.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 introduces a blind forced-choice study with 25 users judging 20 images for three methods, yielding 1,500 responses. Additional protocols cover manual edits on 50 challenging images, NUS evaluation following the CAM protocol with two specified edits, and a lambda sweep over 1, 2, 4, and 8. Existing smartphone splits and evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table S5 adds loss-weight sensitivity analysis for CAM and RAW Diffusion, while Section 4.4 tests robustness to image-specific edits. These extend the retained component, sampling-range, cyclic-loss, dehazing, and local-tone-mapping analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new participant counts describe evaluation design; preference percentages and hyperparameter sweeps do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All retained quantitative table entries are unchanged, including v1 Table S4 matched to v2 Table S6. New outcomes include 83% overall user preference, manual-edit results such as CAM's 22.11 dB baseline versus 24.36 dB with edit-aware loss, and NUS and lambda-sweep scores. NUS results also show reduced RAW PSNR and a Sony Edit B PSNR tie at 33.26 dB. These are additional experiments, not improvements to previously reported scores.

M1.justification: The four-module sampled ISP, reconstruction objectives, and target-edit fine-tuning procedures remain unchanged in Equations (1)-(11) and (S1)-(S3). The additional sampling-threshold disclosure does not establish an actual algorithm revision.

P1.justification: Local rewrites clarify ISP access and shorten related work. v2 adds Sections 4.3, 4.4, and supplementary Section S4, renumbers additional ablations to S5, and revises the conclusion. The abstract, overall narrative, and method exposition remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5, S4, and S5 and renumbers the existing cyclic-loss table to S6. Figures 3 and 4 each shrink from six examples to four; the two displaced RAW Diffusion examples move into Figure S2, replacing two previous examples. Figure 5 moves from page 8 to page 7. The overall visual format and core diagrams remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Cheng, Prasad, and Brown's 2014 work as the NUS dataset reference. Existing research positioning against RAW-fidelity objectives and unedited cyclic consistency remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulations and assumptions, including normalized, demosaiced, denoised three-channel RAW inputs, are retained. Neither version adds or revises a theorem, proof, or substantive derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the paper's practical editing claims: NUS experiments extend the single-camera evidence, the blind user study directly tests perceptual matching, and manual image-specific edits address the restriction to fixed edit recipes. Failure conditions and quantified training overhead also improve transparency. These gains address important evidentiary gaps in v1, despite limited uncertainty reporting and the inconsistent white-balance norm specification.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds a user study, image-specific editing experiments, NUS camera evaluations, and loss-weight sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments, target-edit fine-tuning, and ablations, including Tables 2-4 and S1-S4.

Section 4.5 replaces the purely prospective closed-loop discussion with an available optional recovery mechanism while retaining the open-loop execution limitation. Existing reconstruction and sim-to-real limitations remain.

D1.justification: Figure 9 newly provides an example rollout context with waypoint, gripper, object-state, duration, and screenshot fields. Table 1 specifies a ±2 cm alignment tolerance previously left unquantified.
